articles.title: Maple Syrup Urine Disease
articles.markdown: # Maple Syrup Urine Disease # Introduction Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) is an inborn error of metabolism characterized by impaired catabolism of the branched-chain amino acids, including leucine, isoleucine, and valine ((Figure 1)).  The disease is named for the sweet, maple syrup–like odor of the patient's urine. # Pathogenesis MSUD, also known as branched-chain ketoaciduria, is an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism that occurs due to branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex deficiency.  This thiamine-dependent enzyme complex is located in the mitochondria of various tissues (eg, muscle, liver, kidney, brain).  It catabolizes the branched-chain amino acids into substrates that can be used in the tricarboxylic acid cycle ((Figure 2)). Branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex deficiency causes branched-chain amino acids and their metabolites to accumulate, resulting in ketoacidosis.  Serum levels can rise very rapidly during periods of generalized catabolism (eg, illness, fasting).  Excess leucine can cause abnormal myelination, cerebral edema, and decreased neurotransmitter production.  In addition, sotolone, an isoleucine metabolite, gives urine its characteristic odor. # Clinical presentation In classic MSUD, untreated newborns develop the following symptoms: - <48 hours of life:  Irritability, poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, and dystonia. - Approximately 4 days of life:  Apnea, seizures, and cerebral edema. - 7-10 days of life:  Coma and central respiratory failure. Throughout this time, the urine and cerumen take on a sweet, maple syrup–like odor.  Formula-fed newborns may have a quicker onset of more severe symptoms because there are typically higher concentrations of branched-chain amino acids in formula compared to breast milk. The timing and severity of symptoms depend on the underlying genetic mutation, which determines the amount of remaining branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex activity, if any.  Patients with more enzyme activity typically develop milder symptoms, which include poor growth and developmental delays, later in childhood. Patients with MSUD are prone to acute metabolic exacerbation episodes due to increased protein catabolism, resulting in an acute rise in serum branched-chain amino acids levels.  These episodes are typically caused by physical stress (eg, infection, injury, surgery, fasting) or dietary noncompliance.  Symptoms generally include epigastric pain, vomiting, anorexia, and muscle fatigue during these metabolic exacerbations. # Evaluation and diagnosis All newborns are routinely screened for MSUD within 24-48 hours of birth by using tandem mass spectrometry to measure levels of leucine and isoleucine.  However, because the mass-to-charge ratio of these branched-chain amino acids is similar to hydroxyproline, this test cannot reliably differentiate MSUD from benign isolated hydroxyprolinemia.  Therefore, the diagnosis is confirmed by quantitative plasma amino acid analysis using liquid chromatography to measure levels of leucine, isoleucine, and valine, which can be 2-4 times the normal level.  In addition, alloisoleucine, a stereoisomer of L-isoleucine that is detectable after day 6 of life, is measured.  However, a presumptive diagnosis of MSUD is often made before confirmatory test results are obtained based on clinical features (eg, vomiting, lethargy, urine/cerumen odor) and ketonuria, which is detectable 48-72 hours after birth. Genetic testing is available to identify the underlying genetic mutation and carrier risk for family members. # Differential diagnosis - **Phenylketonuria** ((Figure 3)):  Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency causes hyperphenylalaninemia.  Patients typically develop seizures after phenylalanine is introduced in breast milk or standard formula.  Additional features include skin hypopigmentation, microcephaly, and a musty body/urine odor. - **Urea cycle disorders**:  These occur due to a deficiency in any enzyme used to convert nitrogen to urea (eg, ornithine transcarbamylase ((Figure 4))), resulting in hyperammonemia.  Newborns typically develop poor feeding, vomiting, and lethargy within the first few days of life.  Central hyperventilation causing respiratory alkalosis is also characteristic. - **Galactosemia** ((Figure 5)):  Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency causes galactosemia.  Patients develop vomiting, lethargy, and poor feeding shortly after being introduced to galactose-containing breast milk or formula.  Additional signs and symptoms include jaundice, hepatomegaly, and cataracts. # Management Management consists of lifelong dietary restrictions of branched-chain amino acids (ie, use of specialized formulas and medical foods) and supplementation of valine and isoleucine in small quantities that allow for growth and development while preventing acute metabolic decompensation.  Thiamine pyrophosphate, an intracellular derivative of thiamine, increases the stability of the branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex.  In some cases of MSUD, thiamine supplementation can prolong residual branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex enzyme activity and improve symptoms. Acute metabolic exacerbations are managed with rapid inhibition of protein catabolism through the following strategies: - Protein restriction for 24-72 hours. - Intravenous glucose with or without insulin (to suppress catabolism). - Symptomatic management (eg, antiemetics, intravenous fluids). - Correction of metabolic acidosis and electrolyte disturbances. In severe cases, dialysis may be required to remove branched-chain amino acids and their metabolites. The liver expresses at least 10% of all branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex activity.  Therefore, liver transplantation may be considered for refractory MSUD that cannot be managed through dietary restriction. # Prognosis Classic MSUD progresses quickly and is often fatal without treatment (within 2 months).  For the best prognosis, therapy should begin before symptoms appear or shortly after they develop.  Outcomes depend on maintaining an appropriate plasma branched-chain amino acid concentration, and patients remain at lifelong risk for neurotoxicity in the setting of acute metabolic decompensation due to transient increases in plasma leucine levels. # Complications If untreated, classic MSUD can quickly cause cerebral edema (due to increased branched-chain amino acids in the brain) and irreversible damage within 7-10 days of life.  This may result in lifelong neurologic sequelae such as seizures, developmental delay, or cerebral palsy.  Elevated plasma leucine in patients with MSUD can also cause T-cell suppression and increased susceptibility to fungal infections (eg, recurrent esophageal candidiasis).  Acute metabolic exacerbations can cause acute pancreatitis due to inflammation from circulating branched-chain amino acids. # Summary Maple syrup urine disease is a life-threatening metabolic disorder that results in elevated serum leucine, isoleucine, and valine levels.  Affected newborns classically present within the first few days of life with irritability, poor feeding, and sweet-smelling urine.  Diagnosis is made by quantitative plasma amino acid analysis, and management is lifelong dietary restriction of branched-chain amino acids.  Early detection and dietary restriction can prevent irreversible neurologic damage. ​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌

articles.title: Lysosomal Storage Diseases
articles.markdown:
# Lysosomal Storage Diseases # Introduction Lysosomal storage diseases are inherited metabolic disorders that occur due to lysosomal enzyme deficiencies.  These deficiencies impair lysosomal metabolism, resulting in the accumulation of various metabolic substrates within the lysosome.  Over time, these substrates cause clinically significant cellular and tissue dysfunction. # Pathophysiology Lysosomes are cytoplasmic organelles that contain enzymes (ie, acid hydrolases) required for the degradation of various macromolecules (eg, mucopolysaccharides, sphingolipids).  In lysosomal storage diseases, enzyme deficiencies result in impaired metabolism of these macromolecules, allowing them to accumulate within the lysosome.  Over time, accumulation of these substrates results in cellular dysfunction.  Patients are typically asymptomatic at birth but develop symptoms as the substrate accumulates.  The clinical presentations of each lysosomal storage disease vary, but common features include dysmorphic features, hepatosplenomegaly, progressive neurodegeneration, neuropathy, abnormal tone, and ataxia. Lysosomal storage diseases are categorized by the type of substrate that accumulates.  This article will discuss the major categories of lysosomal storage diseases, including mucopolysaccharidoses, sphingolipidoses, and inclusion cell (I-cell) disease. # Mucopolysaccharidoses Mucopolysaccharidoses are characterized by a deficiency in the enzymes required for the metabolism of mucopolysaccharides, which are long, unbranched polysaccharides attached to a protein core.  They are primarily found in mucus, joint fluid, and the extracellular matrix of certain types of connective tissues (eg, vitreous humor of the eye).  The most common mucopolysaccharidoses include Hurler and Hunter syndromes ((Table 1)). ## Hurler syndrome Hurler syndrome (type I mucopolysaccharidosis) occurs due to impaired metabolism of dermatan and heparan sulfate. - Inheritance pattern:  Autosomal recessive. - Deficiency:  **α-L-iduronidase**. - Accumulated substrate:  **Dermatan and heparan sulfate**. Hurler syndrome is characterized by severe developmental delay and intellectual disability, **corneal clouding**, and **coarse facial features** (eg, frontal bossing, broad nose, flat midface).  Hepatosplenomegaly and **coronary artery disease** (due to deposition of dermatan and heparan sulfate within the vessels) are common.  Death typically occurs in early childhood (age <10) due to cardiac complications (eg, myocardial infarction). ## Hunter syndrome Hunter syndrome (type II mucopolysaccharidosis) occurs due to impaired metabolism of dermatan and heparan sulfate. - Inheritance pattern:  X-linked recessive. - Deficiency:  **Iduronate sulfatase**. - Accumulated substrate:  **Dermatan and heparan sulfate**. Hunter syndrome, the only X-linked mucopolysaccharidosis, is characterized by a milder phenotype than Hurler syndrome.  Clinical features include aggressive behavior but not corneal clouding.  Death typically occurs in adolescence or early adulthood. # Sphingolipidoses Sphingolipidoses are characterized by deficiencies in the enzymes required for the metabolism of sphingolipids (eg, glycosphingolipids, phosphosphingolipids) ((Figure 1)), complex lipids that are essential components of cell membranes.  The most common sphingolipidoses are discussed below ((Table 2)). ## Fabry disease Fabry disease occurs due to impaired metabolism of globotriaosylceramide ((Table 3)). - Inheritance pattern:  X-linked recessive. - Deficiency:  **α-galactosidase A**. - Accumulated substrate:  **Globotriaosylceramide**. Fabry disease, the only sphingolipidosis that is X-linked, typically presents in childhood and early adolescence with **neuropathic pain** due to globotriaosylceramide deposition in nerve tissue.  Angiokeratomas and telangiectasias often develop in late adolescence.  Multiorgan involvement occurs in adulthood, and patients are at increased risk for **cardiac disease** (eg, left ventricular hypertrophy) and **cerebrovascular disease** (eg, transient ischemic attack, stroke).  In addition, globotriaosylceramide accumulation in the glomerulus and distal renal tubule can cause proteinuria and polyuria, respectively, and can progress to renal failure. ## Tay-Sachs disease Tay-Sachs disease occurs due to impaired metabolism of GM2 ganglioside. - Inheritance pattern:  Autosomal recessive. - Deficiency:  **ꞵ-hexosaminidase A**. - Accumulated substrate:  **GM2 ganglioside**. Patients with Tay-Sachs disease develop normally for the first few months of life because the gradual accumulation of GM2 ganglioside in neuronal lysosomes does not initially cause cellular dysfunction.  However, by age 6 months excess GM2 ganglioside leads to **loss of previously achieved developmental milestones** (eg, no longer able to roll over or sit independently).  Other clinical findings include macrocephaly, **seizures**, spasticity, and an exaggerated startle reflex. Ganglioside accumulation occurs in the retina but spares the fovea, which lacks ganglion cells.  As a result, the retina appears opaque, whereas the unaffected fovea remains bright red due to the underlying choroid, leading to the classic fundoscopic finding of a **cherry-red spot at the macula** ((Figure 2)).  Patients have poor vision, and **progressive neurodegeneration** typically leads to death at age 2-5. ## Gaucher disease Gaucher disease occurs due to impaired metabolism of glucocerebroside ((Table 4)). - Inheritance pattern:  Autosomal recessive. - Deficiency:  **ꞵ-glucocerebrosidase**. - Accumulated substrate:  **Glucocerebroside**. The clinical presentation of Gaucher disease is related to the accumulation of glucocerebroside within the lysosomes of macrophages as they engulf cellular debris.  These lipid-laden macrophages, known as **Gaucher cells** ((Figure 3)), have a characteristic wrinkled tissue paper appearance and secrete lysosomal proteases and cytokines that disrupt cellular function.  Patients can present at any age with various clinical manifestations, including: - Severe hepatosplenomegaly. - Pancytopenia (eg, pallor, fatigue, easy bleeding). - Bone pain:  Following bone marrow infiltration, Gaucher cells release lysosomal enzymes and inflammatory mediators that cause bone pain (which is worse at night) and osteopenia that can lead to joint collapse and pathologic fractures. - Delayed puberty and poor growth. - CNS involvement:  Can lead to spasticity, muscle spasms, and loss of motor skills. ## Niemann-Pick disease Niemann-Pick disease occurs due to impaired metabolism of sphingomyelin. - Inheritance pattern:  Autosomal recessive. - Deficiency:  **Sphingomyelinase**. - Accumulated substrate:  **Sphingomyelin**. Sphingomyelin accumulates in lysosomes, which can be visualized as enlarged, vacuolated cells, often referred to as **lipid-laden foam cells** ((Figure 4)).  Foam cells accumulate in the liver, spleen, and CNS, leading to hepatosplenomegaly and progressive neurologic symptoms (eg, hypotonia, absent reflexes, neurodegeneration). After a period of normal development in early infancy, patients lose previously achieved developmental milestones (eg, no longer able to roll over or sit independently).  In addition, sphingomyelin accumulation in the retinal ganglion cells leads to retinal opacification, which gives the appearance of a **cherry-red macula**.  Niemann-Pick disease is progressive, and death usually occurs by age 3. ## Krabbe disease Krabbe disease occurs due to impaired metabolism of galactolipids formed during white matter myelination. - Inheritance pattern:  Autosomal recessive. - Deficiency:  **Galactocerebrosidase**. - Accumulated substrate:  **Galactocerebroside** and **psychosine** (galactosylsphingosine). Krabbe disease is characterized by progressive neurodegeneration, peripheral neuropathy, and **optic nerve atrophy** due to loss of myelin.  Optic nerve atrophy can be visualized as optic nerve pallor on fundoscopic examination.  The disease typically presents in infancy, and death often occurs by age 2. ## Metachromatic leukodystrophy Metachromatic leukodystrophy occurs due to impaired metabolism of cerebroside sulfate. - Inheritance pattern:  Autosomal recessive. - Deficiency:  **Arylsulfatase A**. - Accumulated substrate:  **Cerebroside sulfate**. The clinical presentation of metachromatic leukodystrophy is central and peripheral nervous system demyelination, leading to neurologic regression, seizures, and ataxia. # Inclusion cell (I-cell) disease Unlike mucopolysaccharidoses and sphingolipidoses, each of which occurs due to a specific acid hydrolase enzyme deficiency, I-cell disease involves **deficiencies of multiple lysosomal enzymes**.  In I-cell disease, acid hydrolase enzymes are transported to the extracellular space, rather than the lysosomes.  Normally, acid hydrolase enzymes undergo posttranslational modification in the Golgi apparatus, including phosphorylation of mannose residues by a phosphotransferase enzyme.  This mannose-6-phosphate tag marks the enzyme for transport to the lysosome.  In I-cell disease, a defect in the phosphotransferase enzyme results in enzyme transfer to the extracellular space, and various substrates accumulate in the lysosomes, forming the characteristic **inclusion bodies**. I-cell disease demonstrates an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern, and the clinical presentation includes **failure to thrive**, **recurrent respiratory tract infections**, and **cognitive deficits** in the first year of life, along with characteristic physical features (eg, **coarse facies**, corneal clouding, hepatosplenomegaly). # Diagnosis Diagnosis involves a thorough history (including birth history and family history) and physical examination.  Certain conditions are associated with specific histologic features, and further evaluation depends on the suspected disease.  Enzyme assays may be necessary to measure enzyme activity in leukocytes or fibroblasts.  Genetic testing is often performed to identify the underlying mutation. # Management and prognosis In general, the prognosis for lysosomal storage disease is poor, with death occurring in childhood or adolescents for most patients.  Management is generally supportive (eg, physical therapy, vision/hearing support), but enzyme replacement therapy is available for patients with Gaucher disease, Fabry disease, Hurler syndrome, and Hunter syndrome.  These therapies improve symptoms and slow progression, leading to a more favorable prognosis.  Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation may prevent disease progression in some conditions. # Summary Lysosomal storage diseases are inherited metabolic disorders that occur due to lysosomal enzyme deficiencies, resulting in the accumulation of various metabolic substrates within the lysosome.  Clinical presentation varies, but common features include dysmorphic features, hepatosplenomegaly, progressive neurodegeneration, and ataxia.  Prognosis is poor overall, and management involves supportive care.  Enzyme replacement therapies are available for certain diseases. ​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌

articles.title: Lipid Metabolism And Overview Of Dyslipidemias
articles.markdown:
# Lipid Metabolism And Overview Of Dyslipidemias # Introduction Dyslipidemias are disorders characterized by abnormal lipid levels in the blood, including cholesterol, triglycerides (TGs), and lipoproteins.  These abnormalities are often chronic and are frequently associated with complications, including atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD).  Dyslipidemias most commonly arise from interactions between genetic and environmental factors but also can be inherited in a monogenic fashion (familial disorders).  This article discusses lipid classification and metabolism, etiology of dyslipidemias and complications including atherosclerosis, and clinical presentation and screening.  Management of dyslipidemia is presented in a separate article. # Main categories of lipids Lipids discussed in this article include cholesterol and TGs; because they are insoluble, lipids are carried within lipoproteins.  This section provides an overview of cholesterol, TGs, and lipoproteins (with their associated surface apolipoproteins). ## Cholesterol - **Synthesis:**  Cholesterol is endogenously synthesized or consumed through diet.  It is most commonly synthesized in the liver and intestines; the rate-limiting step is the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate by the enzyme HMG-CoA reductase ((Figure 1)). - **Functions:**  Cholesterol is important for cell membrane integrity and is a precursor to steroid hormones, bile salts, and other compounds (eg, myelin). - **Homeostatic regulation:**  Hepatic synthesis of cholesterol is decreased during increases in exogenous (dietary) cholesterol (negative feedback regulation).  Circulating cholesterol is primarily cleared by the liver; blood cholesterol levels are primarily regulated by expression of cholesterol-binding hepatocyte receptors (discussed further below). ## Triglycerides - **Synthesis:**  TGs are endogenously synthesized or consumed through diet.  TGs are formed by esterification of fatty acids (eg, saturated, unsaturated) with glycerol; in contrast, when needed (eg, for energy), TGs undergo lipolysis within tissue and in the circulation to become free fatty acids (FFAs) and glycerol. - **Functions:**  TGs serve as an important form of **energy storage** in the body.  FFAs derived from TGs can be used for ATP production (eg, beta-oxidation within mitochondria).  Glycerol is used by the liver (glycerol kinase) for glucose formation via gluconeogenesis ((Figure 2)).  Conversely, fatty acids can be reesterified in cells (eg, adipose tissue) into TGs; these stored TGs can subsequently be mobilized for energy (eg, during exercise). - **Homeostatic regulation:**  Dietary TGs are lipolyzed by pancreatic lipase.  In addition, lipoprotein lipase (LPL) located within the endothelium promotes lipolysis of TGs for uptake within cells, effectively decreasing circulating FFA levels ((Figure 3)).  In contrast, hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) promotes lipolysis of stored TGs for release into the circulation, increasing circulating FFA levels.  Excess FFAs are taken up by the liver. ## Lipoproteins and apolipoproteins Lipids are insoluble and therefore are carried within the core of lipoproteins ((Figure 4)).  Lipoproteins deliver TGs and cholesterol to tissues then return to the liver (binding to hepatocyte receptors) for processing, storage, and recycling.  Lipoproteins are classified based on density (determined by their relative proportions of cholesterol, TGs, and proteins), which in turn determines their primary functions ((Table 1)). Each class of lipoproteins has specific **apolipoproteins** (eg, Apo B-48), which assist with assembly, enzymatic signaling, transport, and hepatocyte binding ((Figure 5)).  Apo deficiencies (eg, genetic syndromes) are implicated in pathogenesis of dyslipidemias, as discussed in the subsequent sections. The following section details how lipids and lipoproteins are metabolized. # Lipid metabolism Pathways for metabolism of dietary lipids (primarily involving chylomicrons) and endogenously synthesized lipids (primarily involving hepatic synthesis of VLDL and HDL) are each discussed in the following sections. ## Transport of dietary lipids: Chylomicrons TGs and cholesterol consumed through diet are metabolized via the following steps: - **Fat emulsification and micelle formation:**  The presence of dietary TGs and cholesterol in the gut triggers bile secretion into the small intestine, which emulsifies fat droplets (increase surface area) to facilitate further enzymatic processing ((Figure 6)).  TGs are lipolyzed by pancreatic lipase, forming FFAs and monoglycerides, which aggregate into micelles ((Figure 7)). - **Chylomicron formation and circulation:**  Micelles are absorbed by enterocytes, where FFAs are reassembled into TGs and packaged along with cholesterol esters and **Apo B-48** into chylomicrons.  Chylomicrons cannot enter the bloodstream due to their large size; instead, they exit into the lymphatic circulation via lacteals, eventually emptying via the thoracic duct into the left subclavian vein. - **TG uptake into cells, clearance of chylomicron remnants, and cholesterol recycling:**  Assisted by **Apo C-II**, LPL facilitates lipolysis of TGs within chylomicrons for cellular uptake.  TG-depleted chylomicron remnants enter the liver by receptor-mediated endocytosis, a process requiring **Apo E** and Apo B-48 to interact with the remnant receptor.  Cholesterol within chylomicrons is recycled for production of bile acids or other lipoproteins. ## Endogenous lipid transport: VLDL and LDL Endogenous lipid metabolism begins in the liver with VLDL synthesis, formed by TGs and a small amount of cholesterol.  After exiting the liver, VLDL undergoes the following steps: - TGs contained in VLDL undergo lipolysis (LPL action, supported by Apo C-II), in a manner similar to chylomicron processing, for uptake and storage in tissue. - As TG content of VLDL is progressively depleted, it becomes IDL and then cholesterol-rich LDL. - LDL enters cells via r**eceptor-mediated endocytosis**, a process requiring binding of Apo B-100 to the LDL receptor (located on hepatocytes and certain other peripheral tissue, such as adrenocortical cells).  The hepatic LDL receptor is the greatest contributor to cholesterol clearance from the circulation (~70% of LDL clearance); its expression is in part controlled by the serine protease proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (**PCSK9**) and is subject to negative feedback: - **High intracellular cholesterol:**  PCSK9 binding to the LDL receptor increases, causing receptor degradation, decreasing LDL receptor expression and hepatic cholesterol uptake.  The net effect is increased circulating LDL. - **Low intracellular cholesterol:**  PCSK9 binding to the LDL receptor decreases, and LDL receptor expression and hepatic uptake increases.  The net effect is decreased circulating LDL. ## Reverse transport of cholesterol to the liver: HDL HDL, synthesized in the liver and intestines, serves 2 important functions in lipid metabolism: - **Scavenges intracellular cholesterol** (eg, from macrophages, other lipoproteins):  This process requires entry of HDL into the cell (involving binding of Apo A-1 to the cell surface ATP-binding cassette transporter-1) and an esterification of free cholesterol by lecithin cholesterol-acyl transferase (LCAT).  HDL carries this esterified cholesterol to the liver, binding to hepatocyte surface scavenger receptors to enter hepatocytes. - **Supports function of other lipoproteins:**  HDL is a carrier of Apo C-II and E, passing them to other lipoproteins (eg, VLDL, chylomicrons) to enable lipolysis of TGs and hepatic clearance. When TG levels are high, HDL accepts TG from VLDL and LDL in exchange for cholesterol, a process catalyzed by cholesterol ester transferase protein (**CETP**).  The resulting TG-rich HDL is unstable and prone to breakdown of HDL, with a net effect of decreasing HDL concentration and impairing HDL transport of cholesterol to the liver. Several key enzymes involved in endogenous cholesterol synthesis and transport are summarized in this table ((Table 2)). # Common patterns of dyslipidemia Common patterns seen in dyslipidemia and their causes are presented in this table ((Table 3)). # Dyslipidemias and atherosclerosis A primary clinical consequence of dyslipidemia involves its association with ASCVD. ## Role of LDL Chronic exposure to excess LDL is causally linked to ASCVD.  LDL generates ASCVD through the following steps: - LDL (especially small, dense LDL) can penetrate the endothelial barrier and accumulate under the subendothelial space, a crucial step in atherogenesis ((Figure 8)).  It undergoes reactive oxygen species modification, becoming ox-LDL. - Ox-LDL is taken up by macrophages and rapidly accumulates (because uptake of ox-LDL is not subject to normal feedback inhibition), resulting in formation of foam cells (lipid-laden macrophages) and proliferation of smooth muscle cells with increased production of extracellular matrix proteins (eg, collagen, proteoglycans) - The ensuing inflammatory cascade leads to the development of the lesions typical of atherosclerosis, starting from the fatty streaks within the intima (composed mainly of lipid-laden foam cells) that transition into atherosclerotic plaques, such as fibrous cap atheromas and fibrous plaques.  These can become calcified and obstruct blood flow, or can rupture and lead to acute thrombosis. ## Role of HDL and TGs High TG and low HDL levels are often seen in combination with high LDL.  Their effects on the pathogenesis of ASCVD are as follows: - **HDL** has antiatherogenic properties (eg, scavenging excess cholesterol from macrophages before it can be oxidized) and appears to increase nitric oxide production to improve vascular function. - **TG** has theoretical proatherogenic effects because high levels are associated with increased CETP activity and decreased HDL and reverse cholesterol transport. No direct causal link between either high TG or low HDL and ASCVD has been established, although both laboratory abnormalities are often seen in other conditions increasing risk for ASCVD (eg, metabolic syndrome). # Clinical presentation The clinical manifestations of dyslipidemia vary depending on the specific lipid abnormality, severity of the disorder and the presence of associated conditions.  In most cases, dyslipidemia is diagnosed in asymptomatic patients during routine lipid screening (eg, lipid panel), obtained during health maintenance visits (eg, in asymptomatic patients).  In other cases (especially with familial syndromes), patients may manifest with dyslipidemia-associated complications (eg, ASCVD) or signs on physical examination.  This section covers common asymptomatic and symptomatic manifestations of dyslipidemia. # Screening in asymptomatic patients The optimal time to screen for dyslipidemia depends on the presence of other ASCVD risk factors for ASCVD (eg, family history, obesity, presence of hypertension). - **No ASCVD risk factors present:**  Low-risk, asymptomatic patients are generally recommended to undergo one-time screening in childhood and early adulthood (age 9-11 and between age 17 and 21). - **Other ASCVD risk factors present:**  Patients with a family history of familial hypercholesterolemia or other risk factors should initiate screening earlier (early childhood, or when the risk factor is identified). Because age is a primary risk factor for ASCVD, frequent (eg, annual) monitoring of lipids is not usually recommended for low-risk, younger patients (no ASCVD risk factors, age <35 for men and age <45 for women) because it will usually not affect management (ie, lifestyle management for prevention is universally recommended for such patients as first-line treatment).  However, for motivated patients interested in monitoring lipid values to inform lifestyle changes and prevention, lipid screening may be performed earlier. # Symptomatic presentations In some cases, patients with severe elevations in LDL or triglycerides (often reflecting familial syndromes) may manifest with premature ASCVD (eg, childhood, teenage years), pancreatitis, and/or characteristic physical examination findings. - **Atherosclerosis:**  Manifestations can involve the coronary, cerebral (especially internal carotid), and/or systemic (eg, ileal, popliteal) circulation; symptoms can range from myocardial infarction, aortic aneurysm or dissection, ischemic stroke, or limb symptoms of peripheral artery disease (claudication, nonhealing ulcers) to sudden cardiac death. - **Fatty liver disease:**  Accumulation of lipids (especially TG) within hepatocytes results in hepatic steatosis, the first stage in nonalcoholic fatty disease ((Figure 9)).  Chronic metabolic inflammation and oxidative stress (eg, from obesity and insulin resistance) downregulates the nuclear receptor protein peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-alpha, which normally promotes FFA beta-oxidation.  Reduced beta-oxidation of FFAs leads to further lipid accumulation and lipotoxicity, ultimately inciting hepatocyte necrosis, inflammation, and fibrosis (eg, progression to steatohepatitis and cirrhosis). - **Pancreatitis:**  Increased TGs are lipolyzed by pancreatic lipase in pancreatic capillaries; the resulting FFAs are highly inflammatory and cause cellular damage, inflammation, and necrosis.  The serum TG level generally is >1,000 mg/dL (eg, familial syndromes) to be a potential cause of pancreatitis (lower levels may be associated with pancreatitis with concomitant excess alcohol intake). ## Physical examination findings Physical manifestations of dyslipidemia are most often seen in patients with familial hypercholesterolemia and other genetic syndromes.  Presence of any of these findings warrants obtaining a diagnostic lipid panel: - **Xanthoma** is a flat, yellowish deposit of cholesterol that presents as lipid-laden histiocytes in the dermis; it can form in the skin or in tendons (eg, Achilles tendon).  It may be tuberous (over knees, elbows), eruptive (acute onset), or tendinous (over tendons). - **Xanthelasma** is a type of xanthoma usually found on the medial eyelids ((Figure 10)); it presents as dermal accumulations of benign-appearing macrophages with abundant, finely vacuolated (foamy) cytoplasm containing cholesterol (free and esterified), phospholipids, and triglycerides.  Unlike other types of xanthomas, xanthelasma does not always signal severe dyslipidemia; it can be seen in milder cholesterol elevations or also seen in ~50% of healthy patients.  Chronic cholestatic processes including obstructive biliary lesions and primary biliary cholangitis result in hypercholesterolemia due to leakage of bile back into the circulation, leading to the formation of xanthelasmas. - **Arcus corneae** appears as an opaque ring or arc around the cornea; although it can occur in older adults as a benign finding, its presence in children or younger adults (eg, age <40) suggests an underlying dyslipidemia (eg, familial syndrome).  Lipemia retinalis (milky-appearing retinal vasculature) may also occur. - **Lipemic serum** is often a clue to high chylomicron levels, indicative of high circulating chylomicrons in the blood, and often indicate a genetic defect. # Risk factors Most cases of dyslipidemia are acquired through a polygenic mechanism involving interaction of possible genetic factors with environmental triggers (eg, diet, lifestyle behaviors, obesity).  Dyslipidemia may also be the result of another comorbid condition (eg, insulin resistance) or part of a monogenic familial syndrome. ## Lifestyle factors Lifestyle is a major factor influencing the risk for acquiring dyslipidemia in the general population (eg, 50%-60% of attributable risk).  Factors that adversely impact lipid profile include diet (eg, high saturated fat/trans fat intake, high sugar intake), sedentary lifestyle, excessive alcohol intake, and smoking. ## Insulin resistance Insulin resistance (eg, diabetes mellitus, obesity) is associated with increased VLDL, elevated LDL, and low HDL.  This occurs due to aberrant insulin action.  Normally, insulin upregulates LPL, which increases FFA uptake in adipose tissue and lowers blood TG and FFA levels, while inhibiting HSL (which releases stored FFAs and promotes increased TG levels).  Insulin resistance leads to the following effects: - Impaired LPL activity and increased HSL activity lead to an increase in circulating FFAs. - Acquisition of excess FFAs by the liver causes increased VLDL and TG levels. - Increased TG levels stimulate CETP to transfer TGs to HDL, resulting in lower HDL levels. Increased TGs also affect the morphology of LDL, leading to the generation of small dense LDL, which is more strongly associated with atherogenesis and inflammation. ## Familial syndromes Dyslipidemias are inherited as familial syndromes through a primarily monogenic (eg, autosomal recessive or dominant) or polygenic fashion involving mutations or dysfunction of various apolipoproteins, lipoproteins, receptors, or enzymes required for optimal lipid metabolism.  These familial dyslipidemias and their syndromes are often associated with specific physical examination findings or other manifestations.  Common genetic syndromes are presented in this table ((Table 4)). # Summary Dyslipidemias represent a diverse group of lipid disorders that manifest with high LDL, low HDL, and/or high triglycerides.  They involve defects in lipid metabolism and enzymatic processing, lipoproteins and apolipoproteins, lipid transport, and/or cellular receptor binding, which can result from genetic and lifestyle factors.  Although many patients with dyslipidemia are asymptomatic, some experience sequelae of atherosclerosis, pancreatitis, skin and tendon findings, and fatty liver disease. ​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌​​​​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌

Lipoproteins

Structure & synthesis

Function & clearance

VLDL

  • Formed in liver
  • Contains ↑ TGs, ↓ cholesterol
  • Transports TGs
  • Becomes IDL as TG content reduces
  • Requires Apo C-II (LPL co-factor) & ApoE

LDL

  • Formed when IDL is depleted of TGs; also formed in liver
  • Contains ↑ cholesterol, ↓ TG
  • Transports cholesterol
  • Mainly cleared by liver; can be taken up by other tissues
  • Requires LDL-R & apo-B100

HDL

  • Formed in intestine & liver
  • Begins as nascent HDL (↓ TG & ↓ cholesterol); mature HDL has more cholesterol
  • Scavenges excess cholesterol & returns to liver
  • Supports function & clearance of other lipoproteins
  • Requires Apo A-I

Chylomicron

  • Formed in intestines from dietary lipids; ↑↑ TGs & ↓ cholesterol
  • Transports TGs from diet
  • Becomes chylomicron remnants when TG content depleted
  • Requires Apo B-48, ApoE & Apo C-II (LPL cofactor)

Apo B-48 = apolipoprotein B-48; Apo B-100 = apolipoprotein B-100; Apo C-II = apolipoprotein C-II; ApoE = apolipoprotein E; IDL = intermediate-density lipoprotein; LDL-R = low-density lipoprotein receptor; LPL = lipoprotein lipase; TG = triglyceride.

Key enzymes involved in cholesterol transport & synthesis

HMG-CoA reductase

  • Rate-limiting step in endogenous cholesterol production
  • ↑ Cholesterol synthesis

PCSK9

  • Binds to & promotes degradation of LDL-R
  • ↓ LDL-R & ↑ cholesterol levels

LPL

  • Lipolyzes TGs within lipoproteins into FFAs for cellular uptake → catabolizes VLDL & chylomicrons into remnants
  • ↓ Level of FFAs & TG in the blood

CETP

  • Transfers cholesteryl esters from HDL to LDL/VLDL
  • ↑ TG content of HDL → ↓ quality & ↓ levels of HDL

LCAT

  • Esterifies free cholesterol for transport by HDL
  • ↑ Reverse transport of cholesterol to liver

CETP = cholesteryl ester transfer protein; FFA = free fatty acid; LCAT = lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase; LDL-R = low-density lipoprotein receptor; LPL = lipoprotein lipase; PCSK9 = proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9; TG = triglyceride.

Common patterns of dyslipidemias & their causes

High LDL (eg, >100-130 mg/dL)

  • ↑ LDL formation (eg, excess VLDL or Apo-B hepatic synthesis)
  • ↓ LDL clearance (eg, ↓ LDL-R expression, ↑ PCSK9, ↓ LDL-R binding caused by defective Apo B)

High TGs (eg, >150 mg/dL)

  • ↑ Hepatic VLDL synthesis
  • ↓ Chylomicron or VLDL clearance (eg, defective Apo E)
  • ↓ HDL activity (eg, ↑ CETP activity)
  • ↓ LPL activity (eg, defective Apo C-II → ↓ TG lipolysis)
  • Worsened by metabolic inflammation (eg, insulin resistance)

Low HDL (eg, <40-50 mg/dL)

  • Most commonly a sequela of ↑ LDL & TG
  • Isolated ↓ HDL can occur if ↓ synthesis (eg, defective Apo A-1)

Apo A-1 = apolipoprotein A-1; Apo B = apolipoprotein B; Apo C-II = apolipoprotein C-II; Apo E = apolipoprotein E; CETP = cholesteryl ester transfer protein; LDL-R = low-density lipoprotein receptor; LPL = lipoprotein lipase; PCSK9 = proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9; TG = triglyceride.

Important inherited hyperlipoproteinemias

(type I)

Chylomicrons

(type II A)

  • ApoB-100

LDL

  • Tendon xanthomas
  • Xanthelasmas

Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia
(type III)

Chylomicron & VLDL remnants

  • Premature atherosclerosis
  • Tuboeruptive & palmar xanthomas

(type IV)

  • Polygenic

VLDL

articles.title: Lac Operon
articles.markdown: # Lac Operon # Introduction Bacteria regulate gene expression in response to environmental conditions (eg, nutrient availability) by controlling whether RNA polymerase transcribes specific genes.  One common strategy is the operon, a group of functionally related genes transcribed together and regulated as a unit.  The *lac* operon, first described in *Escherichia coli*, is a prototypical inducible operon that uses a negative feedback mechanism for transcriptional regulation in prokaryotes.  It enables bacteria to express genes required for lactose metabolism only when lactose is available and glucose is limited, aligning gene expression with energy efficiency. # Structural organization of the *lac* operon Bacteria can use either glucose or lactose as a carbon source, but glucose is metabolically preferred.  The *lac* operon enables the cell to activate lactose metabolism when glucose is unavailable and to avoid unnecessary enzyme production when lactose is absent. The *lac* operon is a polycistronic transcriptional unit, meaning multiple genes are transcribed together as a single mRNA.  It includes 3 structural genes related to lactose metabolism: - ***lacZ***:  Encodes beta-galactosidase, which hydrolyzes lactose into glucose and galactose and converts a small fraction of lactose into allolactose. - ***lacY***:  Encodes lactose permease, which facilitates lactose entry into the cell. - ***lacA***:  Encodes thiogalactoside transacetylase, which is not essential for lactose metabolism but may detoxify nonmetabolizable galactosides. Upstream of the structural genes are regulatory DNA elements that control transcription by determining RNA polymerase access.  They include the following: - The **promoter (lacP)** is where RNA polymerase binds to initiate transcription. - The **operator (lacO)** is a DNA sequence that is the binding site for the *lac* repressor, which blocks transcription when bound. - The **catabolite activator protein (CAP) binding site** is located upstream of the promoter and serves as a docking site for an activator protein that enhances transcription of genes required for lactose metabolism when cAMP concentrations are high.  A separate, constitutively expressed gene, *lacI,* encodes the ***lac*** **repressor**, which is produced continuously and diffuses to act on the operator. These elements determine whether transcription of the downstream genes occurs by controlling RNA polymerase access and efficiency. # Regulatory logic of the operon Regulation of the *lac* operon reflects 2 questions. 1. Is lactose present?  (Is expression of the genes required for lactose metabolism currently necessary?) 2. Is glucose available?  (Can a preferred energy source be used instead of lactose?) The inputs are handled by 2 interacting control systems: - A **repressor**, which blocks transcription unless lactose is present (negative control). - An **activator**, which increases transcription when glucose is low (positive control). This creates a 2-step regulatory logic: Lactose determines whether transcription is blocked or allowed, and glucose determines whether transcription is low or high. ## Induction by lactose (allows transcription when lactose is present) When lactose is absent, the *lac* repressor is bound to the operator and transcription of genes required for lactose metabolism is blocked ((Figure 1)).  When lactose is present, a small amount enters the cell and is converted to allolactose.  Allolactose acts as an inducer by binding the repressor and causing a conformational change that prevents operator binding and allows transcription to proceed ((Figure 2)). The *lac* operon is therefore classified as inducible; expression is activated by the presence of substrate. ## Activation by low glucose (increases transcription when glucose is low) When glucose levels are low, intracellular cAMP levels rise.  cAMP binds to CAP, and the cAMP–CAP complex binds to its site upstream of the promoter.  This complex interacts with RNA polymerase, stabilizes the open complex, and substantially increases the rate of transcription initiation ((Figure 3)). Intracellular cAMP levels are inversely related to glucose availability: - High glucose levels lead to low cAMP levels, resulting in minimal CAP binding and basal or low transcription. - Low glucose levels lead to high cAMP levels, resulting in active CAP binding and strongly enhanced transcription. This mechanism couples *lac* operon expression to cellular energy status, ensuring that lactose metabolism is upregulated only when glucose is scarce. # Integration of regulatory inputs Because both control systems operate simultaneously, transcription of lactose metabolism genes depends on the combination of lactose and glucose availability: - **No lactose, high glucose**:  The repressor is bound and CAP is inactive; transcription is off. - **No lactose, low glucose**:  The repressor is bound and CAP is active; transcription is off. - **Lactose present, high glucose**:  The repressor is unbound and CAP is inactive; low-level transcription occurs ((Figure 4)). - **Lactose present, low glucose**:  The repressor is unbound and CAP is active; high-level transcription occurs ((Figure 5)). CAP activity alone cannot drive transcription if the repressor remains bound.  Both conditions must be satisfied simultaneously for high-level expression.  This dual control ensures that lactose metabolism genes are strongly expressed (ie, high-level transcription) only when both lactose is present and glucose is low. ## Functional dynamics of induction Induction is not instantaneous.  Because some *lac* repressor molecules periodically dissociate from the operator even in the absence of allolactose, basal transcription continuously produces low levels of permease and beta-galactosidase.  When lactose becomes available, this basal activity allows the following events to take place: - Initial lactose uptake via basal permease. - Conversion of a small fraction of lactose to allolactose via basal beta-galactosidase. - Allolactose binding to the repressor, releasing the operator and increasing transcription. - Increased production of permease and beta-galactosidase, allowing more allolactose to be generated. This constitutes a positive feedback loop that amplifies and sustains operon activation when lactose is present.  It also explains why induction is not all-or-none at the single-cell level but instead builds progressively as intracellular allolactose accumulates. # Effects of mutations - **Repressor or operator defects**:  Mutations that prevent the *lac* repressor from binding the operator result in transcription that is always allowed, regardless of lactose availability (constitutive expression). - **Promoter defects**:  Mutations that impair RNA polymerase binding to the promoter decrease transcription of genes required for lactose metabolism, even when regulatory conditions would otherwise permit expression. - **CAP or CAP binding site defects**:  Mutations that disrupt CAP function or its binding site prevent increased transcription when glucose is low, so transcription remains low despite the presence of lactose. - **Structural gene mutations**:  Mutations in *lacZ*, *lacY*, or *lacA* prevent proper lactose uptake or metabolism, so the operon may be transcribed normally but lactose cannot be effectively used. # Inducible vs repressible operons The *lac* operon is an inducible system under negative control, with additional positive regulation.  This contrasts with repressible operons, such as those governing amino acid biosynthesis, in which gene expression is typically on by default and is turned off by the end product, which acts as a corepressor. # Summary The *lac* operon regulates transcription of genes required for lactose uptake and metabolism by integrating lactose and glucose availability.  Lactose determines whether transcription is blocked or allowed by controlling repressor binding to the operator, whereas glucose determines how strongly those genes are transcribed through cAMP–CAP activity.  This creates a graded, condition-dependent response: Transcription is blocked when lactose is absent, allowed at a low level when lactose is present but glucose is high, and increased when lactose is present and glucose is low.  These effects are mediated by DNA elements that control RNA polymerase access and activity, allowing for coordinated, condition-dependent expression of multiple genes from a single promoter. ​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​

articles.title: Homocysteine And Homocystinuria
articles.markdown:
# Homocysteine And Homocystinuria # Introduction Homocysteine is a sulfur-containing intermediary amino acid formed during methionine metabolism.  In normal patients, homocysteine levels remain low because the amino acid is rapidly recycled via remethylation to methionine (requires vitamin B12 and folate) or broken down by transsulfuration to cysteine (requires vitamin B6).  Vitamin (cofactor) deficiency or enzymatic defect can cause homocysteine to accumulate in the blood (hyperhomocysteinemia), increasing the risk of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events.  The most severe form of impaired homocysteine metabolism (homocystinuria) is associated with multiorgan manifestations (eg, lens dislocation, marfanoid body habitus, developmental delay, thrombotic events) that begin in infancy or early childhood. # Homocysteine formation Homocysteine is generated from methionine via a 3-step process ((Figure 1)), as follows: - **Methionine → S-adenosyl methionine** (SAM) is a rate-limiting, magnesium- and energy-dependent step that primes SAM to become a **methyl donor** for a wide variety of reactions. - SAM → S-adenosyl homocysteine (SAH) is the key enzymatic step of this pathway marked by the donation of a methyl group from SAM to an acceptor molecule, such as: - Nucleic acids for gene silencing in epigenetics (DNA) or regulation of protein translation (RNA). - Proteins for regulating gene expression via histone methylation. - Small molecules (eg, creatine) and lipids (eg, phosphatidylcholine) as part of energy metabolism and cell membrane production. - Neurotransmitters (eg, epinephrine, melatonin, dopamine) as part of synthesis or deactivation. - SAH → **homocysteine** + adenosine is the final step of the process, decreasing SAH to prevent competitive inhibition of the SAM → SAH step.  Elevated homocysteine levels exert a negative feedback loop on this cycle via the buildup of SAH (which then inhibits the conversion of SAM → SAH).Homocysteine is potentially toxic at elevated levels and is metabolized through the remethylation and transsulfuration pathways. # Homocysteine metabolism Homocysteine can be recycled to methionine via remethylation or broken down into cysteine via transsulfuration. ## Remethylation pathway Homocysteine can be recycled back to methionine via remethylation. The **methionine synthase** pathway, ubiquitous in cells, is considered the primary recycling mechanism.  It uses the active form of **folate** (5-methyltetrahydrofolate \[5-MTHF\]) as a methyl donor, with **vitamin B****12** as a cofactor.  Genetic polymorphisms that reduce the generation of 5-MTHF from tetrahydrofolate, via alterations in the enzyme **methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR)**, are associated with hyperhomocysteinemia. A backup pathway that converts homocysteine to methionine without requiring folate or vitamin B12 relies on betaine–homocysteine methyltransferase (BHMT).  BHMT is primarily active in the liver and kidneys and is absent in the heart and brain. ## Transsulfuration pathway Homocysteine can also be broken down into cystathionine and then cysteine via a 2-step process, as follows: - **Homocysteine** → cystathionine is mediated by **cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS)**, which requires **vitamin B****6** as a cofactor and is stimulated by the accumulation of SAM (ie, sufficient methyl donors from the methionine cycle). - Cystathionine → **cysteine** is mediated by an enzyme (cystathionase) that also requires vitamin B6 as a cofactor. Cysteine plays many important roles in metabolism, including: - Precursor for glutathione, an important antioxidant. - Disulfide bridges in complex proteins. - Precursor for coenzyme A, a cofactor required for the Krebs cycle. - Precursor for taurine, a crucial amino acid in the heart/retina and for bile salt conjugation. # Hyperhomocysteinemia Hyperhomocysteinemia is a common disorder (up to 5%-10% of the population) characterized by elevated homocysteine levels in the blood.  It is typically caused by a **vitamin** (cofactor) **deficiency** or a **genetic enzyme deficit**, which impairs homocysteine metabolism. ## Impaired remethylation - **Folate or vitamin B****12** **deficiency**:  A folate metabolite (5-MTHF) and vitamin B12 are required for methionine synthase activity. - **MTHFR polymorphisms** (**most common genetic** cause of hyperhomocysteinemia):  MTHFR converts tetrahydrofolate to 5-MTHF, which is a required precursor for methionine synthase.  A large percentage of the population (up to 30%) has a genetic polymorphism that makes MTHFR work poorly at elevated temperatures (thermolabile), leading to moderate hyperhomocysteinemia. - Methionine synthase deficiency (very rare):  Because methionine synthase is the primary enzyme that recycles homocysteine to methionine, genetic deficiency of methionine synthase is associated with marked elevations of blood and urine homocysteine (homocystinuria). ## Impaired transsulfuration - **Vitamin B****6** **deficiency**:  Vitamin B6 is a required cofactor for both enzymatic steps in transsulfuration. - **CBS deficiency**:  CBS drives the first enzymatic step in the conversion of homocysteine to cysteine.  CBS deficiency is the most common cause of **homocystinuria** (discussed in the next section), which is marked by massive elevation of homocysteine in the blood and urine. Elevations in plasma homocysteine can also be seen in chronic kidney disease (reduced clearance/impaired metabolism), as a medication adverse effect (eg, fibrates, nicotinic acid, metformin, methotrexate), and with cigarette smoking. ## Clinical consequences: Hyperhomocysteinemia and vascular injury Elevated homocysteine levels are associated with vascular injury (eg, intimal thickening, smooth muscle hypertrophy, elastic lamina disruption), possibly due to oxidative stress (which damages endothelial cells), direct endothelial toxicity, impaired nitric oxide signaling, and increased platelet activation. These effects promote a prothrombotic state, leading to an increased risk for coronary artery disease, venous thromboembolism, and ischemic stroke.  In some individuals, elevated homocysteine levels contribute to premature cardiovascular disease, particularly when traditional risk factors are absent.  However, lowering homocysteine levels has not been shown to reliably prevent cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, or thrombotic events; therefore, routine testing of homocysteine levels is not typically undertaken as part of the prevention or treatment of these conditions. # Homocystinuria Homocystinuria is a rare group of genetic diseases characterized by massively elevated homocysteine levels in the blood, leading to spillover in the urine.  The most common cause is an **autosomal recessive** mutation in **CBS**.  Because this enzyme blocks the homocysteine transsulfuration pathway, its deficiency prevents conversion of homocysteine to cystathionine, leading to elevated homocysteine and methionine levels.  Homocystinuria is also seen with deficiency of methionine synthase (very rare), leading to impaired homocysteine remethylation. ## Clinical consequences: Pleiotropy Homocystinuria is a more severe and consequential form of hyperhomocysteinemia that affects multiple organ systems due to the toxic effects of homocysteine on connective tissue, vascular structures, and the nervous system.  The disease illustrates the genetic principle of pleiotropy, in which a mutation in a single gene produces diverse, unrelated phenotypic traits affecting multiple organ systems.  It typically presents in infancy or early childhood with significant abnormalities, including: - **Skeletal abnormalities**:  Patients often develop skeletal findings resembling those seen in connective tissue disorders.  Many are tall with long fingers (arachnodactyly) and may have a sunken or protruding chest (pectus excavatum/carinatum).  These features produce a marfanoid appearance, although the underlying molecular defect differs from that seen in Marfan syndrome. - **Ectopia lentis**:  A hallmark ocular finding is ectopia lentis, in which the lens of the eye becomes displaced or dislocated (most often downward and inward) due to weakened or broken zonular fibers.  This results in visual impairment (eg, myopia, astigmatism, diplopia) at a young age. - **Developmental delay**:  Patients frequently have intellectual impairment and may have seizures.  Risk is reduced with early treatment. - **Thrombotic events**:  **Thromboembolism** is the **leading cause of death** in patients with homocystinuria and may occur at an early age.  Strokes or myocardial infarction can occur in adolescents or young adults due to damage to the endothelium from massively elevated homocysteine levels. ## Differentiation from Marfan syndrome Because homocystinuria and Marfan syndrome both present with tall stature, skeletal abnormalities, and lens dislocation, the conditions share a differential diagnosis ((Table 1)).  However, homocystinuria typically has downward lens dislocation, intellectual disability/developmental delay, and increased risk of thromboembolism.  In contrast, Marfan syndrome is typically associated with upward lens dislocation (due to stretched, rather than broken, zonules), no significant thrombotic risk, and progressive aortic root dilation. # Treatment Treatment of classic homocystinuria (CBS deficiency) includes the following: - **Vitamin B****6**:  Approximately 50% of patients respond to high doses of vitamin B6, which stimulates partially active CBS.  This alone may be enough to control homocysteine levels in these cases. - **Low-methionine diet**:  Reducing dietary intake of methionine limits the amount of homocysteine produced.  Patients must avoid or strictly limit meat, poultry, fish, eggs, dairy, nuts, and beans; instead, they are given a "methionine-free" medical formula that contains the other 19 essential amino acids. - **Cysteine supplementation**:  Because cysteine cannot be generated from homocysteine in most patients with homocystinuria, supplementation with cysteine (an essential amino acid) is required. - **Supplements to increase homocysteine remethylation:** - **Betaine supplementation**:  Betaine supplementation increases homocysteine recycling to methionine via the BHMT pathway (does not require vitamin B12 or folate). - **Vitamin B****12****/folate supplementation**:  Supplementation with these cofactors may increase conversion of homocysteine to methionine via the methionine synthase pathway. Early initiation of these therapies helps limit or delay disease manifestations.  Therefore, testing should be undertaken as soon as possible, and genetic counseling should be provided for first-degree relatives of those who are affected. Enzyme replacement therapy and gene therapy may someday provide more durable interventions. # Summary Homocysteine is an intermediate amino acid produced during methionine metabolism.  In normal patients, homocysteine is rapidly recycled via remethylation to methionine (requires vitamin B12 and folate) or is broken down by transsulfuration to cysteine (requires vitamin B6).  Disruption of these pathways (eg, vitamin deficiency, enzyme defect) leads to the accumulation of homocysteine in the blood.  Hyperhomocysteinemia is associated with an increased risk of cerebrovascular and cardiovascular events; however, lowering homocysteine levels does not seem to reduce the risk (nonmodifiable risk factor). The most severe form of impaired homocysteine metabolism is homocystinuria.  It is caused primarily by an autosomal recessive gene mutation in cystathionine beta-synthase, which prevents conversion of homocysteine to cysteine.  Patients typically have multiorgan manifestations (eg, lens dislocation, marfanoid body habitus, thrombotic events) that begin in childhood.  Early interventions to decrease homocysteine levels, such as a vitamin B6 challenge, methionine-free diet, cysteine supplementation, and stimulation of the remethylation pathway, can reduce or delay symptoms. ​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​
