articles.title: Cellular And Molecular Aspects Of Aging
articles.markdown:
# Cellular And Molecular Aspects Of Aging

# Introduction

Aging is a universal process characterized by a gradual loss of functional reserve across multiple organ systems.  From a molecular perspective, aging is due to accumulated genomic and metabolic insults that impair homeostasis.  These changes lead to cellular dysfunction, tissue changes, and eventually, clinically apparent organ system decline.  To properly care for older adults, clinicians must distinguish between physiologic aging and pathologic conditions.

# Mechanisms

Aging involves the gradual buildup of molecular damage that interferes with cell function.  Although several experimental interventions (eg, senolytic agents) are under investigation, no clinically approved therapy has been shown to slow, halt, or reverse these fundamental mechanisms.

## Molecular events

-   **Genomic damage**:  The average human cell sustains roughly 100,000 DNA lesions per day from environmental insults, endogenous free radicals, and natural replication errors.  With advancing age, DNA damage (eg, base oxidation) increases, and DNA repair (eg, base excision repair, mismatch repair) capacity declines, leading to a greater chance of mutations.
-   **Mitochondrial dysfunction**:  Electron transport chain function (eg, mitochondrial DNA mutations) deteriorates with age, leading to a drop in ATP efficiency and an increase in reactive oxygen species production.  The NAD⁺ pool declines because it is regenerated less efficiently within mitochondria, which impairs antioxidant enzymes and further limits DNA repair.
-   **Proteostatic stress**:  Cells invest heavily in proper protein folding and in the clearing of misfolded or damaged proteins.  With age, the folding machinery (chaperones) declines, causing misfolded proteins to accumulate, activating stress responses (initially prosurvival but later proapoptotic).  In parallel, the cell's waste disposal pathways (ubiquitin-proteasome, autophagy-lysosome) slow down because their components are damaged by oxidation.  A brownish residue called **lipofuscin** (aggregates or proteins, lipids, and iron) accumulates in lysosomes, serving as a marker of cellular waste buildup ((Figure 1)).
-   **Extracellular matrix cross-linking**:  Extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins constantly undergo random **glycation**, whereby sugar molecules covalently bind to their amino groups (ie, Maillard reaction).  Unlike regulated enzymatic glycosylation, this process serves no physiologic purpose.  Over time, these reactions form advanced glycation end products **(AGEs)**, which are stable and generally irreversible protein modifications.  Concurrent oxidation (glycoxidation) can result in cross-linking of collagen and elastin, leading to matrix stiffening.  AGEs are also proinflammatory and profibrotic because they activate dedicated receptors on immune cells and fibroblasts.

## Cellular and tissue events

These events lead to detrimental changes in cells and tissues.  There are 3 general outcomes:

-   **Cell loss**:  When injury outpaces repair, cells can adaptively shrink (atrophy) or undergo regulated death (apoptosis).  The impact is greatest in tissues with limited mitotic capacity, such as neurons, skeletal muscle, cardiac myocytes, nodal pacemaker cells, and nephrons.  When lost, these cells are normally replaced by stem or progenitor cells.  With aging, however, stem cells progressively lose their self-renewal capacity (stemness) because of accumulated DNA damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, and proteostatic stress.
-   **Cell senescence**:  Not all damaged cells undergo apoptosis or atrophy.  Many become senescent, a state of permanent cell cycle arrest that functions as a cancer safeguard by halting further division.  Senescence can be triggered by repeated cellular injury, activation of oncogenes, or, simply, attainment of the natural replication limit (eg, **telomere shortening**).  Although it is protective against malignant transformation, senescence comes at a cost: Senescent cells accumulate with age and secrete a mixture of proinflammatory chemokines, profibrotic factors, and proteases known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), which degrades surrounding tissue and impairs the function of nearby healthy cells ((Figure 2)).
-   **Malignancy**:  As mutations accumulate, some cells progress from dysplasia to neoplasia.  Normally, such cells are eliminated through DNA damage checkpoints and immune surveillance.  With aging, however, these safeguards are weakened, increasing the risk of cancer.

The ECM also changes.  AGE cross-links stiffen collagen and elastin, elastic fibers fragment, and profibrotic signaling from the SASP promotes collagen deposition.  In some tissues, misfolded proteins deposit as amyloid (eg, transthyretin in myocardium and tendons).  These processes collectively reduce compliance and elasticity (eg, diastolic dysfunction, decreased bladder capacity, decreased tendon and joint range of motion).

# Organ systems

Normal aging produces relatively predictable changes across all organ systems.  These changes can overlap with mechanisms of disease and may someday prove modifiable by reversing the molecular and cellular lesions previously discussed.  This section highlights expected patterns of aging to help distinguish typical trajectories from clinically concerning pathology.

## Neurologic/cognitive

Normal aging brings gradual neuronal atrophy that affects gray matter (cell bodies) more than white matter (myelinated axons).  Whole brain volume typically shrinks by 0.5% per year after midlife, accelerating after age 65.

-   **Gray matter** volume loss is diffuse but tends to be greatest in the hippocampi (responsible for new learning and long-term memory) and frontoparietal association cortices (responsible for executive function and working memory).  As a result, cognitively normal older adults usually have preserved knowledge and vocabulary but struggle more with recalling recent conversations, multitasking, and making complex decisions.
-   **White matter** hyperintensities accumulate due to chronic small vessel ischemia, leading to slowed communication between brain regions.  One consequence is the classic hesitant, or magnetic, gait of an older individual due to impaired relay from intention to movement.  This arises because conduction slows from the premotor cortex (planning), through the periventricular white matter tracts, and to the motor cortex (execution).

Although cemented abilities such as vocabulary and general knowledge remain intact, processing and retrieval speed is reduced (ie, **accurate but slower**).  Mild cognitive impairment is *not* considered part of the normal aging spectrum because it requires an absolute deficit (eg, ≤25/30 \[normal: ≥26\] on Montreal Cognitive Assessment) ((Table 1)).  Brain imaging often shows modest cortical thinning with slightly widened sulci (deeper grooves).  Mild ventricular enlargement is common and remains proportional to the degree of atrophy, unlike the more extensive dilation seen with normal pressure hydrocephalus (disproportionate) ((Figure 3)).

The aging brain is also more vulnerable to acute dysfunction.  Stressors such as illness, sleep disruption, anticholinergic medications, or unfamiliar environments can precipitate **delirium**, an acute confusional state with fluctuating attention and alertness.  Sleep provides restorative protection, but aging is associated with changes in sleep architecture (eg, less slow-wave \[N3\] and REM sleep, more arousals) that blunt the brain's recovery capacity.

## Visual

Normal aging produces characteristic ocular changes that affect the cornea, lens, anterior chamber, vitreous, and retina ((Table 2)).

-   The **cornea** flattens slightly due to decreased epithelial cell density and loss of aquaporin function, leading to a mild refractive error.  Corneal sensitivity decreases, which can predispose to abrasions.  Peripheral lipid deposition (arcus senilis) is common and usually benign in older adults (vision sparing).  Lacrimal gland function decreases, leading to evaporative dry eye.
-   The **lens** thickens and becomes more rigid due to glycation and cross-linking, leading to a decreased ability to focus on near objects (eg, **presbyopia**) because the ciliary body has more difficulty bending the lens.  Progressive nuclear sclerosis **(cataract)** scatters incoming light, diminishing contrast and increasing glare and halos (eg, seen when driving at night).  Blue color perception declines due to mild lens yellowing from oxidation of lens proteins (crystallins).
-   In the **anterior chamber**, aqueous outflow through the trabecular meshwork declines modestly with age, leading to a slight rise in intraocular pressure.  Although this is usually benign, it increases the risk of primary open-angle glaucoma, an important cause of preventable vision loss.
-   The **vitreous** is a uniform gel comprising water, collagen, and hyaluronic acid.  With aging, the gel completely liquifies in certain areas (eg, lacunae).  Precipitated collagen fibrils form visible strands (eg, floaters).  Stress is not uniformly distributed, leading to traction on the retina, increasing the risk of detachment, tears, and macular holes.
-   The **retina** exhibits photoreceptor loss, predominantly of rod cells (eg, impaired night vision and slower adjustment to dim light).  The retinal epithelium accumulates lipofuscin and drusen, focal, plaque-like protein deposits that contribute to age-related macular degeneration.

Most age-related ocular changes (mild refractive shifts, presbyopia, glare, slower dark adaptation) are considered normal and usually do not threaten vision.  Cataracts are the leading cause of reversible visual impairment worldwide, and age-related macular degeneration is the main cause of central vision loss.

## Auditory

**Presbycusis** is the most common cause of age-related hearing loss ((Table 3)).  It is a bilateral, symmetric, sensorineural decline that progresses slowly over decades.  It stems from the degeneration of cochlear hair cells and neurons, especially those detecting high frequencies; therefore, older patients often struggle with consonant discrimination ("s," "t," "f") and speech in noisy environments, increasing reliance on lip-reading.  Unlike conductive losses (eg, cerumen impaction), presbycusis does not improve with louder volume but can respond to hearing aids.  Hearing loss in older adults is linked to isolation, depression, and greater cognitive decline, underscoring the need for early recognition and treatment.

## Cardiovascular

Normal aging leads to changes in the vasculature, valves, heart muscle, conduction system, and autonomics ((Table 4)):

-   Large **arteries stiffen** as medial elastin is degraded and collagen is cross-linked.  Functionally, this produces systolic hypertension because the arteries dissipate pulse energy less effectively.  The aortic leaflets frequently develop calcification, termed aortic sclerosis (ie, no significant gradient).  In some patients, this progresses to calcific aortic stenosis (eg, elevated gradient, symptoms).
-   The left ventricle adapts to the increased vascular stiffness and afterload by undergoing concentric hypertrophy, often with interstitial fibrosis, leading to a smaller cavity size and **diastolic dysfunction** (ie, impaired filling pressure but preserved ejection).  Fibrosis can also degrade the **conduction system**, predisposing to sinus node dysfunction, atrioventricular block, and bundle branch blocks.  The left atrium often enlarges due to diastolic dysfunction (higher filling pressure) and fibrosis, predisposing to atrial fibrillation.  The term "presbycardia" is sometimes used to describe this constellation of changes ((Figure 4)).
-   Autonomic responsiveness decreases, so maximal heart rate (HR<sub>max</sub>) falls (eg, HR<sub>max</sub> ≈ 220 − age) and baroreceptor reflexes are blunted (eg, orthostatic hypotension with alpha-blockers, tricyclic antidepressants, and other medications)

Resting **cardiac output** is generally preserved with healthy aging, but maximal cardiac output decreases due to lower HR<sub>max</sub> and blunted stroke volume reserve (~20%-30% lower in older vs young adults).

## Respiratory

Normal aging leads to several changes in respiratory mechanics ((Figure 5)):

The lung parenchyma loses elastic recoil due to elastin degradation and alveolar septal loss over time.  As a result, small airways collapse earlier during expiration, leading to mild airtrapping (eg, increased residual volume \[RV\]).  However, overall lung size (total lung capacity \[TLC\]) remains relatively constant after age 25.  Therefore, vital capacity, the difference between TLC and RV, steadily decreases by roughly 30 mL/year on spirometry ((Figure 6)).

Earlier airway closure causes microatelectasis (ie, invisible on standard chest imaging), whereas age-related alveolar septal loss modestly reduces surface area and capillary blood volume.  Together, microatelectasis and surface loss lead to slightly decreased oxygen transfer, reflected by a mild decrease in the diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide and an age-dependent increase in the alveolar-arterial (A-a) gradient (eg, expected A-a gradient ≈ age / 3 ≈ age / 4 + 4).

Other functional changes include lower pulmonary reserve (eg, increased risk of respiratory failure with infection or anesthesia) and weakened cough and mucociliary clearance (eg, increased risk of aspiration and pneumonia).

## Renal

Normal aging leads to a gradual loss of nephrons, with compensatory hypertrophy of remaining nephrons.  Renal atrophy is greater in the cortex (glomerulosclerosis) than in the medulla (tubulointerstitial fibrosis).

-   Renal blood flow falls by roughly 10% per decade starting in midlife due to rising glomerular resistance (eg, hyaline arteriolosclerosis, atherosclerosis, endothelial dysfunction).  As a result, the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) declines by approximately 10 mL/min/1.73 m<sup>2</sup> per decade, with wide variability ((Figure 7)).
-   Decline in tubular functions leads to impaired concentrating and diluting capacity, which predisposes patients with poor oral intake to dehydration.  Reduced ammoniagenesis increases the risk of metabolic acidosis under stress.  Renin and aldosterone levels decrease, raising the risk of hyperkalemia (eg, with ACE inhibitors).

Because muscle mass also decreases with aging, serum creatinine can remain apparently normal despite a significant reduction in GFR.  Generally, creatinine-based estimated GFR overestimates renal function, especially in older patients with sarcopenia.  Drugs cleared by urinary excretion are prone to accumulating and may require more careful titration (eg, digoxin, metformin).

## Genitourinary/pelvic

Normal aging alters bladder function, outlet resistance, and pelvic support.

-   Bladder capacity falls due to wall stiffening (eg, increased collagen).  Simultaneously, the detrusor muscle weakens, so postvoid residuals increase and patients are at increased risk for acute **urinary retention**, especially when using medications with anticholinergic activity (eg, antihistamines).  Retention affects men more than women, due to concurrent outlet resistance from prostatic hyperplasia.  With high retained volumes, **overflow incontinence** can occur (eg, dribbling).
-   At the same time, detrusor activity increases, leading to sensations of urgency.  An effective on-demand continence response depends on healthy periventricular white matter (for rapid control), mobility (to get to the toilet), and strength of pelvic floor muscles, including the urethral sphincter.  These are compromised in older patients, leading to **urge incontinence**.
-   In women, pelvic floor laxity and reduced urethral closure (from postmenopausal atrophy) predispose to **stress incontinence** (eg, leakage with exercise, laughter, or sneezing).  Pelvic organ prolapse can also cause physical obstruction and overflow incontinence.
-   **Asymptomatic bacteriuria** is common (~20% at random) due to urinary stasis and decreased mucosal immunity.  This generally does not require treatment by itself but can predispose patients to episodes of symptomatic bacterial cystitis.

## Gastrointestinal

Normal aging leads to decreased gastrointestinal motility and altered oral drug metabolism; however, absorptive and secretory function largely remains intact.

-   In the upper gastrointestinal tract, oropharyngeal **swallowing** becomes less coordinated (presbyphagia) due to periventricular white matter disease (eg, coordination), muscle weakness (eg, tongue, pharynx), and impaired mastication (eg, poor dentition).  The esophagus becomes less peristaltic, hiatal hernia (eg, crural muscle weakening) is more common, and the lower esophageal sphincter relaxes; these changes predispose to gastroesophageal reflux and pill esophagitis.
-   Gastric acidity and small bowel absorption capacity are generally preserved.  Pancreatic exocrine function is generally preserved (eg, maintaining absorption of proteins and fats).  Gallbladder contractility decreases and bile acid cholesterol content increases, favoring biliary sludging and cholelithiasis.
-   Hepatic drug metabolism changes, mainly due to decreased liver blood flow ((Table 5)).  First-pass metabolism decreases, leading to higher oral bioavailability of certain medications (eg, morphine, propranolol, verapamil), which may result in greater sedation or hypotension at a given dose.  Conversely, clearance (eg, cytochrome oxidase activity) decreases, which prolongs drug half-life.
-   Colonic motility slows and is worsened by low physical activity or constipating drugs (eg, anticholinergics, calcium channel blockers, iron).  At the same time, the rectal sphincter weakens, so stool retention can paradoxically lead to leakage (overflow fecal incontinence).

Dysphagia, weight loss, iron deficiency anemia, and malabsorption are *not* features of normal aging and should prompt diagnostic evaluation.

## Endocrine/metabolic

With normal aging, basal hormone levels are often near normal except for androgens and estrogens.  However, deficits are more easily unmasked by stressors such as acute illness.

-   **Glucose**:  Visceral adiposity rises and lean mass falls, producing **insulin resistance**.  In addition, early-phase (meal-stimulated) insulin release is blunted, leading to higher postprandial glucose despite normal fasting levels.  Counterregulation to hypoglycemia (eg, glucagon, cortisol, and catecholamine response) is weaker, predisposing patients to hypoglycemia with fasting, illness, or antidiabetic medications.
-   **Thyroid axis**:  With age, tissue 5′-deiodinase activity gradually declines, so conversion of T4 (prohormone) to T3 (active hormone) becomes less efficient.  As a result, serum T3 levels slowly fall, whereas free T4 levels generally remain stable.  TSH can drift upward due to a reset in the hypothalamic-pituitary feedback setpoint.  This combination creates a laboratory picture that resembles subclinical hypothyroidism (ie, mildly elevated TSH, normal T4) but represents an aging-related change in normal value limits rather than true thyroid disease.  It usually does not warrant treatment because the adverse effects of thyroid hormone supplementation (eg, atrial fibrillation, bone loss) outweigh the benefits.
-   **Adrenal axis**:  The diurnal cortisol rhythm flattens (ie, peaks are lower, troughs are higher), yet maximal output to stress is usually preserved.  In contrast, dehydroepiandrosterone declines steadily, reducing the availability of androgen precursors.
-   **Gonadal axis**:  In women, menopause brings a permanent decline in ovarian estrogen and progesterone production, leading to vasomotor symptoms, bone loss, and genitourinary atrophy.  Vasomotor symptoms can last for an average of 7-10 years after the final menstrual period.  In men, free testosterone falls due to testicular atrophy, which is associated with changes in energy, perceived wellness, and muscle mass.
-   **Bone mineral axis**:  Cutaneous vitamin D synthesis declines due to epidermal thinning, reduced perfusion, and depletion of precursor steroids.  In parallel, renal 1-alpha hydroxylation and intestinal calcium absorption also decline.  These changes can lead to secondary hyperparathyroidism (especially with underlying chronic kidney disease), tilting the bone balance toward resorption.  The result is progressive bone mineral loss (~1% per year in men, >2% per year in women).

## Hematologic

Bone marrow cellularity declines with age as hematopoietic cells are progressively replaced by fat (eg, marrow cellularity % ≈ 100 − age).

-   **Erythropoiesis (formation of red blood cells)** falls modestly, resulting in mild normocytic anemia.  Because of fibrofatty replacement, the marrow is less responsive to erythropoietin, so circulating erythropoietin generally rises with aging.  In addition, iron is less bioavailable due to elevated hepcidin (upregulated by chronic inflammation).  Superimposed illness can unmask anemia easily.
-   **Myelopoiesis (formation of white blood cells)** is generally preserved.  However, immune cells have qualitative immunologic defects (discussed in the next section).
-   **Thrombopoiesis (platelets)** remains intact with age, with stable platelet and megakaryocyte counts.  However, platelet reactivity increases, particularly in response to prothrombotic stimuli (eg, infection, inflammation), leading to an increased risk of acute cardiovascular events during stress.

In addition, many older adults develop a degree of **clonal hematopoiesis** due to age-acquired mutations in precursor cells.  This state is usually asymptomatic, but it carries a higher risk of hematologic malignancy (eg, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, myelodysplastic syndrome).

## Immunologic

Normal aging is associated with immunosenescence, affecting both innate and adaptive defenses.

-   With respect to **innate immunity**, neutrophils, natural killer (NK) cells, and macrophages remain quantitatively intact, but their function declines.  Neutrophils and macrophages exhibit reduced chemotaxis, phagocytosis, and microbial killing (eg, weaker respiratory burst), whereas NK cells show diminished cytotoxicity.  Older adults often have a **blunted** systemic inflammatory response due to the decreased production of acute phase cytokines.  Fever, leukocytosis, and tachycardia may be muted or absent during infection.
-   In terms of **adaptive immunity**, both T and B cells are affected.  Thymic involution begins in late childhood and continues until death.  By age 70, the thymus is reduced to approximately 10% of its original size, leaving little capacity to quickly generate new T cells.  Older adults therefore rely heavily on memory T-cell pools, which limits their ability to respond to novel antigens.  B-cell function also declines, partly due to a lack of T-cell assistance.  Serum total immunoglobulin levels are generally preserved, but the ability to produce high-affinity antibodies is reduced.  Together, these changes underlie diminished vaccine responsiveness, greater susceptibility to infectious disease (eg, pneumonia, influenza), and reactivation of latent viruses (eg, varicella-zoster virus).

## Musculoskeletal

Normal aging alters bone, muscle, and connective tissue.

-   **Bone** skews toward resorption, as previously described, increasing the risk of osteopenia, osteoporosis, and fragility fractures.
-   **Skeletal muscle** atrophies with age, with **fast-twitch (type II) fibers** being most affected.  This compromises the body's ability to make rapid and powerful postural adjustments, which are essential for maintaining balance.  The Timed Up and Go (TUG) test (rise from chair, walk 3 m \[10 ft\], turn, and sit back down as quickly as possible) can often capture this deficit.  Sarcopenia is defined as a measurable age-related reduction in muscle power (eg, on the TUG test), muscle, or both.
-   **Cartilage and tendons** accumulate cross-links (eg, AGE, amyloid) and microdamage, whereas intervertebral discs dehydrate and lose height, producing degenerative joint disease and spinal stiffness.

Together, these changes impair mobility, balance, and motor power, raising the risk of falls and fractures.

## Dermatologic

Skin is among the most visible markers of aging.

-   Epidermal turnover slows, and dermal fibroblasts produce less collagen and elastin, leading to thinning, dryness, and impaired wound healing.  Melanocyte density decreases (eg, to <25% of youthful levels by age 70), producing graying hair and hypopigmented macules.  However, benign focal proliferations of melanocytes can cause lentigines (liver spots).
-   Elastic fiber fragmentation and hyaluronan degradation lead to laxity and wrinkles.  Subcutaneous fat is lost in some areas (face, hands, shins) but redistributed in others, resulting in sagging and predisposing to pressure injury.  Senile purpura (solar or actinic purpura), which is characterized by intermittent ecchymotic lesions primarily on the hands and forearms, arises due to blood vessel fragility after years of sun-related damage to the dermis, sometimes with residual brownish discoloration from hemosiderin deposition; platelet counts and coagulation tests are typically normal.
-   Immune surveillance declines (fewer Langerhans cells \[skin macrophages\] and reduced cutaneous T-cell function), making it easier for ultraviolet damage to induce actinic keratoses, basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma.

# Summary

Aging is driven by the gradual accumulation of molecular and cellular damage that leads to irreversible loss of organ function and reserve ((Table 6)).  At the molecular level, genomic instability, mitochondrial dysfunction, proteostatic stress, and extracellular matrix cross-linking underlie much of the decline.  At the cellular level, apoptosis, senescence, and diminished stem cell renewal translate into progressive organ system vulnerability.  Clinically, these changes manifest as predictable patterns:

-   Cognitive aging typically produces slower processing and retrieval but preserves knowledge, vocabulary, and independence in daily activities.
-   Visual aging brings presbyopia (difficulty with near focus), increased glare, cataracts, and risk of macular degeneration and glaucoma.
-   Auditory aging manifests as presbycusis (high-frequency hearing loss and impaired speech discrimination), which can lead to increased social isolation and cognitive decline.
-   Cardiovascular changes include arterial stiffening, diastolic dysfunction, conduction disease, and diminished maximal heart rate and cardiac output reserve.
-   Respiratory aging involves the loss of lung elastin, leading to gradually elevated residual volume and loss of vital capacity.
-   Renal aging involves a progressive decline in glomerular filtration rate, which often occurs despite stable serum creatinine levels (due to decreased muscle mass).
-   Bladder and pelvic floor changes predispose to incontinence, retention, and asymptomatic bacteriuria.
-   Endocrine and metabolic adaptations include insulin resistance and mild subclinical changes in thyroid hormone profile.
-   Hematologic and immune changes decrease hematopoiesis (fatty replacement of the bone marrow), diminish vaccine response, and increase infection and malignancy risk.
-   Musculoskeletal aging involves sarcopenia, bone loss, and connective tissue cross-linking, which, together, reduce strength and range of motion, increasing fall and fracture risk.

Distinguishing normal aging from pathologic disease is critical to avoiding both overtreatment and undertreatment, especially because some features overlap with clinical disorders.

articles.title: Cell Division: Meiosis, Mitosis, And Cell Cycle Regulation
articles.markdown: # Cell Division: Meiosis, Mitosis, And Cell Cycle Regulation # Introduction The cell cycle facilitates the duplication and segregation of the cell's genetic information to form 2 identical daughter cells.  The 2 major phases of the eukaryotic cell cycle are interphase and M (mitotic) phase.  The cell spends approximately 90% of its life cycle in interphase, which is divided into G1 (first gap), S (synthesis), and G2 (second gap) phases.  Mitosis involves nuclear division to form genetically identical daughter cells.  Meiosis is a specialized form of cell division that leads to the formation of gametes (ova, sperm), which can then participate in sexual reproduction. # Interphase Interphase is characterized by the following phases ((Figure 1)): - **G1 phase**:  Characterized by presynthetic cell growth, organelle duplication, and the production of proteins necessary for DNA replication.  After G1, a subset of cells enters a specialized resting state called **G0**, where the cell cycle is arrested for a variable period: - Some cells (eg, differentiated neurons, erythrocytes, skeletal/cardiac muscle cells) enter G0 permanently (regenerating from stem cells). - Stable (quiescent) cells (eg, hepatocytes) can move from G0 to G1 when stimulated. - Labile cells (eg, bone marrow, hair, intestinal epithelium) have a short G1 and do not enter G0; they tend to be very sensitive to chemotherapy. - **S phase**:  Consists of DNA replication. - **G2 phase**:  Involves replenishing energy stores (for ATP synthesis), synthesizing proteins, assembling molecular machinery needed for cell division, and repairing errors made in DNA replication.  Organelles are prepared for partitioning into daughter cells. # M phase Two events happen concurrently during M phase:  **mitosis** and **cytokinesis** ((Figure 2)).  Mitosis involves nuclear division, and cytokinesis involves cytoplasmic division to form 2 genetically identical daughter cells, each with an identical set of chromosomes. ## Mitosis During late S and G2 phases, the cell commits to division and completes preparations for mitosis.  Each daughter cell receives an identical set of unduplicated chromosomes.  Mitosis is divided into 4 stages ((Figure 3)): - **Prophase**:  Chromosomes condense (chromatin compaction), with each chromosome consisting of 2 identical sister chromatids joined at a centromere.  Nucleoli disappear.  The nuclear envelope breaks down.  The mitotic spindle forms from centrosomes, and spindle fibers attach to kinetochores near the centromeres.  Nonkinetochore spindle fibers elongate the cell.  Centrosomes migrate to opposite poles. - **Metaphase**:  Chromosomes align along the metaphase plate.  Centrosomes are at opposite ends of the cell. - **Anaphase**:  Sister chromatids separate and are pulled toward opposite poles by shortening spindle fibers. - **Telophase**:  Two daughter nuclei form as nuclear envelopes reform around each set of chromosomes.  Chromatin decondenses, and nucleoli reappear.  The remaining spindle fibers are dismantled.  Mitosis concludes with the formation of 2 identical daughter nuclei. ## Cytokinesis Cytokinesis is a process separate from but overlapping with mitosis.  In eukaryotic cells, it begins during late anaphase.  A **cleavage furrow** forms near the metaphase plate, marked by a contractile ring of actin and myosin.  The ring contracts to pinch the cell into 2, each with its own nucleus, cytosol, and organelles. # Cell cycle regulation Intrinsic timing mechanisms monitor internal and external conditions and include **checkpoints** to ensure proper completion of each stage before progression ((Figure 4)).  The 3 most important checkpoints occur at: - **G1/S transition**:  The transition from G1 to S phase (initiation of DNA replication) is controlled by a combination of cell size and nutrient status, exposure to growth factors, and proper surveillance and repair of damaged DNA (with tumor suppressor protein p53 causing cells with mutant DNA to arrest until the damage is repaired). - **G2/M transition**:  At the transition from G2 to M phase, the cell checks for DNA damage again and repairs replication errors before they can be passed on to daughter cells during mitosis. - **M phase**:  An additional spindle checkpoint ensures that duplicated chromosomes separate appropriately during cell division. ## Cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases Checkpoints are regulated by **cyclins** and **cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs)**: - Cyclins fluctuate in abundance during the cell cycle and are degraded by proteolysis after use. - CDKs are constitutively present at relatively constant levels but active only when bound to a cyclin partner. Activated cyclin-CDK complexes are able to phosphorylate proteins, advancing the cell through various cell cycle stages.  There are 3 major types of regulatory cyclins: - **G1/S cyclins**:  Bind CDKs at the end of G1 and commit the cell to replication. - **S cyclins**:  Peak during S phase; required for replication. - **M cyclins**:  Peak at G2/M transition; promote mitotic events. ## Example:  Retinoblastoma, p53, and CDKs Progression through the G1/S checkpoint is controlled in part by CDK4 and CDK6, which are activated by cyclin D ((Figure 5)).  The mechanism involves the tumor suppressor **retinoblastoma (Rb) protein**, which normally exists in 2 functional states: - Active (dephosphorylated):  Rb binds and inhibits E2F transcription factors, preventing the transcription of genes necessary for S-phase entry.  This form of Rb is predominant in quiescent (G0) cells or in terminally differentiated cells, in which cell-cycle progression is arrested. - Inactive (phosphorylated):  Inactivation occurs following stimulation by growth factors, which induce activation of cyclin D and its associated CDKs (CDK4 and CDK6) as well as cyclin E and its associated CDK (CDK2).  Phosphorylation of Rb causes it to release E2F, allowing transcription of S-phase genes and progression through the G1/S checkpoint. After mitotic division, the Rb protein is dephosphorylated and remains active until the cell is again stimulated to enter the next cycle.  This mechanism is exploited in some types of cancer treatment (eg, CDK4/6 inhibitors for breast cancer). Progression through the G1/S checkpoint is also tightly regulated in response to DNA integrity, with the tumor suppressor protein **p53** playing a central role.  When DNA damage is detected, p53 becomes stabilized and activated, leading to transcriptional upregulation of genes that inhibit CDK activity (eg, p21).  This inhibition prevents progression into S phase, allowing time for DNA repair.  If the damage is irreparable, p53 can initiate apoptosis to eliminate the damaged cell.  **Apoptosis** is a programmed form of cell death (distinct from necrosis) in which caspases (activated from inactive procaspases) initiate a cascade leading to DNA fragmentation, cell shrinkage, and formation of apoptotic blebs that separate into apoptotic bodies; these are then phagocytosed by neighboring cells or phagocytes (eg, macrophages), allowing for controlled cell removal without damage to surrounding tissue. These regulatory mechanisms ensure that cells do not replicate damaged DNA and help maintain genomic stability.  Changes in these mechanisms also underlie some hereditary cancer syndromes (eg, Li-Fraumeni cancer syndrome due to germline mutation in the p53 tumor suppressor gene, causing breast cancer, sarcomas, leukemias, and others). # Meiosis Whereas mitosis produces 2 genetically identical daughter cells and maintains the chromosome number across divisions, meiosis is a specialized form of cell division that reduces the chromosome number by half and gives rise to gametes (sperm and ova), enabling sexual reproduction. Ploidy refers to the specific number of complete sets of chromosomes in a cell.  Human somatic (nonreproductive) cells contain 2 sets of chromosomes—one from each parent—and are classified as diploid (2n = 2 x 23 = 46 chromosomes); gametes contain a single set and are classified as **haploid** (**1n** = 1 x 23 = 23 chromosomes).  Fertilization restores diploidy by combining 2 haploid gametes to form a diploid zygote. Meiotic division occurs in 2 sequential stages:  meiosis I and meiosis II.  Like mitosis, each stage is subdivided into 4 phases. ## Meiosis I - **Prophase I**:  Homologous chromosomes undergo **synapsis**, aligning side by side.  **Crossing over** (exchange of DNA between equivalent maternal and paternal segments) occurs between homologous chromatids ((Figure 6)). - **Metaphase I**:  The pairs of homologous chromosomes (called tetrads because each consists of 4 chromatids) align along the metaphase plate. - **Anaphase I**:  Homologous chromosomes are separated and pulled to opposite poles.  **Sister chromatids remain attached**, in contrast to mitosis. - **Telophase I and cytokinesis**:  Two haploid daughter cells are formed.  Each contains chromosomes composed of **2 connected sister chromatids**. ## Meiosis II - **Anaphase II**:  Sister chromatids are separated and move to opposite poles. - **Telophase II and cytokinesis**:  The formation of **haploid gametes** is complete, with each gamete containing 1 complete set of chromosomes. Through this 2-step process, diploid cells give rise to haploid gametes (gametogenesis) ((Figure 7)); the process starts before birth but is arrested until puberty ((Figure 8)).   The failure of chromosome pairs to separate properly during cell division is called **nondisjunction**.  This could be due to a failure of homologous chromosomes to separate in meiosis I or a failure of sister chromatids to separate during meiosis II or mitosis. # Summary Cell division occurs through the cell cycle, which includes interphase (G1, S, G2) and M phase, facilitating the replication and segregation of genetic material.  Mitosis produces 2 genetically identical diploid daughter cells through a sequence of stages—prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase.  Cell cycle progression is regulated by checkpoints at G1/S and G2/M transitions, and during mitosis, with control mediated by cyclins, cyclin-dependent kinases, and tumor suppressors such as Rb and p53.  In contrast to mitosis, meiosis generates haploid gametes through 2 successive divisions (meiosis I and II) that reduce chromosome number and introduce genetic diversity. ​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌

articles.title: Cell Biology: Secretory Pathway (Endoplasmic Reticulum And Golgi Apparatus)
articles.markdown: # Cell Biology: Secretory Pathway (Endoplasmic Reticulum And Golgi Apparatus) # Introduction This article focuses on the cell's secretory pathway, which consists of 3 organelles ((Figure 1)): - The **smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER)**, which makes lipids and steroid hormones. - The **rough ER** (RER), which makes secreted and transmembrane proteins. - The **Golgi apparatus**, which sorts and traffics proteins and lipids to their final destinations. A related article covers the waste disposal and recycling (ie, proteasome, lysosomes, endosomes, peroxisomes) of the cell.  These 2 pathways are inseparable.  For example, many transmembrane proteins, and those secreted extracellularly, are reinternalized for degradation in lysosomes. # Overview The ER and Golgi apparatus belong to the endomembrane system, a continuous network that begins at the nuclear envelope and extends outward toward the cell periphery.  The ER membrane is directly continuous with the outer nuclear membrane, and its lumen is continuous with the perinuclear space.  From the ER, newly synthesized proteins and lipids move forward in vesicles to the Golgi apparatus, which is organized as a polarized stack near the nucleus.  The cis face receives cargo from the ER, whereas the trans face dispatches it toward the plasma membrane, lysosomes, or secretory vesicles.  This arrangement ensures that the luminal side of the ER and Golgi apparatus corresponds to the extracellular side once vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane, preserving the orientation of membrane proteins and secreted molecules. # Smooth endoplasmic reticulum ## Function The SER is a tubular network of lipid membranes serving as the site of **lipid synthesis** (of steroid hormones, phospholipids, and cholesterol).  It supplies lipid membranes throughout the cell, including the contiguous RER, vacuoles, and plasma membrane.  In addition, SER has specialized functions in specific organs: - Hepatic SER is the site of phase I metabolism **(cytochrome P450 oxidase)**, converting lipophilic drugs (which accumulate in the lipid sink of the ER) into more hydrophilic metabolites, preparing them for biliary or renal excretion. - Cardiac and skeletal muscle SER (known as sarcoplasmic reticulum) is tightly woven around the myofibrils ((Figure 2)), where it **sequesters calcium** for controlled release in response to excitation-contraction signaling (eg, ryanodine receptor \[RyR\]). - Adrenal cortex, thyroid follicular, and gonadal SERs are prominent because they are steroid hormone–producing cells.  (The rate-limiting step of steroid hormone synthesis begins in the mitochondria, but the majority of steps are completed in the SER.) ## Dysfunction Diseases originating in the SER include **congenital adrenal hypoplasia** (eg, 21-hydroxylase \[CYP2A1\] deficiency: blocked cortisol and aldosterone synthesis but androgen excess) and **malignant hyperthermia** (eg, *RYR* mutation: inappropriate calcium release and muscle contraction, inhibited by dantrolene). Similarly, because corticosteroid-producing cells (in the adrenals, gonads, and liver) characteristically contain a well-developed SER, **androgen-secreting tumors** (eg, ovarian, adrenal) tumor can lead to manifestations such as virilization. # Rough endoplasmic reticulum ## Function The RER is contiguous with the SER but is studded with ribosomes, giving it a grainy appearance on electron microscopy.  It is the site for the synthesis of **secreted** and **transmembrane** proteins.  Such proteins require a lipophilic vesicle to integrate or pass through the plasma membrane (eg, for secretion).  The RER's continuity with the SER enables the transfer of lipid components that form vesicular coats to serve this purpose ((Figure 3)).  This is in contrast to soluble cytosolic proteins, which are synthesized by free ribosomes in the cytoplasm and do not require lipid vesicles. Because it specializes in protein export, RER is most prominent in secretory cells such as plasma cells (eg, antibodies), pancreatic acinar cells (eg, digestive enzymes), hepatocytes (eg, plasma proteins, clotting factors), and goblet cells (eg, mucins). RER protein processing is as follows ((Figure 4)): - RER-synthesized peptides begin their translation on free ribosomes in the cytosol.  Proteins are synthesized from their N (amino) to C (carboxy) termini. - For secreted or transmembrane proteins, the first (nascent) 15-30 amino acids serve as a signal peptide that engages a **signal recognition particle** (SRP); this process temporarily pauses translation and guides the ribosome-peptide complex to the RER. - Once the complex is docked to the RER, translation resumes, threading the growing peptide into the RER lumen through a pore (translocon).  Defects in SRP docking result in elongation arrest, leading to the accumulation of incomplete peptides in the cytosol. - The RER enzymes add **cotranslational** and **posttranslational modifications** such as N-linked glycosylation (to facilitate proper protein folding), proline hydroxylation (for collagen secretion), and GPI anchors (for membrane integration). ## Dysfunction Defective RER processing is involved in several conditions, including: - **Cystic fibrosis**, in which the most common mutation (*ΔF508*) results in a misfolded chloride channel (CFTR protein) that is retained in the RER and unable to reach the plasma membrane. - Several forms of **amyloidosis**, in which chronic ER overload due to overproduction of abnormal proteins (eg, immunoglobulin light chains in myeloma, serum amyloid A in chronic inflammation) overwhelms RER capacity, leading to extracellular deposition of incompletely folded proteins as insoluble fibrils. - Most congenital disorders of glycosylation involving the accumulation of improperly N-glycosylated and subsequently misfolded proteins, leading to multisystem organ dysfunction. Some of the clinically significant syndromes due to overproduction of peptide hormones by the RER include: - Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (characterized by increased water reabsorption in the renal collecting ducts), due to overproduction of vasopressin. - Hypoglycemia due to overproduction of insulin by certain pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (insulinomas). - Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastric acid hypersecretion and recurrent peptic ulcer) due to excess secretion of gastrin from pancreatic or small intestine gastrinomas. - Galactorrhea (pathologic mammary milk production) due to a prolactin-secreting lactotroph pituitary adenoma. # Golgi apparatus The Golgi apparatus appears as a stack of flattened cisternae on electron microscopy, typically located just beyond the ER.  The Golgi apparatus appears as a zone of perinuclear clearing on hematoxylin and eosin staining because it does not take up the dye.  This zone is especially prominent in **plasma cells**, which have extensive ER and Golgi to support their high rate of immunoglobulin production. The Golgi apparatus has 3 major functions: - Protein finalization (adding further posttranslational modifications to mature proteins received from the RER). - Protein sorting (directing proteins to their final destinations). - Protein retrograde transport (to replenish ER proteins). ## Protein finalization On receiving proteins from the RER, the Golgi apparatus adds further **posttranslational modifications**, namely: - O-linked glycosylation (eg, surface glycoproteins, immunoglobulins, mucins). - O-linked sulfation (eg, chemokine receptors). - Mannose-6 phosphorylation (eg, lysosomal acid hydrolases). Deficient O-glycosylation of IgA1 leads to **IgA nephropathy**, with features of impaired mucosal immunity (eg, recurrent respiratory infections) and immune complex deposition in the glomerular mesangium (eg, nephritic syndrome).  Chronic exposure to **cigarette smoke** damages the Golgi and ER membranes and impairs O-glycosylation in airway goblet cells, leading to abnormally thick mucus (eg, chronic bronchitis). ## Protein sorting The Golgi apparatus then sorts and traffics the RER-synthesized proteins based on specific signal peptides. - Plasma membrane proteins have **no specific sequence** (default secretory pathway).  A signal is not required because the lipid vesicles naturally fuse with the plasma membrane (with assistance from specialized SNARE proteins). - Resident ER proteins (eg, chaperones, disulfide isomerases) have an **ER retention signal** (KDEL or KXXX) and are directed back to the ER via retrograde transport (discussed later). - Lysosomal enzymes (acid hydrolases) carry a **mannose-6 phosphate** tag. A notable example of aberrant Golgi apparatus sorting is **I-cell disease** (aka mucolipidosis type II), resulting from defective mannose-6-phosphate tagging, which directs digestive enzymes into lysosomes ((Figure 5)).  Consequently, lysosomes are unable to hydrolyze waste, leading to the accumulation of undigested debris (inclusion bodies), resulting in severe multisystem organ dysfunction. ## Protein retrograde transport Vesicular traffic through the Golgi apparatus is bidirectional.  In forward **(anterograde)** transport, proteins leave the RER in vesicles coated in **COPII** (coat protein complex II), enter the cis Golgi apparatus, and progress through the stack before exiting the trans face toward the plasma membrane, lysosomes, or secretory vesicles. However, this flow is leaky: some proteins that belong in the RER (eg, chaperones, translocon components) escape into the forward pathway.  To maintain ER function, the Golgi apparatus continuously retrieves these proteins and returns them in **COPI**\-coated vesicles, a process termed **retrograde** transport. This retrograde Golgi transport is exploited by several extracellular bacterial toxins (eg, Shiga, diphtheria, and cholera toxins) to avoid lysosomal degradation, reentering the cytosol to attack their targets (eg, ribosomes and G-protein subunits). ## Golgi apparatus–independent sorting Proteins synthesized by free ribosomes in the cytosol do not pass through the Golgi apparatus for sorting.  However, they are included in this section for completeness.  Specifically: - Cytosolic proteins (eg, glycolytic enzymes, tubulin, actin) have no specific sequence (default pathway). - Nuclear proteins (eg, histones, DNA polymerase) have a nuclear localization signal (NLS) (typically PKKKRKV). - Mitochondrial proteins (eg, Krebs cycle enzymes) have a mitochondrial targeting sequence (MTS) (15-30 basic and positively charged amino acids). - Peroxisomal proteins (eg, catalase) carry a peroxisomal targeting signal, which is recognized by PEX proteins. # Summary The secretory pathway, consisting of the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus, is responsible for the synthesis, modification, and trafficking of secreted, transmembrane, and organelle-associated proteins, as well as lipids, within the cell.  The smooth endoplasmic reticulum produces lipids and steroid hormones and has additional functions, including detoxifying lipophilic drugs (eg, cytochrome P450 enzymes) and storing intracellular calcium (eg, sarcoplasmic reticulum in muscle).  The rough endoplasmic reticulum, studded with ribosomes, synthesizes proteins, ensures proper folding, and performs essential posttranslational modifications (eg, N-linked glycosylation).  Rough endoplasmic reticulum dysfunction is implicated in cystic fibrosis (misfolded CFTR protein) and congenital glycosylation disorders.  The Golgi apparatus recognizes protein localization sequences and traffics them to their correct destinations throughout the cell.  Golgi apparatus dysfunction is implicated in I-cell disease (defective mannose-6 phosphate) tagging of acid hydrolase enzymes, resulting in lysosomes full of undegraded debris. ​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​

articles.title: Cell Biology: Purine And Pyrimidine Metabolism
articles.markdown: # Cell Biology: Purine And Pyrimidine Metabolism # Introduction Nucleotides are the monomeric building blocks of RNA and DNA.  They consist of the following 3 components: - **Nitrogenous base**:  Either 2-ring purines (adenine, guanine) or single-ring pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine; uracil in RNA). - **Pentose sugar backbone**:  Either ribose or deoxyribose.  The purine or pyrimidine base attached to sugar is called a **nucleoside**.  Ribonucleosides are used in RNA (eg, adenosine, guanosine, cytidine, uridine), whereas deoxyribonucleosides (eg, deoxyadenosine, deoxyguanosine, deoxycytidine, deoxythymidine \[usually written as just "thymidine"\]) are used in DNA. - **Phosphate groups**:  1, 2, or 3 phosphates.  A nucleoside with at least 1 phosphate is a **nucleotide** (eg, AMP, deoxyadenosine diphosphate \[dADP\]).  Only the triphosphate forms of nucleotides are incorporated into nucleic acids (eg, deoxyadenosine triphosphate \[dATP\] in DNA, ATP in RNA). Additional nitrogenous bases not incorporated into DNA or RNA but essential in metabolism include hypoxanthine (purine) and orotate (pyrimidine).  Their corresponding nucleosides are inosine and orotidine. This figure summarizes the composition of purine and pyrimidine nucleotides ((Figure 1)). Based on the sugar component, nucleotides are classified as ribonucleotides or deoxyribonucleotides.  Deoxyribonucleotides are used primarily for DNA synthesis, whereas ribonucleotides participate in RNA synthesis, as well as several other functions, including: - **Coenzymes and electron carriers** (eg, NAD⁺/NADH, CoA). - **Second messengers** (eg, cyclic AMP, cyclic GMP) used in various hormonal signaling pathways (eg, glucagon). - **Sources of energy** (eg, ATP, guanosine triphosphate \[GTP\]). - **Allosteric regulators**, which modulate enzyme activity in metabolism. # De novo nucleotide synthesis Purines (adenine, guanine) and pyrimidines (cytosine, uracil, thymine) can be synthesized de novo or via salvage pathways.  In both cases, the pentose sugar (ribose 5-phosphate) backbone is derived from glucose entering the pentose phosphate pathway ((Figure 2)).  Additional inputs include: - **Purines**:  Glutamine, glycine, and aspartate (nitrogen and/or carbon sources), N10\-formyltetrahydrofolate (carbon source derived from folate), and carbon dioxide. - **Pyrimidines**:  Aspartate, glutamine, and carbon dioxide. ## Ribonucleotide synthesis The first, common step in de novo purine and pyrimidine ribonucleotide synthesis (eg, AMP, GMP, uridine monophosphate \[UMP\]) is "activation" of ribose 5-phosphate to a high-energy form, **5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate (PRPP)**.  This activation is catalyzed by **PRPP synthetase**. Purine and pyrimidines are then synthesized from PRPP via distinct pathways. **Purine synthesis** ((Figure 3)) occurs in the cytosol of hepatocytes, where carbon and nitrogen atoms are added directly to the PRPP scaffold, forming inosine monophosphate (IMP) as the first purine nucleotide.  Key steps include: - **Committed, rate-limiting step**:  PRPP amidotransferase transfers an amide nitrogen from glutamine to PRPP, forming 5-phosphoribosylamine. - **Subsequent additions**:  Carbons and nitrogens are contributed by glycine (both C and N), N10\-formyltetrahydrofolate (2 carbons), aspartate (N), and carbon dioxide. - **Synthesis of IMP**:  IMP acts as a branch point; it can be converted to either AMP (requiring aspartate and GTP) or GMP (requiring glutamine and ATP). **Pyrimidine synthesis** ((Figure 4)) occurs mainly in the cytosol of hepatocytes, with one step in the inner mitochondrial membrane.  In contrast to purine synthesis, the pyrimidine ring is synthesized separately (as orotate) and then attached to PRPP to form UMP, the first pyrimidine nucleotide.  Key steps include: - **Committed, rate-limiting step**:  Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS II) synthesizes carbamoyl phosphate in the cytosol using glutamine, carbon dioxide, and ATP.  (CPS II is distinct from mitochondrial CPS I, which participates in the urea cycle and uses free ammonia.) - **Formation of orotate (orotic acid)**:  Aspartate transcarbamoylase and dihydroorotase generate dihydroorotate, which is oxidized by dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (the only mitochondrial enzyme in this pathway) to form orotate. - **Conversion to UMP**:  Orotate is attached to PRPP by orotate phosphoribosyltransferase in an irreversible step that releases pyrophosphate, producing orotidine monophosphate (OMP).  OMP is decarboxylated by OMP decarboxylase to UMP. Once the monophosphate forms of purine and pyrimidine nucleotides are synthesized, they are phosphorylated to the diphosphate and triphosphate forms by nucleoside monophosphate and diphosphate kinases (eg, AMP → ADP → ATP; UMP → UDP → UTP; GMP → GDP → GTP). The pyrimidine nucleotides for cytidine and thymidine are synthesized via distinct pathways: - **Cytidine nucleotides**:  UMP is phosphorylated to uridine diphosphate (UDP) and uridine triphosphate (UTP); and cytidine triphosphate (CTP) synthetase then converts UTP to CTP by glutamine-dependent amination.  Cytidine diphosphate (CDP) and cytidine monophosphate (CMP) are interconverted from these pools by specific kinases and phosphatases as needed. - **Thymidine nucleotides**:  Synthesis occurs from UMP only in the deoxyribonucleotide form for DNA synthesis, as described next. ## Deoxyribonucleotide synthesis Deoxyribonucleotides (used in DNA synthesis) originate from the conversion (reduction) of ribonucleotides.  This process is facilitated by **ribonucleotide reductase (RNR)** and other enzymes: - **RNR** acts on **ribonucleoside diphosphates** only (eg, ADP, UDP), converting them to deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates (eg, dADP, dUDP). - **Kinases** (eg, nucleoside diphosphate kinase) phosphorylate these deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates to form the triphosphate forms (eg, dCDP → dCTP). - **DNA polymerase** (DNA-synthesizing enzyme) acts on these triphosphate forms only (eg, dATP, dCTP) to synthesize DNA. ## Thymidine nucleotide synthesis Thymine is used only in DNA; therefore, thymidine nucleotides exist exclusively in the deoxyribonucleotide form.  They are derived from UMP as follows: - **RNR** reduces **UDP** (from de novo UMP) **into dUDP**, which then is phosphorylated to dUTP. - **UTP diphosphatase (dUTPase)** immediately hydrolyzes **dUTP into dUMP**.  This action keeps dUTP pools low, which is essential to preventing accidental misincorporation of dUTP within DNA (which can lead to fragility and breaks). - **Thymidylate synthase** methylates **dUMP into deoxythymidine monophosphate (dTMP)**.  This reaction uses N5,N10\-methylenetetrahydrofolate (N5,N10\-methylene-THF) reductase as the single-carbon donor, oxidizing THF to dihydrofolate.  This unique oxidation step, not seen in purine synthesis, links thymidine (and DNA) synthesis with folate metabolism.  In particular, the enzyme dihydrofolate reductase, which regenerates THF, and adequate folate intake are crucial for continued dTMP and DNA synthesis ((Figure 5)). ## Regulation of nucleotide synthesis Purine biosynthesis is tightly regulated at multiple levels. - **PRPP amidotransferase** (rate-limiting enzyme) is allosterically inhibited by AMP, GMP, and IMP. - **PRPP synthetase**, which generates PRPP from ribose 5-phosphate, is stimulated by inorganic phosphate (substrate) and inhibited by end products (eg, AMP, GMP, ADP, guanosine diphosphate \[GDP\]).  At branch points, AMP and GMP also provide negative feedback to limit their own synthesis from IMP. Pyrimidine synthesis is regulated via the inhibition and activation of CPS II, which catalyzes the rate-limiting step.  CPS II is activated by PRPP and inhibited by UTP through feedback inhibition. # Degradation and salvage pathways Degraded DNA or RNA results in the release of free bases and/or nucleosides, which can be salvaged to resynthesize purine or pyrimidine nucleotides.  A proportion of nucleotides (especially dietary) is not salvaged but instead further degraded in the liver to waste products. - **Pyrimidine bases** are ultimately degraded to water-soluble end products (eg, beta-alanine and beta-aminoisobutyrate) that are easily excreted or reused. - **Purine bases** are ultimately degraded to uric acid, an insoluble waste product.  Excess uric acid can accumulate in tissues; therefore, purine salvage is clinically critical compared to pyrimidine salvage. ## Purine salvage Purine salvage involves reattaching the purine base to PRPP via specific phosphoribosyltransferases: - **Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT)** attaches hypoxanthine to PRPP to produce IMP (which can be converted to AMP or GMP as described previously) or guanine to PRPP to form GMP. - **Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase** converts adenine to AMP. In addition, adenosine can uniquely be salvaged as a nucleoside (ie, not just at the adenine base stage) by adenosine kinase, which phosphorylates adenosine directly to form AMP. The salvage pathway provides an additional regulatory check on excess de novo purine synthesis by increasing PRPP consumption and generation of end products (AMP, GMP, IMP) that directly inhibit purine synthesis enzymes. ## Purine degradation Purine degradation ((Figure 6)) first begins with dephosphorylation of the nucleotides IMP, AMP, and GMP to the nucleoside form (inosine, adenosine, guanosine). - Inosine is degraded to hypoxanthine, whereas guanine is deaminated directly to xanthine.  Hypoxanthine and xanthine are sequentially oxidized by xanthine oxidase to **uric acid**, which is excreted in the urine. - Adenosine (nucleoside) can be deaminated by **adenosine deaminase (ADA)** to inosine, which is then converted to hypoxanthine → xanthine.  This is the nucleoside pathway. - Alternately, adenosine nucleotides (eg, ADP, ATP) can be dephosphorylated to AMP, which is then deaminated by AMP deaminase to form IMP.  IMP is then degraded (ie, inosine → hypoxanthine → xanthine).  This is the nucleotide pathway. Uric acid is the final product of the pathway because humans lack uricase (urate oxidase).  At physiologic pH, uric acid circulates as a more soluble monosodium urate salt that is filtered at the glomerulus.  The majority is reabsorbed, with a small portion excreted in urine. ## Pyrimidine degradation and salvage Pyrimidine salvage occurs through nucleoside kinases (eg, thymidine kinase, uridine-cytidine kinase), which phosphorylate pyrimidine nucleosides back to their nucleotide monophosphate forms. Degradation of cytosine and uracil yields beta-alanine, whereas degradation of thymine yields beta-aminoisobutyrate; both products are easily excreted in urine or repurposed in intermediary metabolism.  As a result, defects in pyrimidine salvage and degradation are rare and generally less clinically significant than purine salvage deficiencies. # Clinical applications Genetic deficiencies of nucleotide salvage or degradation enzymes lead to impaired DNA synthesis or buildup of toxic end products, underlying characteristic syndromes.  In addition, medications targeting nucleotide synthesis are often therapeutic targets in the treatment of tumors, infections, and autoimmune diseases (eg, rheumatoid arthritis), which are associated with pathologic growth and replication of tumor or foreign cells. ## Defects in purine pathways - **Lesch-Nyhan syndrome** ((Figure 7)):  Caused by complete HGPRT deficiency, characterized by inability to salvage the purine bases guanine and hypoxanthine.  Guanine and hypoxanthine accumulate along with PRPP, leading to loss of inhibitory checks on de novo purine synthesis.  De novo purine synthesis increases, and, as bases are degraded, uric acid accumulation results.  Key features of this X-linked condition include gouty arthritis, nephrolithiasis, choreoathetosis, and self-mutilating behavior. - **Gout** ((Figure 8)):  Occurs due to the precipitation of excess monosodium urate crystals in joints, which triggers an intense inflammatory response and associated pain.  Causes include increased purine synthesis (eg, partial HGPRT deficiency, leading to increased de novo synthesis); increased cellular turnover, resulting in increased purine degradation (eg, leukemia, tumor lysis syndrome); and/or excess dietary purines (eg, meats, alcohol).  It can also occur due to the kidneys' underexcretion of uric acid (eg, renal insufficiency, use of diuretics) - **ADA deficiency**:  Results from the inability to degrade adenosine, leading to severe combined immunodeficiency.  Ineffective adenosine degradation leads to toxic adenosine accumulation and dATP formation within lymphocytes (where ADA is most highly active).  Excess dATP inhibits RNR, preventing DNA formation and cell division, leading to marked lymphopenia. ## Defects in pyrimidine pathways - **Orotic aciduria**:  Caused by a deficiency of UMP synthase (which catalyzes the conversion of orotate to UMP), leading to inhibited DNA synthesis.  Patients have megaloblastic anemia unresponsive to vitamin B12 or folate supplementation, growth delay, and elevated urinary orotic acid without hyperammonemia (because CPS I activity is preserved).  Oral uridine supplementation bypasses the defect as uridine is converted to UMP via nucleoside kinases. ## Medications affecting purine metabolism - **Allopurinol and febuxostat**:  Inhibit xanthine oxidase to reduce production of xanthine and uric acid ((Figure 9)). - **Azathioprine**:  Converted intracellularly to 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP), a "false purine" analogue of IMP acted on by HGPRT to form active metabolites (eg, thio-IMP), thereby blocking purine (and therefore DNA/RNA) synthesis.  Coadministration of xanthine oxidase inhibitors, which prevent 6-MP degradation ((Figure 10)), amplifies this effect.  6-MP also directly inhibits PRPP amidotransferase, the rate-limiting step of purine synthesis, by mimicking the feedback effect of IMP ((Figure 11)). - **Rasburicase**:  A recombinant form of urate oxidase (absent in humans), which converts uric acid to the more soluble allantoin.  It is administered during chemotherapy for cancers with rapid cell turnover (eg, leukemia) to prevent uric acid buildup and tumor lysis syndrome. ## Medications blocking pyrimidine synthesis - **5-Fluorouracil**:  Acts as a pyrimidine analogue that irreversibly inhibits thymidylate synthase, blocking dTMP synthesis. ## Medications affecting both purine and pyrimidine metabolism - **Sulfonamide antibiotics**:  Block bacterial folate synthesis, which prevents the production of tetrahydrofolate and inhibits purine and pyrimidine synthesis. - **Methotrexate**:  Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, the enzyme needed to regenerate tetrahydrofolate, thereby halting purine synthesis (at the formyl-THF step) and pyrimidine synthesis (at the step of dTMP formation via thymidylate synthase). - **Nucleoside analogues**:  Block viral replication by integrating into viral DNA ((Figure 12)).  Acyclovir is a guanine nucleoside analogue that is phosphorylated first by viral thymidine kinase and then by host kinases to the active triphosphate form.  Once incorporated into viral DNA, it causes chain termination.  Zidovudine mimics thymidine; it can be phosphorylated by host kinase to the triphosphate form, where it inhibits HIV reverse transcriptase. - **Hydroxyurea**:  Inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, preventing conversion of ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides.  This blocks both purine and pyrimidine deoxynucleotide synthesis. # Summary Purine and pyrimidine metabolism provides the essential building blocks for DNA and RNA, integrating inputs from amino acids, folate derivatives, carbon dioxide, and the pentose phosphate pathway.  Purines are synthesized directly on a 5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate (PRPP) scaffold to form inosine monophosphate, whereas pyrimidines are built separately as orotate before being attached to PRPP to yield uridine monophosphate.  Regulation occurs through feedback inhibition at key enzymes (PRPP amidotransferase for purines, carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II for pyrimidines), whereas salvage pathways recycle bases (clinically important for purines to prevent toxic accumulation of uric acid).  Defects in these pathways or in the therapeutic targeting of their enzymes underlie a range of important clinical syndromes and treatments of neoplastic, infectious, and immunoproliferative disorders. ​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​

articles.title: Cell Biology: Overview Of Cell Structure
articles.markdown:
# Cell Biology: Overview Of Cell Structure

# Introduction

Cellular architecture has many important correlations to human health and disease.  This article outlines the structure and functional organization of the cell, with details covered in separate articles.

# Cell organization

Human cells are highly compartmentalized, with each structure performing specific functions.  The nucleus contains and regulates access to the genetic code.  The cytoplasm surrounds the nucleus and serves as the site of translation, metabolism, and signaling.  Within the cytoplasm, membrane-bound organelles have specific roles in biosynthesis, degradation, and energy production.

## Nucleus

The nucleus is the command center of the cell, containing the nuclear genome and regulating gene expression.  It consists of the following:

-   The **nuclear envelope**, the outer membrane of the nucleus, is a double-membrane structure perforated by small pores that regulate transport between the nuclear matrix and the cytoplasm (eg, of RNAs, nuclear proteins, and transcription factors).  Its outer membrane is contiguous with the rough endoplasmic reticulum, which has ribosomes attaches to its cytoplasmic surface.
-   The **nucleosome** contains DNA wrapped around histone octamers (chromatin).  Chromatin, which helps modulate gene transcription (DNA to RNA), exists as unpacked euchromatin (transcriptionally active) and densely packed heterochromatin (transcriptionally inactive).
-   The **nucleolus** is a dense intranuclear region where ribosomal RNA (rRNA) is transcribed and ribosomal subunits are assembled.  Copies of the 45S pre-rRNA gene are arranged in clusters (nucleolar organizing regions) on multiple chromosomes; these regions come together in the nucleus to form the nucleolus.  RNA polymerase I functions exclusively within the nucleolus to transcribe the 45S pre-rRNA gene into a single transcript that is subsequently processed into mature 18S, 5.8S, and 28S rRNAs.   Ribosomal proteins, which are synthesized in the cytoplasm, are transported into the nucleolus, where they combine with rRNA to form immature 40S and 60S subunits.  These subunits are then shuttled via nuclear pores to the cytoplasm, where they ultimately participate in protein synthesis.
-   **Nucleoplasm**, the internal fluid matrix of the nucleus, provides the medium for diffusion and contains:
    -   Nucleotides (building blocks of DNA and RNA), S-phase enzymes (eg, DNA polymerase, helicase, topoisomerase), DNA repair enzymes, and DNA-associated proteins (eg, transcription factors).
    -   Pre-mRNA processing enzymes (eg, spliceosome proteins, poly-A polymerase, 5′ methyl capping transferases).
    -   Cell cycle checkpoint proteins (eg, cyclins, cyclin-dependent kinases) that participate in cell cycle regulation.

## Cytoplasm

Whereas gene expression and genome maintenance occur in the nucleus, most biosynthetic reactions, protein translation, and intracellular signaling occur in the cytoplasm, both in the cytosol and in membrane-bound organelles.  The cytoplasm contains:

-   The **cytosol**, which is the aqueous intracellular solution where many biochemical reactions (eg, glycolysis, nucleotide synthesis), RNA processing and degradation, and signal transduction (eg, second messengers) take place.
-   **Free ribosomes**, which are complexes of rRNA and protein that synthesize soluble cytosolic proteins.
-   **Cytosolic inclusions**, which are normal temporary storage compartments for nutrients (eg, glycogen, lipid droplets) or secretory granules for preformed bioactive mediators (eg, histamine granules, neurotransmitter vesicles).

## Subcellular organelles

Organelles are membrane-bound or protein-complex compartments with specialized roles.  They include:

-   Secretory pathway organelles (**endoplasmic reticulum** and **Golgi apparatus**) for synthesis, posttranslational modification, and trafficking of membrane-bound or secreted proteins to their correct location.
-   Disposal pathway organelles (**proteasomes**, **lysosomes**, **endosomes**, **peroxisomes**) for degradation of proteins, damaged organelles, cellular debris, and ingested pathogens.
-   **Mitochondria**, which contain their own genomes (mitochondrial DNA) and ribosomes, for oxidative phosphorylation, fatty acid beta-oxidation, and apoptosis regulation via cytochrome c release.

## Cytoskeleton

The cytoskeleton is an array of filamentous proteins that determine cell shape, motility, and intracellular transport.  It includes:

-   **Microfilaments** (actin) for cell motility and shape shifting.
-   **Intermediate filaments** (various proteins) for structural reinforcement.
-   **Microtubules** (tubulin) for intracellular transport, cell division (eg, mitotic spindle), and cilia.

## Cell surface

The cell surface consists of the plasma membrane and associated structures that mediate barrier function, molecular transport, and cell surface signaling.  It includes the:

-   **Glycocalyx**, which is an outer carbohydrate-rich coat that protects cells from chemical or mechanical injuries (eg, extracellular enzymes, shear stress), mediates adhesion, and regulates innate immune recognition (eg, ABO antigens).
-   **Plasma membrane**, which is a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins.  Its structure is described by the fluid mosaic model, in which lipids and proteins can move laterally within the membrane.  The relative proprtions of proteins and lipids vary according to function (eg, protein-rich membranes support transport and enzymatic activity; lipid-rich membranes support insulation).  Each phospholipid molecule is amphipathic, with a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic fatty acid tails.  The hydrophilic heads face the extracellular fluid and cytosol, whereas the hydrophobic tails are directed inward, forming the core of the bilayer.  This arrangement allows the cell membrane to function as a selectively permeable barrier.
    -   Cholesterol is interspersed within the membrane and modulates membrane fluidity and stability. 
    -   Glycolipids are present in smaller amounts, particularly in the outer leaflet.
    -   Membrane proteins may be integral or peripheral and function as channels, transporters, receptors, enzymes, and junctional proteins (eg, occludins, cadherins, connexins).
-   **Membrane microdomains**, which are tiny regions for receptor clustering, endocytosis, or focused signaling compartmentalization.  They include:
    -   Lipid rafts (eg, Fc epsilon receptor–IgE \[FCεR-IgE\] clustering in mast cells).
    -   Clathrin-coated pits (eg, internalization of transferrin).
    -   Caveolae (eg, insulin receptor and GLUT4 translocation).

# Integrated systems

Most cell processes span multiple locations.  Some examples are listed.

## Metabolic pathways

Major biochemical pathways have dual cytosolic and mitochondrial phases:

-   **Amino acid catabolism** involves transamination in the cytosol (eg, alanine transaminase) and deamination in mitochondria (eg, glutamate dehydrogenase) to release free ammonia.
-   The **urea cycle** involves mitochondrial enzymes (eg, ornithine transcarbamylase) that initiate ammonia detoxification and cytosolic enzymes (eg, arginase) that complete the conversion of ammonia to urea for excretion.
-   **Gluconeogenesis** begins in mitochondria (eg, pyruvate carboxylase) and continues in cytosol (eg, phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase) to generate free glucose.
-   **Heme synthesis** involves mitochondrial (eg, aminolevulinic acid synthase) and cytosolic steps.
-   **Pyrimidine synthesis** occurs primarily in the cytosol but requires a key mitochondrial enzyme (dihydroorotate dehydrogenase).
-   **Beta-oxidation** involves fatty acyl-CoA activation in the cytosol, transport into mitochondria via the carnitine shuttle, and beta-oxidation within the mitochondrial matrix.  Separately, very-long-chain fatty acids are initially shortened in peroxisomes before entering mitochondria.

Metabolic processes confined to the cytosol include **glycolysis** and the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP).   Red blood cells (RBCs), which lack nuclei and mitochondria, use glycolysis to generate ATP and the oxidative phase of the PPP to generate NADPH, which regenerates reduced glutathione for antioxidant defense; the nonoxidative phase of the PPP involves transketolase, which uses thiamine (vitamin B1) as a cofactor to shuttle 2-carbon fragments between sugar molecules.  Lack of mitochondrial metabolism makes RBCs uniquely susceptible to pyruvate kinase deficiency (hemolysis due to ATP depletion) and glucose-6-phosphate-dehydrogenase deficiency (hemolysis due to hemoglobin oxidation).

## Corticosteroid hormones

Corticosteroid hormone **synthesis** (eg, cholesterol to pregnenolone) begins in the mitochondria and then proceeds largely in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (eg, additional modifications to produce cortisol, aldosterone, testosterone, estrogen, and others).  Corticosteroid hormone **signaling** begins with cytosolic receptors, followed by nuclear translocation to regulate gene transcription.

## Apoptosis

Apoptosis begins in the mitochondria (eg, cytochrome c release), amplifies in the cytoplasm (eg, caspase cascade), and culminates in the nucleus (eg, DNA fragmentation, chromatin condensation.

## Gene expression

Gene expression begins with transcription and pre-mRNA processing in the nucleus, followed by translation of mRNA by cytoplasmic ribosomes (for soluble cytosolic proteins) or rough endoplasmic reticulum–bound ribosomes (for secreted or membrane-bound proteins)

## Cell cycle

Cyclins are synthesized in the cytoplasm and translocate to the nucleus at key transitions in the cell cycle to activate cyclin-dependent kinases.  For instance, cyclin B accumulates in the cytoplasm during the G<sub>2</sub> phase and enters the nucleus only at the M phase (mitosis) to trigger nuclear envelope breakdown.

# Summary

The nucleus is the central regulatory hub for gene expression and cell cycle control, which are coordinated via chromatin states, the nucleolus (ribosomal RNA), and nuclear-cytoplasmic transport.  The cytoplasm contains free ribosomes dedicated to synthesizing soluble cytosolic proteins, whereas specialized inclusions provide temporary storage for nutrients or bioactive compounds.  Membrane-bound organelles are organized into distinct systems:  Secretory organelles (endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus) process and traffic secreted or membrane-bound proteins, disposal organelles (lysosomes, proteasomes, and peroxisomes) degrade macromolecules and damaged structures, and mitochondria drive energy production and regulate apoptosis.  The cytoskeleton maintains cell shape, facilitates intracellular transport, and enables mitotic division.  At the cell surface, the glycocalyx and plasma membrane microdomains enable receptor signaling.  Many essential cellular processes span multiple compartments.

​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​​‌​​​‌​​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌

articles.title: Cell Biology: Mitochondria
