articles.markdown: # Cell Biology: Mitochondria # Introduction Mitochondria are double-membraned organelles best known for generating ATP via oxidative phosphorylation.  However, they also regulate apoptosis and many aspects of metabolism.  Mitochondria are dynamic structures that continuously undergo movement, fission, and fusion in response to cellular energy demands.  Dysfunctions in mitochondrial processes underlie several diseases, and various drugs exhibit mitochondrial toxicity. # Mitochondrial structure Mitochondria have a unique architecture that supports compartmentalization of their functions ((Figure 1)): - **Outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM)**:  Contains porins and is permeable to small molecules.  This membrane also contains proteins that regulate mitochondrial apoptosis and hosts the rate-limiting enzyme of corticosteroid hormone synthesis. - **Intermembrane space (IMS)**:  Serves as a reservoir for protons (which are ultimately used for energy production) and signaling proteins. - **Inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM)**:  Functions as a primary site for energy production through the electron transport chain (ETC) complexes and ATP synthase, which are described in more detail later in this article.  Its highly folded structure (into cristae) increases surface area. - **Mitochondrial matrix**:  Contains mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), ribosomes, and enzymes of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and fatty acid beta-oxidation, with long-chain fatty acids transported into mitochondria via the carnitine shuttle.  The mitochondrial matrix also hosts the rate-limiting enzymes of heme biosynthesis (eg, delta-aminolevulinate synthase) ((Figure 2)) and the urea cycle (eg, ornithine transcarbamylase), which detoxifies ammonia ((Figure 3)).  It contains significant calcium stores (primarily as calcium phosphonate), which helps the endoplasmic reticulum to buffer intracellular calcium. # Mitochondrial genome Each mitochondrion typically has 5-10 copies of a circular **mitochondrial genome**, which resembles bacterial plasmids.  The mtDNA encodes 13 of the 90 subunits of the ETC complexes.  It is inherited maternally and lacks histones and robust DNA repair mechanisms, making it vulnerable to mutations and deletions that accumulate with age or oxidative stress. However, most mitochondrial proteins (99% of ~1,700 proteins) are encoded by **nuclear DNA** and imported posttranslationally into the mitochondria via translocase complexes. # Bioenergetics and oxidative phosphorylation The primary function of mitochondria is to generate ATP through oxidative phosphorylation, which couples the oxidation of metabolic substrates to the phosphorylation of ADP ((Figure 4)): - **TCA (Krebs) cycle**:  Located in the matrix, this cycle oxidizes acetyl-CoA (from glucose, fatty acids, or amino acids) to produce NADH and FADH2. - **ETC**:  Composed of **complexes I-IV** in the IMM, the ETC receives electrons from NADH and FADH2 (eg, from the TCA cycle and fatty acid beta-oxidation), which are transferred through the complexes, pumping protons into the IMS and creating a proton gradient. - **ATP synthesis**:  The resulting electrochemical gradient (proton motive force) drives protons through **ATP synthase (complex V)**, producing ATP. Leakage of electrons, particularly at complexes I and III, can produce reactive oxygen species (ROSs). # Mitochondrial dynamics: Fusion, fission, and mitophagy Although they are often depicted as solitary organelles, mitochondria constantly undergo fusion (joining) and fission (splitting), which are important processes for quality control, adaptation to metabolic demand, and cell cycle progression. ## Fusion Fusion relieves stress (eg, oxidized ETC proteins, depleted mtDNA) by allowing partially damaged mitochondria to mix their contents with healthy ones.  This can prevent mitochondrial apoptosis by restoring energy production and OMM integrity.  Inherited defects in fusion proteins (eg, Mfn-2, Opa-1) result in abnormally small or fragmented mitochondria and contribute to conditions such as early-onset peripheral neuropathy (Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease) and autosomal dominant optic atrophy. ## Fission Fission facilitates mitosis, distribution, and removal of aged or dysfunctional mitochondria.  Inherited defects in fission proteins (eg, Drp-1) result in abnormally enlarged but hypofunctional mitochondria, leading to neurodegeneration (eg, hypotonia, seizures, optic atrophy). ## Mitophagy Mitophagy is a specialized form of autophagy that eliminates dysfunctional mitochondria, preventing the accumulation of ROSs and mutated mtDNA.  This process involves PTEN-induced kinase-1 (**PINK1**) and **Parkin**, which mark dysfunctional mitochondria for degradation through a ubiquitin-mediated pathway (activated by loss of mitochondrial membrane potential).  Some forms of familial early-onset Parkinson disease are related to biallelic loss of PINK1 or Parkin. # Mitochondria in apoptosis and cell signaling Mitochondria are central mediators of the **intrinsic apoptosis pathway** ((Figure 5)).  With cellular stress or DNA damage, the OMM becomes permeabilized, releasing the following pro-apoptotic factors: - **Cytochrome c**, when released into the cytosol, binds to Apaf-1 and procaspase-9, forming the apoptosome and initiating caspase-dependent apoptosis. - **Bcl-2 family proteins** regulate OMM permeabilization.  Pro-apoptotic (Bax, Bak) and anti-apoptotic (Bcl-2, Bcl-xL) proteins balance cell survival and death. Mitochondria also participate in calcium signaling, redox homeostasis, and innate immunity.  For example, mtDNA released during cellular damage can activate inflammasomes or stimulate type I interferon responses, linking mitochondrial dysfunction to chronic inflammation. # Mitochondrial biogenesis and regulation Mitochondrial biogenesis refers to the growth and assembly of mitochondria in response to cellular needs.  The primary regulator is peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α), which interacts with transcription factors to upregulate mitochondrial genes.  Biogenesis is stimulated by exercise, cold exposure, and certain hormones (eg, thyroid hormone, catecholamines).  Dysregulation is implicated in aging, metabolic syndrome, and muscle wasting. # Clinical correlates ## Mitochondrial disorders Defects in mitochondrial-genome encoded proteins affect the most energetically active tissues (especially the brain, retina, and skeletal muscle).  Symptoms increase with metabolic stress (eg, infection).  Disorders include the following: - Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fiber (**MERRF**) is characterized by myoclonus, seizures, and cerebellar ataxia.  Muscle histology shows compensatory proliferation of defective mitochondria, lending a ragged appearance to the sarcolemma ((Figure 6)). - Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes (**MELAS**) manifests with recurrent cerebral metabolic infarctions (ie, neuron death despite adequate perfusion) resembling acute stroke but with neuroimaging showing lesions that do not respect vascular territories. - **Leber hereditary optic neuropathy** presents in late adolescence with acute or subacute painless central vision loss due to optic nerve atrophy. - **Kearns-Sayre syndrome** involves large mtDNA deletions affecting multiple ETC subunits.  It presents with extraocular muscle dysfunction (ophthalmoplegia) and retinal degeneration.  The unusual combination of external and internal ocular findings is highly specific. These disorders follow a maternal inheritance pattern ((Figure 7)); mtDNA is normally transmitted exclusively from the mother to all offspring (paternal mitochondria do not usually survive in the ovum following fertilization).  Clinical expression varies due to heteroplasmy, which is the proportion of mutated to normal mitochondria within each cell. Defects in nuclear encoded mitochondrial proteins include the following: - **Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency** results in an inability to convert pyruvate to acetyl-CoA to enter the TCA cycle, forcing cells to rely on anaerobic glycolysis for energy production.  It presents with lactic acidosis, neurodevelopmental delay, hypotonia, and elevated alanine starting in infancy (due to transamination of excess pyruvate via hepatic alanine transferase). - **Leigh syndrome** (subacute necrotizing encephalomyelopathy) involves defects in ATP synthase (complex V) and other ETC subunits.  It presents in early life with psychomotor regression, hypotonia, brainstem dysfunction, and bilateral symmetric basal ganglia lesions. - Multiple mitochondrial dysfunctions syndrome (**MMDS**) involves mutations in iron-sulfur cluster proteins (essential cofactors for parts of ETC complexes).  It results in severe encephalopathy, hypotonia, respiratory failure, and death, typically in infancy. - mtDNA depletion syndrome (**MDS**) involves defects in mtDNA polymerases or repair enzymes, leading to severe reductions in mtDNA copy number.  Expressivity is highly variable and may include lactic acidosis, encephalomyopathy, and liver failure. These disorders display nuclear inheritance (eg, autosomal recessive, autosomal dominant, X-linked). Secondary mitochondrial dysfunction occurs in common disorders not primarily due to mitochondrial gene mutations.  They include: - **Parkinson disease**:  Sometimes associated with impaired mitophagy (PINK1 and Parkin mutations). - **Type 2 diabetes mellitus**:  Associated with altered mitochondrial metabolism and biogenesis. - **Cancer**:  Where metabolic reprogramming (Warburg effect) may involve mitochondrial function. - **Aging**:  Where accumulation of mtDNA mutations and increased ROSs contribute to cellular senescence. In addition, although not specifically mitochondrial disorders, defects in fatty acid transport or beta-oxidation impair mitochondrial energy production.  Beta-oxidation yields FADH2 and NADH for ATP production and generates acetyl-CoA for use in the TCA or ketone body production. - **Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency** is the most common enzymatic defect in fatty acid beta-oxidation.  Patients may remain asymptomatic until a significant fast, when they are unable to oxidize fatty acids to maintain glucose and ketone body (eg, acetoacetate) production (eg, by the liver).  Therefore, manifestations of MCAD deficiency include hypoketotic hypoglycemia (eg, undetectable acetoacetate), mild hepatomegaly, and liver dysfunction. - **Primary carnitine deficiency** results in fatty acids not being transported into mitochondria as acyl-carnitine (carnitine shuttle), preventing their beta-oxidation to acetyl-CoA.  As a result, cardiac and skeletal myocytes cannot generate ATP from fatty acids, and the liver cannot synthesize ketone bodies (eg, acetoacetate), resulting in myopathy, cardiomyopathy, and hypoketotic hypoglycemia. ## Mitochondrial toxins **ETC inhibitors** directly antagonize respiratory complexes I-V, resulting in reduced ATP production despite adequate oxygen delivery (eg, cellular dysoxia).  Well-known ETC poisons include the following: - **Cyanide (CN)** inhibits cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV).  Patients exhibit a rapid onset of neurologic changes, lactic acidosis, and cardiovascular collapse.  Venous oxygen saturation is abnormally high (due to the inability of tissues to utilize oxygen), producing a cherry-red skin hue. - **Carbon monoxide (CO)** also inhibits cytochrome c oxidase (while simultaneously binding hemoglobin and outcompeting oxygen).  CO toxicity presents similarly to CN poisoning but progresses more gradually, with headache, confusion, lactic acidosis, and cardiac dysrhythmias.  Patients also have a pinkish hue with abnormally elevated venous oxygen saturation. - **Metformin** inhibits NADH dehydrogenase (complex I) and pyruvate decarboxylase ((Figure 8)).  Patients can develop spontaneous lactic acidosis when drug levels accumulate due to renal insufficiency, particularly in the setting of tissue hypoperfusion (eg, heart failure exacerbation). - **Propofol** also inhibits NADH dehydrogenase (in addition to fatty acid beta-oxidation enzymes).  Propofol infusion syndrome (seen with prolonged, high doses) can produce lactic acidosis, fulminant rhabdomyolysis (eg, elevated creatine kinase, hyperkalemia, and renal failure due to myoglobinuria), and cardiovascular collapse. - **Statins** block coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone) synthesis by inhibiting mevalonate production.  Coenzyme Q10 shuttles electrons between complexes I, II, and III.  Manifestations range from dose-dependent statin myopathy (eg, myalgias, fatiguability) to frank rhabdomyolysis and muscle necrosis. - Several drugs impair synthesis of mtDNA or ribosomes, leading to impaired replication and expression of ETC proteins.  They include the following: - **mtDNA replication inhibitors** include several nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (**NRTIs**) used for treatment of HIV (eg, zidovudine, stavudine, didanosine, zalcitabine).  NRTIs inhibit mtDNA polymerase (DNA polymerase gamma), blocking mitochondrial replication and expression of ETC proteins.  NRTI toxicity presents with lactic acidosis, myopathy, peripheral neuropathy, and lipodystrophy. - **Mitochondrial ribosome inhibitors** include antibiotics that block mitochondrial protein synthesis due to similarities with bacterial ribosomes.  **Linezolid** mitochondrial toxicity can manifest with lactic acidosis and peripheral neuropathy.  **Chloramphenicol** mitochondrial toxicity occurs in neonates (eg, third trimester exposure) due to immature hepatic glucuronidation and resulting drug accumulation; it manifests with cyanosis, flaccidity, and cardiovascular collapse (gray baby syndrome).  **Aminoglycoside** (eg, amikacin, tobramycin) mitochondrial toxicity manifests with permanent sensorineural hearing damage. Uncouplers permeabilize the IMM to protons.  As a result, protons flow back into the matrix instead of driving ATP synthase and the stored energy from the proton gradient is dissipated as heat.  Pharmacologic uncouplers include: - **2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP)** is a weight loss ("fat burner") agent that has largely been banned.  It caused uncontrolled hyperthermia, lactic acidosis, and death in some users, leading to its withdrawal.  However, DNP is still occasionally abused, especially among bodybuilders and individuals with extreme weight loss behavior (eg, anorexia nervosa). - **Aspirin** (and other salicylates) can act as an uncoupler in **overdose**.  Salicylate poisoning manifests with paradoxic hyperthermia (ie, instead of antipyretic effect) and combined metabolic acidosis (from lactate accumulation) and primary respiratory alkalosis (from direct stimulation of the brainstem respiratory center). Thermogenin (uncoupling protein 1) is a physiologic uncoupler found in brown fat, which enables heat production (especially important in neonates, who have limited muscle mass for shivering). # Summary Mitochondria are dynamic, double-membraned organelles responsible for oxidative phosphorylation, intermediary metabolism, and regulation of apoptosis.  Maternally inherited mitochondrial DNA encodes a small minority of electron transport chain proteins, whereas most mitochondrial proteins are derived from the nuclear genome.  In addition to energy production, mitochondria also control the intrinsic apoptosis pathway by preventing cytochrome c from being released into the cytosol.  Mitochondrial fusion and fission prevent accumulation of damaged components and ensure equitable inheritance during cell division.  Mitochondrial genetic defects result in several disorders, generally sharing a clinical picture of spontaneous lactic acidosis, myopathy, and neurodegeneration (eg, brain, retina).  Various drugs and poisons exhibit mitochondrial toxicity, including electron transport chain inhibitors (eg, cyanide, metformin), biogenesis disruptors (eg, antiviral nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, ribosomal inhibitor antibiotics), and uncouplers. ​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌

articles.title: Cell Biology: Junctions And Polarity
articles.markdown: # Cell Biology: Junctions And Polarity # Introduction The 6 types of cell junctions ((Figure 1)), arranged from tightest (barrier-forming) to loosest (communicating), are as follows: - Tight junctions (cell-cell) form a circumferential seal between cell apices. - Adherens junctions (cell-cell) form a belt below tight junctions. - Desmosomes (cell-cell) anchor the lateral surface of cells to each other. - Hemidesmosomes (cell-matrix) attach the basal surface to the basement membrane. - Focal adhesion complexes (FACs) (cell-matrix) are a transient attachment for migratory cells. - Gap junctions (cell-cell) connect cells directly through their cytoplasm. These junctions coordinate adhesion and communication between cells, organizing them into continuous layers that define tissue structure.  This organization establishes cell polarity, which maintains the ordered architecture required for normal tissue physiology and whose loss may lead to disorganized growth and cancer development. # Cell junctions ## Tight junctions (cell-cell) Tight junctions (zona occludens) form a **continuous seal** around the apical circumference of epithelial and endothelial cells, creating a barrier impermeable to water, solutes, and ions (eg, blood-brain barrier, blood-testis barrier, gastric epithelium).  They are composed of transmembrane proteins (claudins and occludins) that dimerize, zipping neighboring cells together. Tight junctions can be disrupted by inflammatory cytokines (eg, TNF-α, IL-1β), bacterial toxins (eg, *Clostridium perfringens*), proteases, and reactive oxygen species.  These noxious stimuli downregulate claudin and occludin expression, thereby facilitating leukocyte migration to sites of injury or infection.  However, the resulting increase in paracellular permeability contributes to edema formation (third spacing) in inflammatory states (eg, burns, sepsis, pancreatitis, acute respiratory distress syndrome). ## Adherens junctions (cell-cell) Adherens junctions (zona adherens) are typically located just below tight junctions, near the apices.  Like tight junctions, they form a **continuous belt** of contact between neighboring epithelial or endothelial cells.  However, unlike tight junctions they do not form a waterproof barrier.  Instead, they function as strong but **dynamic anchors** to allow flexibility during tissue remodeling (eg, embryogenesis, wound healing).  **Reversible** assembly and disassembly are made possible using calcium-dependent protein complexes (eg, cadherins, beta-catenin). Adherens junction disruption is seen in cancer invasion and metastasis, when malignant epithelial cells detach from each other and migrate through underlying tissue planes.  This loss of cohesion is often driven by downregulation of E-cadherin, an adhesion molecule that maintains epithelial architecture.  Its reduction destabilizes cell-cell contacts and promotes the transition to a more motile, mesenchymal phenotype—a process called epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition.  It is seen in a wide range of epithelial malignancies, particularly breast, gastric, pancreatic, and colorectal adenocarcinomas.  In these tumors, low E-cadherin expression is a poor prognostic marker. ## Desmosomes (cell-cell) In contrast to the continuous band formed by tight junctions and adherens junctions, desmosomes form **discrete** intercellular junctions that attach the lateral surfaces of adjacent cells together, providing **tensile strength** to tissues subjected to repetitive mechanical stress (eg, epidermis, myocardium).  Each desmosome is a multiprotein complex that spans the space between 2 neighboring cells and links their cytoskeletons.  On the intracellular side, **intermediate filaments** (eg, keratin in epithelial cells, desmin in muscle cells) anchor a dense cytoplasmic plaque composed of adaptor proteins (eg, desmoplakins).  These plaques connect to transmembrane **cadherins** (eg, desmogleins), which project into the intercellular space and bind to their counterparts on the adjacent cell ((Figure 2)). In **pemphigus vulgaris**, autoantibodies form against desmogleins 1 and 3, which causes keratinocytes within the same cell layer to separate from each other (ie, acantholysis) and form **intraepidermal blisters** ((Figure 3)).  The blisters are **flaccid** because cells easily pull apart from their neighbors, so pressure and fluid do not accumulate underneath.  Immunofluorescence reveals net-like IgG deposition because it highlights desmosomes along the lateral surfaces of cells ((Figure 4)). ## Hemidesmosomes (cell-matrix) Hemidesmosomes form **discrete** junctions that attach the basal surface of epithelial or endothelial cells to their basement membrane.  They are termed *hemi*\-desmosomes because, unlike desmosomes that link 2 adjacent cells, hemidesmosomes connect a cell to the **extracellular matrix** (ECM) using integrin receptors (α6β4) that bind to basement membrane proteins (eg, laminin) via linking proteins (eg, BP180, BP230, plectin) In **bullous pemphigoid**, autoantibodies form against hemidesmosomal proteins (BP180 and BP230), causing the entire epidermis to separate from the underlying dermis and form **subepidermal blisters** ((Figure 5)).  The blisters are **tense** because the overlying skin layers are intact, allowing fluid and pressure to build up underneath.  Immunofluorescence reveals linear IgG deposition because it highlights hemidesmosomes along the basal lamina ((Figure 6)). Similarly, some forms of **epidermolysis bullosa simplex** result from inherited mutations in hemidesmosomal proteins (eg, plectin, BP230).  These mutations produce a similar phenotype to bullous pemphigoid (eg, subepidermal blistering with minor trauma), but the disease is present from birth and does not involve autoantibodies. ## Focal adhesion complexes (cell-matrix) FACs are **transient** basal anchoring structures that form between integrins (aLβ2, α5β1, αvβ3) and ECM proteins (eg, fibronectin, collagen, laminin).  They can be conceptualized as weaker, short-lived counterparts to hemidesmosomes.  FACs are especially prominent in migratory cells (eg, fibroblasts, circulating leukocytes) that need to intermittently tether and release from the ECM during chemotaxis, wound healing, and immune surveillance. Disruption of FACs is involved in **leukocyte adhesion defect** (CD18 \[β2\] integrin defect), which prevents circulating leukocytes from attaching and migrating through the vessel wall to respond to infection.  Manifestations include delayed wound healing, recurrent bacterial infections, persistent neutrophilic leukocytosis, and minimal or absent pus at sites of infection (due to failed neutrophil migration). ## Gap junctions (cell-cell) Gap junctions are cytoplasmic communications formed by **connexins**, which assemble into hexameric channels (connexons).  They allow for direct exchange of ions, metabolites, and small signaling molecules (eg, second messengers such as IP3 and cAMP).  They coordinate electrical and metabolic **coupling** between cells, so they can function in a **synchronized** manner (eg, helping to propagate action potentials between cardiac myocytes). Disruption of gap junctions is involved in genetic ventricular arrhythmias (eg, connexin 43 mutations) and congenital sensorineural deafness (eg, connexin 26 mutations), which impact cell-cell conduction in cardiomyocytes and cochlear hair cells, respectively. # Multijunctional complexes The junctions above localize together in superstructures that integrate mechanical adhesion, barrier function, and intercellular communication. ## Apical junctional complex The apical junction complex (AJC) consists of: - Tight junctions, located most apically. - Adherens junctions, located just below tight junctions. - Desmosomes, located below adherens junctions. AJC is a synergistic structure (ie, it provides more strength than the sum of its individual parts).  It was historically described as a **terminal bar**, a dense band encircling the tops of epithelial cells, and was later resolved by electron microscopy into its 3 distinct elements. ## Intercalated discs Intercalated discs are **exclusive to myocardium** and consist of: - Gap junctions, allowing electrical transmission outside the His-Purkinje conduction system. - Adherens junctions, transmitting contractile force between neighboring ventricular myocytes. - Desmosomes, conferring tensile strength. Intercalated discs allow heart muscle to function as a syncytium, allowing coordinated contraction.  Cell-to-cell conduction through gap junctions is slower than through His-Purkinje fibers.  This slight delay allows the heart to squeeze from apex to base, optimizing systolic ejection.  When the His-Purkinje system is damaged (eg, bundle branch block) or bypassed (eg, accessory pathway), the depolarization wave is forced to spread cell-to-cell more slowly, resulting in a widened QRS complex (eg, >120 ms). # Polarity The coordinated positioning of these junctions defines how cells are oriented within tissues, a concept known as cell polarity.  Cell polarity refers to a functional asymmetry that organizes the cell membrane into distinct regions specialized for different tasks.  It is based on 2 related principles: - Directional function:  Spatial organization that enables processes such as solute transport and secretion to occur in a defined direction. - Tissue orientation:  Maintenance of attachment to underlying support structures, which preserves tissue architecture and prevents dysplastic or invasive growth (eg, early stages of cancer). ## Axes of polarity Polarity can be expressed along several geometric axes: - **Luminal-basal polarity** distinguishes the surface facing the lumen from the surface attached to the basement membrane; this axis dominates in epithelial and endothelial cells. - **Anterior-posterior polarity** distinguishes the leading edge from the trailing edge of migratory cells and of cells with long cytoplasmic extensions (eg, neurons). - **Planar (lateral) polarity** aligns cells within the plane of a tissue, coordinating orientation across neighboring cells.  This alignment is critical for the cochlea (to align stereocilia with incoming sound waves), respiratory tract (to ensure unidirectional ciliary beating), and renal tubules (to direct nephron elongation and loop formation). In addition to these single-cell axes, polarity establishes whole body axes (eg, during embryogenesis) by allowing division to produce asymmetric daughter cells that express different homeobox genes ((Figure 7)). ## Molecular basis At the molecular level, polarity reflects how specific proteins and signaling complexes sort into distinct membrane domains.  For example, in epithelia the apical domain faces the lumen, and the basolateral domain comprises the sides and base of the cell that contact neighboring cells and the basement membrane.  This molecular organization parallels the tissue-level luminal-basal orientation but is defined by protein localization rather than by gross position within the tissue. Polarity at the molecular level is governed by both intrinsic and extrinsic cues: - **Intracellular** cues are mediated by polarity complex proteins, including Par, Crumbs, and Scribble.  These complexes localize to opposing membrane regions:  Par and Crumbs polarize to the apical membrane, whereas Scribble polarizes to the basolateral membrane.  They maintain their boundaries through mutual exclusion and feedback loops. - **Extracellular** cues stabilize polarity but do not create it independently.  They include luminal forces (eg, blood flow), basal contact with basement membrane, and secreted proteins that have extracellular gradients (eg, Wnt, Hedgehog). ## Loss of polarity Normal epithelial cells are highly organized, with distinct apical, lateral, and basal domains.  Loss of apical-basal polarity is a major feature of **epithelial tumors** (ie, **carcinomas**).  Breakdown of polarity occurs in the following stages: - **Dysplasia** occurs in response to chronic inflammation, genetic mutations, carcinogens, or oncogenic viruses (eg, cigarette smoke, alcohol, human papillomavirus).  Affected cells show **partial loss** of polarity (eg, irregular alignment, uneven spacing) due to decreased expression of apical and basal polarity protein complexes.  However, they remain confined above the basement membrane.  These changes are **potentially reversible** with removal of the underlying stimulus. - **Carcinoma** **in situ** represents preinvasive malignancy.  Affected cells often show **complete loss** of polarity (eg, disorganization, crowding, ectopic gland or sheet formation).  The lesion is **irreversible** but remains confined above the basement membrane, making it potentially curable with local excision. - **Invasive carcinoma** is the last stage.  Malignant cells show complete loss of polarity and acquire migratory capacity through epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition.  These changes also allow them to penetrate the basement membrane, invade the underlying stroma, and enter lymphatic channels or blood vessels.  Typically, a grossly visible primary tumor is found, which may be associated with nodal spread or distant metastases. # Summary Cell junctions are specialized structures that regulate permeability, attachment, and polarity.  They are most relevant for epithelial and endothelial cells.  There are 6 main types of junctions: - Tight junctions form a continuous apical seal, creating an impermeable barrier to diffusion. - Adherens junctions form a belt just beneath tight junctions, providing a dynamic (ie, calcium-dependent) but strong link between cells. - Desmosomes form discrete spot-like junctions that anchor the lateral surfaces of adjacent cells together, providing tensile strength. - Hemidesmosomes (fixed) and focal adhesion complexes (transient) attach the basal cell surface to the basement membrane. - Gap junctions enable direct cytoplasmic exchange for synchronized electrical and metabolic activity (eg, heart contraction). Disruption of these junctions can cause capillary leakiness (eg, tight junctions), cancer cell invasion (adherens junctions), blistering skin diseases (desmosomes, hemidesmosomes), and other disorders.  These junctions establish and reinforce cell polarity (ie, apex vs base), which is progressively lost during the transition from dysplasia to invasive carcinoma. ​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌

articles.title: Cell Biology: Disposal And Recycling Pathway
articles.markdown:
# Cell Biology: Disposal And Recycling Pathway # Introduction The disposal and recycling pathway of the cell consists of 4 organelles: - The **proteasome** degrades cytosolic proteins that have been marked by ubiquitination. - **Lysosomes** degrade proteins, lipids, carbohydrates, and organelles. - **Endosomes** send internalized material back to the plasma membrane (for recycling), to lysosomes (for degradation), or to the Golgi apparatus and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (for rerouting). - **Peroxisomes** detoxify reactive oxygen species and metabolize very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs) (which require many redox reactions). A related article covers the secretory pathway organelles (ie, ER, Golgi apparatus) of the cell.  These 2 pathways work together:  The secretory pathway delivers functional proteins, whereas the disposal pathway enforces quality control by clearing misfolded proteins, damaged organelles, and toxic metabolites. # Proteasome ## Function The proteasome is a large, barrel-shaped, ATP-dependent **protease complex** located primarily in the cytosol.  The proteases degrade intracellular proteins that are damaged, misfolded, or obsolete; these proteins are tagged with **polyubiquitin** chains by a class of enzymes known as ubiquitin ligases.  The ubiquitinated protein is then unfolded and fed into the proteasome core for proteolytic degradation ((Figure 1)). The resulting products serve multiple purposes: - Single amino acids can be recycled for new protein synthesis. - Peptide fragments can be presented on major histocompatibility complex I in antigen-presenting cells (eg, intracellular infections, tumor neoantigens). A well-functioning ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) is needed for a vast array of vital processes such as cell cycle regulation (eg, cyclin degradation), stress responses (eg, clearing proteins damaged by oxidation), and overall protein quality control. ## Dysfunction The UPS is activated in **catabolic states** (eg, critical illness, burns), breaking down skeletal muscle protein.  This is initially an adaptive response that liberates amino acids for energy production (eg, providing alanine and glutamine for hepatic gluconeogenesis) to be repurposed for acute phase reactants (eg, C-reactive protein).  However, prolonged activation can lead to muscle wasting and **cachexia** (eg, late starvation, tuberculosis, malignancy). When the UPS is overloaded **(proteostatic stress)**, defective or misfolded/unfolded proteins aggregate in the cell and may ultimately trigger apoptosis.  The UPS is overwhelmed in many chronic inflammatory and neurodegenerative disorders such as: - Parkinson disease (failed clearance of misfolded alpha-synuclein). - Alzheimer dementia (defective clearance of hyperphosphorylated tau and beta-amyloid). **Proteasome inhibitors** (eg, bortezomib, carfilzomib) are a first-line treatment for multiple myeloma, triggering toxic accumulation of immunoglobulin in the malignant plasma cells, inducing proteostatic stress and apoptosis. # Lysosome ## Function The lysosome is a membrane-bound organelle rich in **acid hydrolases** (eg, proteases, nucleases, lipases, glycosidases) that are active at low pH.  The lysosome is involved in several degradation pathways: - **Endocytosis** involves invaginations of the plasma membrane that internalize extracellular materials such as receptor-ligand complexes or viruses.  These vacuoles then fuse with lysosomes, where the contents are degraded ((Figure 2)). - **Autophagy** ("self-eating") involves cytoplasmic vacuoles that enclose damaged organelles and long-lived proteins.  These autophagosomes then fuse with lysosomes for degradation ((Figure 3)).  Autophagy can be ubiquitin dependent (analogous to the proteasome) or ubiquitin independent (regulated by mammalian target of rapamycin \[mTOR\]).  **Mitophagy** is a type of autophagy that removes senile mitochondria (eg, such as those producing excessive free radicals). - **Phagocytosis** involves specialized cells (eg, macrophages) that engulf large particles, including microbes, into phagosomes that subsequently fuse with lysosomes ((Figure 4)). ## Dysfunction Lysosomal storage diseases (LSDs) involve defective lysosomal hydrolases, leading to the intracellular accumulation of glycolipids, glycosaminoglycans, or glycoproteins.  Briefly, LSDs include: - 5 major **sphingolipidoses**, resulting from **intracellular** accumulation of cell membrane sphingolipids ((Table 1)): - **Gaucher** disease, the most common LSD, involves defective beta-glucocerebrosidase, a lysosomal enzyme in **macrophages**, resulting in the accumulation of glucocerebroside as the macrophages perform their normal function of engulfing cellular debris.  This disease presents with hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, osteonecrosis, and Gaucher cells (lipid-laden macrophages resembling crumpled tissue paper) ((Figure 5)). - **Tay-Sachs** disease involves defective hexosaminidase A, resulting in the accumulation of GM2 ganglioside, a sphingolipid specific to **neuronal membranes**.  It presents with neurologic decline in the first few months of life and a cherry-red macular spot, representing the normal unaffected fovea (which lacks ganglion cells) against the pale backdrop of the remaining destroyed retina. - **Niemann-Pick** disease involves defective sphingomyelinase, resulting in the accumulation of sphingomyelin in neural tissue and **reticuloendothelial** organs (eg, liver, spleen).  Like Tay-Sachs disease, Niemann-Pick disease presents with neurologic degeneration in infancy and a cherry-red macula; however, it also causes hepatosplenomegaly. - **Krabbe** disease involves defective galactocerebrosidase, resulting in the accumulation of galactosylsphingosine specific to **myelinated** axons.  It presents with optic nerve atrophy (eg, central pallor), flaccid peripheral neuropathy, and neurologic decline in infancy. - **Fabry** disease, the only X-linked recessive LSD, involves defective galactosidase, resulting in the accumulation of ceramide trihexoside in **small blood vessels** (eg, cutaneous capillaries, cerebral microcirculation, glomeruli).  It presents with angiokeratomas, telangiectasias, early-onset cardiovascular events (eg, stroke), and nephropathy. - The 2 major **mucopolysaccharidoses (MPSs)**, resulting from **extracellular** accumulation of proteoglycans, namely dermatan and heparan sulfate ((Table 2)): - **Hurler** syndrome (severe formo f MPS I) involves defective alpha-L-iduronidase.  It presents with coarse "gargoyle" facies, corneal clouding, developmental delay, hepatosplenomegaly, and coronary artery obstruction (due to extensive interstitial proteoglycan deposition) leading to ischemia, and death in childhood. - **Hunter** syndrome (MPS II) involves defective iduronate-2-sulfatase.  It presents as a milder form of Hurler syndrome but is still lethal by early adulthood. - **I-cell disease**, a mucolipidosis involving global lysosomal dysfunction due to the failed import of **all lysosomal enzymes** caused by an upstream defect in ER and Golgi apparatus trafficking (loss of mannose-6-phosphate tagging).  Because all lysosomal hydrolases are affected, I-cell disease presents with combined features of the listed disorders (eg, neurodegeneration, hepatosplenomegaly, coarse features). # Endosome ## Function Endosomes carry contents between the cell membrane, Golgi apparatus/ER, or lysosomes, depending on whether their internalized cargo is to be recycled to the surface, rerouted, or degraded. - **Receptor recycling** returns internalized surface receptors back to the plasma membrane to reduce the need for de novo receptor synthesis.  It is particularly important for high-turnover systems such as lipoprotein (eg, **LDL receptor**) and iron (eg, transferrin receptor) uptake. - **Lysosome fusion** directs ligand-receptor complexes and pathogens to lysosomes for degradation.  **Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9** inhibitors (eg, alirocumab, evolocumab) are antihyperlipidemic monoclonal antibodies that block LDL receptor endosomes from fusing with lysosomes.  By blocking receptor degradation, they promote recycling to the cell surface, thereby increasing LDL clearance. - **Golgi apparatus/ER rerouting** sends selected internalized proteins back to the *trans*\-Golgi apparatus and ER via retrograde transport to be resecreted by exocytosis.  This pathway is often hijacked by **bacterial protein toxins** (eg, *Shiga* toxin, *Cholera* toxin) to evade lysosomal degradation, allowing them to exit the ER via a backdoor and disrupt their targets in the cytoplasm. In addition to fusing directly, endosomes are also **precursors to lysosomes**, undergoing a process of maturation in which they gradually acidify and acquire lysosomal hydrolase enzymes.  However, in certain cells, the maturing endolysosome is diverted to produce lysosome-related organelles (LROs), which are specialized secretory compartments that store bioactive mediators.  LROs include dense granules in platelets (store ADP, serotonin), melanosomes in melanocytes (store melanin pigment), and azurophilic granules in neutrophils (store myeloperoxidase, lysozyme, defensins, and elastase), and lytic granules in cytotoxic T cells (store perforin and granzyme). ## Dysfunction Defects in LROs result in 2 autosomal recessive disorders with overlapping features: - **Chédiak-Higashi syndrome** involves oculocutaneous albinism (due to defective melanin storage), recurrent pyogenic infections (due to impaired phagolysosome formation), bleeding diathesis (due to absent platelet granules), and progressive neurologic decline (due to the accumulation of old endosomes in neurons).  Giant granules can be observed in circulating neutrophils ((Figure 6)). - **Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome** is similar to Chédiak-Higashi syndrome but does not feature immunodeficiency or neurologic decline.  It presents with oculocutaneous albinism, platelet bleeding diathesis, and early-onset pulmonary fibrosis (due to the accumulation of undigested wax ceramides). These disorders involve systemic manifestations in multiple organs, distinguishing them from simple oculocutaneous albinism, which results from mutations in melanin synthesis genes (eg, tyrosinase) ((Figure 7)) # Peroxisome ## Function The peroxisome houses oxidative enzymes necessary for lipid metabolism and detoxification ((Figure 8)).  Its functions include: - **Beta-oxidation** of VLCFAs (ie, ≥22 carbons) to shorten them prior to further oxidation in mitochondria. - **Alpha-oxidation** of branched-chain fatty acids (eg, phytanic acid). - Synthesis of **bile acids** (requires beta-oxidation of cholesterol). - Reduction of **hydrogen peroxide** (a by-product of fatty acid oxidation) via catalase. - Synthesis of plasmalogens (eg, plasmenylethanolamine), which are critical for **myelin**. ## Dysfunction Peroxisome defects include: - X-linked **adrenoleukodystrophy**, in which defective transport of VLCFAs leads to progressive demyelination and adrenal failure (due to accumulation of VLCFAs in the adrenal cortex). - **Zellweger syndrome**, in which failed peroxisome biogenesis leads to profound neurologic defects (eg, hypotonia, seizures, developmental delay), cholestatic liver failure (due to impaired production of bile acids), and craniofacial abnormalities (eg, widened sutures, large anterior fontanelle), with fatty acid buildup (elevated VLCFA and phytanic acid). - **Refsum disease**, in which the accumulation of phytanic acid (due to impaired alpha-oxidation) leads to retinal degeneration and cerebellar ataxia. # Summary Organelles of the disposal pathway include the proteasome, lysosomes, endosomes, and peroxisomes.  They maintain cellular health by eliminating damaged proteins, organelles, and toxic metabolites.  The proteasome degrades ubiquitinated cytosolic proteins, allowing their amino acids to be used for other purposes (eg, new protein synthesis).  Proteasome dysfunction is implicated in many degenerative diseases in which misfolded proteins accumulate (eg, Parkinson disease, Alzheimer dementia).  Lysosomes digest macromolecules and entire organelles via endocytosis, autophagy, or phagocytosis.  Lysosomal storage diseases (eg, Gaucher, Tay-Sachs, Fabry) lead to the accumulation of glycolipids, glycosaminoglycans, or glycoproteins.  Endosomes traffic internalized materials to lysosomes, the cell membrane, or the Golgi apparatus and give rise to lysosome-related organelles.  Endolysosomal defects result in Chédiak-Higashi and Hermansky-Pudlak syndromes.  Peroxisomes oxidize very-long-chain and branched-chain fatty acids and detoxify reactive oxygen species.  Peroxisome disorders include X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy and Zellweger syndrome. ​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​​‌

articles.title: Cell Biology: Cytoskeleton
articles.markdown: # Cell Biology: Cytoskeleton # Introduction This article covers the cytoskeleton, a scaffolding system composed of filamentous proteins that enable biophysical actions such as vesicle transport, motility, and cell division.  There are 3 major cytoskeletal elements ((Figure 1)): - **Microfilaments** (made of **actin**) are thin, flexible fibers involved in cell shape and motility. - **Intermediate filaments** (made of keratin, vimentin, and other proteins) are strong, ropy fibers that provide mechanical strength. - **Microtubules** (made of **tubulin**) are rigid, hollow tubes used as tracks for intracellular transport, organelle positioning, and mitosis. In addition, the spectrin meshwork is also often considered with these elements. # Microfilaments ## Function Microfilaments are composed of polymerized **actin** monomers forming 2 intertwined strands (F-actin).  They are highly concentrated **beneath the plasma membrane** (ie, cortical actin) and participate in cell: - Shaping (eg, microvilli). - Locomotion (eg, lamellipodia and filopodia for crawling). - Contraction (eg, sarcomeres). - Cytoplasmic partitioning (eg, endocytosis, exocytosis, budding) and mitotic cleavage (ie, cytokinesis). Actin-binding proteins regulate polymerization (eg, profilin), branching (eg, Arp2/3 complex), and severing (eg, cofilin).  Calcium-dependent actin-myosin interactions drive myocyte contraction. **Dysfunction**Defects in actin regulation impair key cellular functions across multiple tissues: - In **immune cells**, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS) is a primary immunodeficiency due to *WAS* gene mutations that lead to defective actin branching.  This impairs T-cell synapse formation, leukocyte chemotaxis, and megakaryocyte fragmentation (to form platelets).  Manifestations include recurrent infections, thrombocytopenia, and secondary eczema (due to Th2 imbalance). - In **neurons**, axonal transport, dendritic remodeling, and neurotransmitter release rely, to varying extents, on dynamic actin rearrangement.  Dysfunction can lead to impaired neural signaling. - In **epithelial tissue**, actin contributes to cell junction stability and wound repair.  Abnormal actin regulation delays wound closure and weakens junctional integrity, which may predispose to barrier dysfunction and poor regenerative capacity. # Intermediate filaments ## Function Intermediate filaments are strong, rope-like fibers that handle mechanical stress, particularly in cells that need to resist deformation (eg, connective tissue, skin, neurons).  Unlike microfilaments or microtubules, which actively polymerize and depolymerize to change cell morphology, intermediate filaments are static and serve a **purely structural** role.  They stabilize the cytoplasmic architecture and anchor organelles in place.  Different cells have different intermediate filament proteins: - Epithelia use **cytokeratin** (eg, stratum corneum). - Mesenchymal cells use **vimentin** (eg, fibroblasts). - Myocytes use **desmin** (eg, cardiac, skeletal, and smooth muscle). - Astrocytes (support cells for neurons) use **glial acid fibrillary protein (GFAP)**. - All nucleated cells use **lamin** (for the nuclear envelope). ## Dysfunction Defects in these intermediate filament proteins lead to loss of tissue integrity. - **Epidermolysis bullosa simplex** is caused by mutations in cytokeratin (eg, skin fragility and intraepidermal blistering with minor trauma). - **Nuclear laminopathies** involve mutations in lamin-A and lamin-C and include Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy (eg, cardiomyopathy, skeletal muscle degeneration, premature joint contractures) and Hutchinson-Gilford **progeria** syndrome (eg, accelerated aging with early-onset vascular disease and osteoporotic fractures). - Several **genetic cardiomyopathies** (both hypertrophic and dilated) involve mutations in desmin or lamin (in addition to sarcomeric proteins such as titin, myosin, and troponin). # Microtubules ## Function Microtubules are hollow cylinders made of alpha- and beta-tubulin dimers.  Microtubules perform the "heavy lifting" within the cell.  Microtubule polymerization and depolymerization depend on guanosine triphosphate hydrolysis, which releases more energy than ATP and enables greater mechanical work.  They also have a polarity (ie, positive and negative ends), which defines the direction of movement.  In particular, microtubules: - Serve as **cargo tracks** for motor proteins such as kinesin (moves toward the positive end) and dynein (moves toward the negative end).  The cargo can be vesicles or even whole organelles ((Figure 2)). - Form **mitotic spindles** for chromosome segregation (emanating from organizing centers at opposite ends of the cell, known as **centrosomes**, each containing 2 centrioles). - Forms **cilia** in the respiratory tract, fallopian tubes, and spermatozoa (where they are called flagella).  The cilia consist of 9 outer microtubules arranged around 2 inner core microtubules (9 + 2) ((Figure 3)).  The microtubules are linked to dynein arms, allowing the cilia to beat in unison and in the same direction. ## Dysfunction Defective microtubule transport causes a wide range of pathologies known as **ciliopathies**. - **Primary ciliary dyskinesias** are a group of disorders caused by mutations in dynein, resulting in loss of ciliary beating or coordination.  Manifestations include **Kartagener syndrome**, which involves bronchiectasis and chronic sinusitis (due to mucostasis causing bacterial overgrowth and recurrent infections), and situs inversus (due to loss of leftward flow of embryonic extracellular fluid).  Infertility is common due to immotile sperm and impaired ovum migration in the fallopian tube. - Autosomal dominant **polycystic kidney diseases** are a group of disorders, mostly due to mutations in polycystin, a ciliary protein involved in renal tubular fluid flow and nephron organization.  Manifestations include the formation of large bilateral renal cysts (dilated nephrons) and extrarenal dilations (eg, hepatic cysts, colonic diverticulosis, cerebral berry aneurysms). - Retinal ciliopathies include **Leber congenital amaurosis** and some forms of retinitis pigmentosa, which are caused by mutations in genes essential for the transport of opsin and retinal pigment within photoreceptor cells.  Manifestations include either congenital blindness or loss of vision early in childhood. Microtubule inhibitors are effective chemotherapy agents because they cause **M-phase arrest** ((Figure 4)).  Tubulin polymerization is inhibited by **vinca alkaloids** (eg, vinblastine, vincristine), so spindles cannot form (mnemonic: "Vinny never builds").  Conversely, depolymerization is inhibited by **taxanes** (eg, paclitaxel, docetaxel), so spindles are frozen in place (mnemonic: "taxes never go away").  Disruption of microtubule function impairs **axonal transport** in neurons, leading to length-dependent peripheral neuropathy, the most common adverse effect of these drugs. In addition to chemotherapy, several other drugs also inhibit polymerization to block the M phase in neutrophils (eg, colchicine), fungal cells (eg, griseofulvin), or helminthic parasites (eg, mebendazole). # Spectrin meshwork ## Function The spectrin meshwork is a flexible, 2-dimensional pentagonal and hexagonal lattice (like the surface of a soccer ball) just below the cell surface, and it is attached to actin filaments via accessory proteins such as **spectrin alpha/beta**, **ankyrin**, **dystrophin**, and protein 4.1.  The spectrin mesh is particularly important in: - **Red blood cells**, where it prevents cell membranes from being stripped as cells pass through narrow capillaries and splenic sinuses. - **Skeletal muscle**, where it anchors the actin cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix to distribute mechanical stress evenly during muscle contraction. ## Dysfunction Spectrin defects result in **hereditary spherocytosis**, in which progressive membrane loss leads to spherical (rather than biconcave) red blood cells.  The spherocytes are less deformable and become trapped in the spleen, where they are destroyed (ie, extravascular hemolysis). **Dystrophin** is a large protein in the spectrin family that links the actin cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix to minimize shear stresses and protect against contraction-induced muscle injury.  Loss of dystrophin in **Duchenne** or Becker muscular dystrophy results in microtears, calcium influx, and myocyte necrosis, causing the muscle body to be replaced by fibrofatty tissue. # Summary The cytoskeleton is a dynamic scaffold that regulates cell shape and provides motor structures for cell movement, division, and intracellular vesicle traffic.  It comprises 3 major constituents: microfilaments, intermediate filaments, and microtubules.  Microfilaments (made of actin) mediate cell shape, motility, and contraction.  Defects in actin polymerization most famously result in Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, a primary immunodeficiency.  Intermediate filaments (made of various cell-specific proteins) provide tensile strength and support.  Defective intermediate filament proteins include nuclear laminopathies (eg, progeria), skin fragility, and heritable cardiomyopathies.  Microtubules (made of tubulin) are critical for cilia formation, vesicle and organelle movement, and mitotic spindle assembly.  Microtubule dysfunction causes ciliopathies, a group of conditions that include Kartagener syndrome and autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.  Microtubule-targeting drugs (eg, vinca alkaloids, taxanes) arrest cells in mitosis but also cause length-dependent peripheral neuropathy due to disrupted axonal transport.  The spectrin meshwork, often considered part of the cytoskeletal system, reinforces the plasma membrane in erythrocytes and muscle cells.  Defective spectrin proteins (eg, ankyrin, dystrophin) lead to hereditary spherocytosis and Duchenne muscular dystrophy. ​‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌

articles.title: Cell Biology: Cytopathology
articles.markdown:
# Cell Biology: Cytopathology # Introduction Cytopathology is the study of diseases based on cell morphology.  This article provides an overview of common cytopathologic changes, such as nuclear and cellular atypia, altered nuclear/cytoplasmic relationships, and cytoplasmic inclusions across various disease processes. # Atypia Cancer disrupts normal nuclear and cytoplasmic morphology because neoplastic cells prioritize rapid proliferation.  Their uncontrolled growth requires extensive DNA replication and transcription (increasing the risk for **nuclear atypia**) at the cost of cell structure (eg, **cellular atypia**). ## Nuclear atypia Nuclear atypia refers to an abnormal nuclear or chromatin structure.  It indicates genetic instability and increased proliferative activity ((Figure 1)) and includes features such as: - Abnormal mitoses (eg, more metaphases, bizarre spindles). - Prominent nucleoli (due to high rates of ribosome production) ((Figure 2)). - Nuclear pleomorphism (ie, variation in size and appearance between nuclei). - Chromatin irregularities, such as hyperchromasia (dark staining) due to increased nuclear DNA content or heterochromasia (coarse, blotchy appearance) due to uneven transcriptional activity. Some chromatin patterns are characteristic of specific cell types, regardless of whether they are benign or malignant:  Clock-face chromatin (radially clumped) is seen in normal plasma cells but also in multiple myeloma (caused by plasma cell proliferation).  Salt-and-pepper chromatin (fine, granular) can be a typical feature of neuroendocrine cells and is retained in neuroendocrine tumors ((Figure 3)). ## Cellular atypia Cellular atypia refers to the abnormal appearance of the entire cell ((Figure 4)).  It includes features such as: - Cellular pleomorphism (ie, irregular size and appearance between cells). - Loss of polarity (eg, nuclei positioned randomly instead of toward the basement membrane) - Loss of differentiating structures (eg, missing cilia on respiratory epithelium, microvilli on enterocytes). **Anaplasia** is the extreme end of cellular and nuclear atypia.  It involves total loss of mature cell markers (eg, loss of cytokeratin in anaplastic tumors of squamous origin), numerous abnormal mitoses, and bizarre pleomorphic giant cells ((Figure 5)). # Nuclear/cytoplasmic relationship ## High nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio A high nuclear/cytoplasmic **(N:C)** ratio indicates a cell that is immature and rapidly dividing:  Its nucleus is large due to unraveled chromatin, high rates of gene transcription, and increased DNA synthesis.  Cytoplasm is scant because rapid division leaves insufficient time for organelles to develop. A high N/C ratio is seen in some normal contexts (eg, erythroblast stage of red blood cell maturation).  However, in malignancy, it typically indicates undifferentiated, anaplastic, and primitive neoplasms (eg, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, small cell lung carcinoma, neuroblastoma) ((Figure 6)).  Because the nucleus is often hyperchromatic (dark blue) and occupies almost the entire cell volume, high-grade malignancies exhibit a **small round blue cell** appearance on hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. ## Nuclear molding Nuclear molding refers to indentation of the nuclear membrane caused by crowding in scant cytoplasm.  It occurs when cells are jammed together in tight sheets.  This feature helps distinguish **small cell lung carcinoma** from other small round blue cell tumors (discussed previously) that also have a high N:C ratio but lack this compression. ## Nuclear/cytoplasmic dyssynchrony Multilobed nuclei reflect asynchrony between nuclear division (mitosis) and cell division (cytokinesis).  Nuclear division depends on DNA replication, whereas cytoplasmic division depends primarily on protein synthesis.  Nutrient deficiencies that selectively affect DNA synthesis (eg, vitamin B12, folate) cause cells to continue adding cytoplasm without dividing, leading to enlargement (ie, **macrocytosis**).  Hematopoietic cells are most severely affected because they have the greatest dependency on DNA synthesis.  The nucleus lags and makes repeated, incomplete attempts to divide (ie, **hypersegmentation**).  Macrocytotic red cells (ie, mean corpuscular volume ≥100 μm3) and hypersegmented neutrophils (ie, ≥6 lobes) are hallmarks of megaloblastic anemia due to vitamin B12 or folate deficiency ((Figure 7)). Of note, granulocytes normally have multilobed nuclei that make them more deformable, allowing them to pass through tissue barriers (eg, 3-5 lobes in neutrophils, 2 lobes in eosinophils).  In addition, the **Pelger-Huët anomaly** is a benign congenital condition with bilobed neutrophils (like pince-nez eyeglasses) due to a minor defect in lamin B, a nuclear envelope protein ((Figure 8)). ## Eccentric nucleus An eccentric (displaced) nucleus is seen in cells with a prominent Golgi apparatus due to copious protein secretion.  It is classically seen in **plasma cells**, where the enlarged Golgi pushes the nucleus to the periphery, resulting in a fried-egg appearance ((Figure 9)).  Eccentric nuclei are also seen in **signet ring cells** (mucinous adenocarcinomas), where intracellular mucin displaces the nucleus ((Figure 10)). ## Multinucleation Multinucleation arises from 2 principal mechanisms: - Repeated nuclear division (ie, mitosis) with lagging cytokinesis, a relatively nonspecific finding seen in many aggressive malignancies. - Cell fusion (**syncytium** formation), a characteristic of several viral infections (eg, measles, respiratory syncytial virus infection).  Viral syncytia facilitate direct viral spread to neighboring cells without exposure to extracellular antibodies.  In blistering cutaneous herpes simplex virus (HSV) and varicella-zoster virus (VZV) lesions (eg, genital herpes, shingles), a Tzanck smear can reveal fused keratinocytes appearing as multinucleated giant cells ((Figure 11)). In addition, several normal cell types, including skeletal myocytes, osteoclasts, and megakaryocytes, are multinucleated. # Specific changes Beyond general patterns of nuclear and cellular atypia, many conditions are associated with **distinctive morphologic changes** that are diagnostically significant. ## Lymphocytes - **Reactive atypia** ("atypical lymphocytosis") refers to large, cytotoxic (CD8+) T cells seen in response to antigenic stimulation, most notably in infectious mononucleosis **(Epstein-Barr virus)**, cytomegalovirus **(CMV)**, or toxoplasmosis.  They represent robust cell-mediated immune activation (eg, IL-2, interferon-gamma).  These lymphocytes are polygonal, have abundant cytoplasm that often molds around adjacent red cells, and possess enlarged nuclei ((Figure 12)).  Despite these enlarged nuclei, their N:C ratio is relatively normal because they also have ample cytoplasm. - **Smudge cells** are ruptured B lymphocytes seen on peripheral blood smear, appearing as exploded cell fragments lacking clear nuclear borders ((Figure 13)).  They are most commonly associated with **chronic lymphocytic leukemia**, reflecting extreme fragility (eg, underproduction of cytoskeletal proteins), leading to mechanical deformation during slide preparation. - **Reed-Sternberg (RS)** cells are large B lymphocytes within lymphoid organs.  They feature abundant cytoplasm and bilobed nuclei with prominent nucleoli, often described as owl's eyes ((Figure 14)).  RS cells secrete cytokines (eg, IL-5, IL-13) that recruit inflammatory cells, creating the characteristic mixed inflammatory background of **Hodgkin lymphoma**. - **Hairy cells** are malignant B lymphocytes with fine, hair-like cytoplasmic projections; they are seen in hairy cell leukemia ((Figure 15)).  They stain with tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) and characteristically infiltrate the red pulp of the spleen (eg, massive splenomegaly) and bone marrow (eg, "dry tap" due to myelofibrosis). - **Sézary cells** are malignant T lymphocytes with cerebriform (convoluted, brain-like) nuclei found in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides) ((Figure 16)).  They are associated with Sézary syndrome, which is characterized by a circulating leukemic phase, lymphadenopathy, diffuse erythroderma, and pruritus. ## Macrophages - **Epithelioid histiocytes** are activated macrophages that take on an epithelial appearance (eg, flat instead of round, fewer phagocytic clefts) in keeping with a shift toward a containment phenotype for walling off pathogens or foreign bodies (eg, earliest stage of granuloma formation). - **Multinucleated giant cells** result from the fusion of multiple macrophages and epithelioid histiocytes in response to persistent activation, such as indigestible foreign bodies, intracellular pathogens that resist degradation (mycobacteria, fungi), or idiopathic granulomas (eg, sarcoidosis). - **Foam cells** are lipid-laden macrophages classically associated with cutaneous xanthomas and atherosclerotic plaques, where they take up excess cholesterol and lipoproteins.  A relatively nonspecific finding, they are also seen wherever macrophages scavenge lipid-rich debris, as in multiple sclerosis (eg, myelin), Whipple disease (eg, *Tropheryma whipplei* cell wall), or Niemann-Pick disease (eg, undegraded sphingolipids) ((Figure 17)). ## Epithelial cells - **Koilocytes** are dysplastic cervical squamous epithelial cells infected by **human papillomavirus**, seen on Pap smears.  They show a characteristic perinuclear halo (due to Golgi expansion) with a wrinkled (raisinoid) hyperchromatic nucleus. - **Clear cells** are malignant cells with copious glycogen and lipid (eg, clear cell renal carcinoma) or mucin (eg, mucinous adenocarcinomas) that are dissolved during routine histologic processing, leaving behind large empty spaces ((Figure 18)). - **Psammoma bodies** are concentrically laminated (onion-skin) nodules of dystrophic calcification seen in epithelial tumors with central infarction and necrosis (eg, papillary thyroid carcinoma, meningioma, serous ovarian carcinoma) ((Figure 19)). # Intracellular inclusions Intracellular inclusions are abnormal collections of proteins or other macromolecules.  They are diagnostically important (and sometimes pathognomonic) findings that can sometimes inform immediate management (eg, Auer rods). ## Aggregated host proteins Damaged, misfolded, or precipitated endogenous proteins can form insoluble inclusions.  They are typically **cytoplasmic** because the cytoplasm is the primary site of protein synthesis and degradation.  Classic examples are listed in the table ((Table 1)): - Hematologic:  **Auer rods** are linear precipitations of myeloperoxidase in myeloblasts; they are seen in acute myeloid leukemia, particularly the acute promyelocytic leukemia (APML) subtype ((Figure 20)).  **Russell** bodies are precipitated immunoglobulin in plasma cells and are seen in multiple myeloma ((Figure 21)). - Neurodegenerative:  **Lewy** bodies are aggregates of misfolded alpha-synuclein in neurons, which are seen in Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia (Figure 22)).  **Neurofibrillary tangles** are accumulations of hyperphosphorylated tau seen in Alzheimer dementia ((Figure 23)). - Hepatic:  **Alpha-1 antitrypsin** (A1AT) globules are accumulations of misfolded, unsecreted A1AT protein that are positive on periodic acid–Schiff stain and diastase resistant ((Figure 24)).  **Mallory** bodies are clumps of degenerated cytoskeletal proteins in hepatocytes and are seen in inflammatory liver disease (eg, alcoholic hepatitis) ((Figure 25)).  **Councilman** bodies are inclusions of apoptotic debris seen in acute viral hepatitis (eg, yellow fever). Auer rods are the most important finding at the point of care.  The presence of numerous Auer rods strongly raises suspicion for APML, a medical emergency with a high risk of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).  Treatment with all-*trans* retinoic acid should be initiated immediately, and coagulation studies are closely monitored, often with preemptive cryoprecipitate transfusion (to supplement fibrinogen) to reduce the risk of DIC. ## Viral replication inclusions Viral proteins and nucleic acids can form **intranuclear** or **cytoplasmic** inclusions, depending on the site of viral replication.  Intranuclear inclusions are generally associated with DNA viruses (which require host polymerase), whereas cytoplasmic inclusions are often associated with RNA viruses (which carry or encode their own RNA-dependent RNA polymerases).  The major examples are listed in the table ((Table 2)): - Rabies virus:  **Negri** bodies are ovoid cytoplasmic inclusions found in neurons (especially hippocampal pyramidal cells) ((Figure 26)) - CMV:  **Owl's eyes** are large intranuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo ((Figure 27)).  The term is also used in nonviral contexts to describe nuclei with prominent nucleoli (eg, Reed-Sternberg cells). - HSV and VZV: **Cowdry type A** bodies are intranuclear inclusions with marginated chromatin. - Molluscum contagiosum virus (a poxvirus):  **Molluscum** (aka, Henderson-Paterson) bodies are large, pink, cytoplasmic inclusions seen in keratinocytes; they are composed of densely amassed virions ((Figure 28)). ## Erythrocyte inclusions Red blood cells are anucleate and lack any organelles, so any inclusions reflect **retained or precipitated material** ((Figure 29)). - Asplenia or hyposplenism (eg, sickle cell disease):  **Howell-Jolly** bodies are nuclear remnants normally removed by splenic macrophages ((Figure 30)). - Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency:  **Heinz** bodies are precipitations of denatured hemoglobin due to oxidative stress ((Figure 31)). - Sideroblastic anemia:  **Pappenheimer** bodies are ferritin (iron) granules that fail to incorporate due to defective heme synthesis ((Figure 32)). - Lead poisoning and thalassemias:  **Basophilic stippling** represents precipitated ribosomes from impaired globin RNA degradation ((Figure 33)). # Summary Pathologic changes in cell structure provide diagnostic clues in human disease.  A high nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio and nuclear atypia are classic features of malignancy.  Basophilic cytoplasm indicates increased ribosomal activity and protein synthesis, as seen in erythroblasts (hemoglobin synthesis) and plasma cells (immunoglobulin synthesis).  Intracellular inclusions such as Auer rods (acute promyelocytic leukemia), Heinz bodies (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency), and Lewy bodies (Parkinson disease) have key specific disease associations. ​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌
