articles.title: Cell Biology: Cell Receptor Signaling
articles.markdown:
# Cell Biology: Cell Receptor Signaling # Introduction This article covers the 4 major categories of receptor signaling: - Intracellular receptors, mainly used for steroid hormone signaling. - G-protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs), mainly used for catecholamines and peptide hormones signaling. - Tyrosine kinase receptors, mainly used for growth factor and cytokine signaling. - Ionotropic receptors, mainly used for excitatory or inhibitory neurotransmission. # Intracellular receptors Intracellular receptors are located within the **cytoplasm** or **nucleus**.  They bind to **small lipophilic molecules** that easily diffuse across the plasma membrane, such as steroid hormones (eg, cortisol, estrogen, progesterone), thyroid hormones, and vitamins A and D.  Intracellular receptors operate by altering **gene expression**, rather than by activating downstream second messengers or protein-protein interactions.  Therefore, they produce slower, sustained physiologic changes that are more difficult to rapidly adjust. These receptors are often called "nuclear hormone receptors" because they act genomically and commonly bind steroid hormones.  However, their activation varies slightly, depending on whether the receptor is in the cytoplasm or the nucleus: - Cytoplasmic receptors (eg, glucocorticoid, mineralocorticoid, sex hormones) float in the cytosol as free monomers.  On binding to their ligand, they **homodimerize**.  The hormone-receptor complex **translocates** to the nucleus and binds specific DNA sequences known as hormone response elements (HREs) ((Figure 1)).  HREs are located within 5′ regulatory regions of genes (eg, promoters) and influence transcription.  Signaling is comparatively slower because new transcription needs to be activated (eg, aldosterone increases sodium channel expression over days). - Nuclear receptors (eg, thyroid hormones \[T3, T4\], vitamins A and D) are **prebound** to DNA as part of repressive complexes until activated by a ligand.  On ligand binding, the receptors form **heterodimers** with the retinoid X receptor (RXR), allowing them to dissociate from DNA, unblocking gene expression.  Receptor signaling is comparatively faster because existing transcription is unblocked (eg, T3 upregulates genes involved in basal metabolic rate over a few hours). Many transcription factors use zinc finger motifs, the most commonly identified DNA-binding domains in humans, to recognize specific genes and alter their activity.  These motifs are composed of amino acid chains bound together around a zinc ion via linkages with cysteine (and sometimes histidine) residues.  This forms a stable, finger-shaped structure containing 2 antiparallel beta strands and an alpha helix.  Unique combinations of amino acids as well as the specific histidine and cysteine linkages determine DNA-binding specificity. # G-protein–coupled receptors GPCRs are **cell surface** receptors that have 7 transmembrane hydrophobic alpha-helical domains ((Figure 2)) and are composed of an alpha subunit (Gα)and a beta-gamma subunit.  GPCRs bind to a wide range of ligands such as peptides and catecholamines that require **fast signaling** (eg, vasoconstriction, bronchodilation, glucose release).  They immediately change cell behavior without directly influencing gene transcription. After the ligand binds: - Gα dissociates from the GPCR, which is accompanied by conversion of guanosine 5′-diphosphate to guanosine 5′-triphosphate. - The released Gα activates a **second messenger** system, which is a cascade of small intracellular molecules that quickly relay and amplify the signal.  The specific type of Gα released (Gαs, Gαi, Gαq, or Gα12/13) determines which second messenger pathway is involved ((Table 1)). ## Gαs and Gαi Gαs and Gαi operate through the **cyclic AMP–protein kinase A (cAMP-PKA)** second messenger system ((Figure 3)).  On ligand binding, adenylate cyclase is stimulated (Gαs) or inhibited (Gαi), leading to increased or decreased cAMP-PKA levels, respectively.  PKA has a vast spectrum of activity depending on the tissue.  For example: - The sympathetic response involves **beta-1** and **beta-2** adrenergic receptors and **glucagon** receptors, which are stimulatory (Gαs).  They increase PKA in the ciliary body (pupillary dilation), pacemaker cells (increased heart rate), airway smooth muscle (bronchodilation), and liver/skeletal muscle (glycogen breakdown). - Trophic pituitary hormones (eg, **TSH**, **ACTH**, **LH/FSH**) have stimulatory Gαs receptors.  They increase PKA in the thyroid gland, adrenal glands, and gonads to increase enzyme activity and hormone production. - The endorphin response involves **mu, delta, and kappa opioid** receptors, which are inhibitory (Gαi).  They decrease PKA in ascending pain pathways, inhibiting the release of nociceptive neurotransmitters such as substance P and glutamate. Other Gαs/Gαi receptors include the alpha-2 adrenergic receptor (Gαi), muscarinic M2 and M4 acetylcholine receptors (Gαi), vasopressin V2 receptor (Gαs), and small peptide receptors (eg, somatostatin, vasoactive intestinal peptide). ## Gαq Gαq operates through the **phosphoinositol–protein kinase C (PKC)** second messenger system ((Figure 4)).  On ligand binding, Gαq stimulates phospholipase C, which hydrolyzes membrane phospholipids into **inositol 1,4,5-triphosphate (IP****3****)** and **diacylglycerol (DAG)**.  IP3 mobilizes **calcium** release from the endoplasmic reticulum, whereas DAG activates **PKC**.  Calcium and PKC have a wide range of actions.  For example: - Smooth muscle contraction requires intracellular calcium and PKC to activate contractile proteins (eg, actin, myosin).  Accordingly, Gαq signaling underlies arteriolar vasoconstriction via receptors that activate this pathway, such as **alpha-1** adrenergic, **angiotensin II**, and **vasopressin** V1 receptors.  Similarly, parasympathetic functions such as gut peristalsis, bladder detrusor contraction, and bronchoconstriction also rely on calcium-dependent contraction; they involve the **M****3** acetylcholine receptor. - Exocytosis often requires a sudden rise in intracellular calcium, which reorganizes the cytoskeleton to pinch off vesicles.  For example, Gαq promotes the exocrine release of digestive enzymes (eg, amylase) from the pancreas via the **cholecystokinin** receptor.  Similarly, mucin is secreted from airway goblet cells via the **M****3** acetylcholine receptor. - Synaptic neurotransmission can be influenced by Gαq.  For example, the **5-HT****2** serotonin receptor promotes excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) because PKC increases the influx of sodium ions (Na+) and decreases the efflux of potassium ions (K+), favoring depolarization.  This has far-reaching effects on mood, memory, and perception. Other Gαq receptors include **histamine** H1 and **bradykinin** B1 receptors, which cause capillary permeability (eg, edema) when the rise in intracellular calcium pulls endothelial gap junctions apart. ## Gα12/13 Gα12/13 proteins operate through the **Rho kinase** system.  Unlike Gαs, Gαi, and Gαq, which rely on second messenger cascades, Gα12/13 activates RhoA and Rho-associated kinase.  Their main function is to activate contractile and cytoskeletal proteins **independently** of intracellular calcium.  This is especially important for processes in which cell shape and tension must be regulated without triggering calcium-dependent activities, such as: - Lymphocyte trafficking (eg, sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor), in which the cell needs to deform without prematurely releasing cytokines. - Fibroblast migration, in which the cells need to contract and move through tissue without simultaneously secreting collagen. - Neuronal pruning (elimination of unused synapses during development), in which the axons and dendrites can be retracted without activating calcium-driven neurotransmitter release. # Tyrosine kinase receptors Tyrosine kinases mediate receptor signaling through **tyrosine phosphorylation** events rather than G-protein second messengers.  They are classified as receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) or non-RTKs (NRTKs) ((Figure 5)). - **RTKs** are **transmembrane receptors** with intrinsic kinase activity.  They homodimerize and **autophosphorylate** themselves when a ligand binds.  Therefore, they are highly specific (one ligand, one receptor) and enable a "vertical" signaling with minimal overlap. - **NRTKs** are **intracellular adapter proteins** that dock with the internal face of other transmembrane receptors and rely on cytoplasmic Janus kinases (JAKs) for tyrosine phosphorylation.  Therefore, they are less specific (one adapter, multiple receptors) and enable "horizontal" signaling that integrates inputs from multiple receptors. Once phosphorylated, the RTKs and NRTKs activate **other kinase pathways** such as rat sarcoma–mitogen-activated protein kinase (Ras-MAPK) ((Figure 6)), phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase–protein kinase B–mammalian target of rapamycin (PI3K-AKT-mTOR) ((Figure 7)), and JAK–signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK-STAT) ((Figure 8)). ## Differences between tyrosine kinases and GPCRs Tyrosine kinases differ from GPCRs in 2 major ways: - GPCRs typically bind small ligands such as catecholamines and short peptides.  In contrast, RTKs and NRTKs bind large proteins such as **cytokines** (eg, IL-2) and **growth factors**. - GPCRs signal through rapid activation of second messenger pathways, leading to immediate functional responses such as secretion and contraction (although continued ligand exposure can also influence secondary changes in gene expression).  In contrast, RTKs and NRTKs initiate signaling via protein phosphorylation cascades.  These cascades can directly influence cell behavior (eg, migration) and slower transcription-dependent processes that govern cell **survival**, **proliferation**, and **hypertrophy**. ## RTKs RTKs are transmembrane receptors themselves.  They include: - Vascular endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGFR). - Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR). - Platelet-derived growth factor receptor (PDGFR). - Fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR). - Insulin receptor (and insulin-like growth factor receptor). These growth factors activate downstream kinase pathways (eg, MAPK) to stimulate protein synthesis and cellular proliferation, which is necessary for normal processes such as angiogenesis and wound healing.  The pathways can become dysregulated in malignancies (eg, constitutively active EGFR in breast and lung cancers), neovascularization (eg, diabetic retinopathy), and fibrosis (eg, excessive PDGF and FGF). ## NRTKs NRTKs are cytoplasmic adapter proteins that dock with other transmembrane receptors.  Their receptor partners include: - T-cell receptor (TCR) and B-cell receptor (BCR). - Cytokine receptors (eg, IL-2R, IL-6R). - Erythropoietin (EPO), granulocyte-monocyte colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), and thrombopoietin (TPO) receptors. NRTKs lack intrinsic kinase activity, so they require JAKs (intracellular tyrosine kinases).  The JAK-STAT pathway promotes **transcription** of genes involved in **leukocyte proliferation** and **hematopoiesis**.  In myeloproliferative disorders such as polycythemia vera, mutations in **JAK2** lead to constitutive activation of the EPO receptor, resulting in erythrocytosis.  Because GM-CSF and TPO receptors also use JAK2, other blood lineages (eg, leukocytes and platelets) are often increased as well. ## Tyrosine kinase inhibitors Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) are small-molecule, orally available drugs that block the tyrosine kinase activity of RTKs and NRTKs.  They can be recognized by their suffix "-tinib."  TKIs are used to treat a wide range of malignancies by blocking cell growth and survival pathways.  TKIs are widely used in the treatment of various malignancies and fibrotic and inflammatory conditions. - RTK inhibitors include **erlotinib** (inhibits EGFR in non–small cell lung cancer), **sunitinib** (inhibits VEGFR and PDGFR in renal cell carcinoma and gastrointestinal stromal tumors), and **nintedanib** (inhibits multiple RTKs, including FGFR in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis). - NRTK inhibitors include **imatinib** (inhibits BCR–Abelson murine leukemia, a fusion kinase created by t\[9;22\] Philadelphia translocation, in chronic myeloid leukemia), **ibrutinib** (inhibits Bruton tyrosine kinase in B-cell neoplasms such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia and mantle cell lymphoma), and **ruxolitinib** (inhibits JAK1/JAK2 in polycythemia vera and various autoimmune inflammatory disorders). # Ionotropic receptors Ionotropic receptors are **ligand-gated ion channels** that allow rapid changes in cell membrane potential, classically in neurons (eg, **synaptic transmission**) but also in other tissues (eg, vasodilation by ADP receptors in vascular smooth muscle).  The receptors open in response to neurotransmitter binding, allowing ions to flow through a pore.  Ionotropic receptors bind 2 excitatory neurotransmitters (glutamate, acetylcholine) and 2 inhibitory neurotransmitters (GABA, glycine). ## Glutamate receptors Ionotropic glutamate receptors are the primary mediators of excitatory neurotransmission in the CNS.  They consist of alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) and NMDA receptors. - **AMPA** receptors bind to glutamate, allowing Na+ influx and K+ efflux, facilitating rapid depolarization, resulting in an EPSP. - **NMDA** receptors require an existing depolarization and glutamate binding to displace a magnesium (Mg2+) plug from the channel ((Figure 9)).  After the channel is unblocked, they allow Na+ and Ca2+ influx, which can produce EPSPs and trigger calcium-dependent pathways (eg, long-term potentiation). ## Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) are located at neuromuscular junctions and throughout the CNS and mediate excitatory neurotransmission.  On binding acetylcholine, they open and allow Na+ influx and K+ efflux.  This ion movement depolarizes the membrane, generating EPSPs (eg, muscle twitch). ## GABA receptors GABA receptors mediate inhibitory neurotransmission in the CNS.  When they bind GABA, the receptors become permeable to Cl− anions.  This leads to hyperpolarization and generation of an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP). ## Glycine receptors Glycine receptors mediate inhibitory neurotransmission, primarily in interneurons in the spinal cord and brainstem.  Like GABA receptors, they are Cl− permeable and hyperpolarize the cell membrane.  IPSPs generated by these receptors help reduce resting motor tone (eg, prevent spasticity). ## Metabotropic modulation Ionotropic receptors are often contrasted with metabotropic receptors (eg, GPCRs), which use second messenger systems ((Figure 10)).  However, metabotropic neurotransmitter receptors (eg, dopamine, serotonin) can modulate the EPSPs and IPSPs generated by ionotropic receptors (eg, glutamate \[NMDA, AMPA\], GABA), allowing for greater synaptic plasticity. # Other receptors ## Transforming growth factor–beta receptor superfamily The transforming growth factor–beta (TGF-beta) receptor superfamily binds to TGF-beta and bone morphogenic protein.  These receptors are **serine/threonine kinases** (distinct from tyrosine kinases) that signal through intracellular **SMAD** proteins, leading to changes in gene transcription. ## Guanylyl cyclases Guanylyl cyclases (GCs) are receptors that operate through the **cGMP–protein kinase G (cGMP-PKG)** pathway ((Figure 11)).  They mediate **nitric oxide** signaling.  Activation of GC increases cGMP, activating PKG, which ultimately leads to the release of myosin light chains from actin, promoting vascular smooth muscle relaxation (ie, **vasodilation)**.  PKG also reduces intracellular calcium levels (by sequestering it within the endoplasmic reticulum), further enhancing its vasodilatory effect. GC is also the receptor for atrial and brain natriuretic peptides, which are released from stretched cardiomyocytes (eg, decompensated heart failure).  In the renal tubules, PKG inhibits sodium reabsorption, leading to enhanced salt and water excretion. # Summary Cells use many receptor systems to regulate physiologic functions ((Table 2)).  They can broadly be categorized into 4 families: - Intracellular receptors are activated by lipophilic molecules (eg, steroid and thyroid hormones) and work by altering gene expression, leading to slow and long-lasting effects. - G-protein–coupled receptors are located on the cell surface and bind to diverse ligands (eg, neurotransmitters, catecholamines, peptides).  They work by activating second messenger systems (eg, cyclic AMP/protein kinase A; inositol 1,4,5-triphosphate/protein kinase C), enabling fast cellular responses such as smooth muscle contraction and glycogenolysis. - Tyrosine kinases, consisting of receptor tyrosine kinases and nonreceptor tyrosine kinases, bind to large proteins such as growth factors and cytokines.  They work by activating phosphorylation (kinase) cascades to regulate cell growth, immune responses, and hematopoiesis. - Ionotropic receptors are ligand-gated ion channels that mediate rapid synaptic transmission by controlling ion fluxes, resulting in excitatory or inhibitory potentials. ​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​‌

# Cell Biology: Cell Death

# Introduction

Cells respond to stress through adaptive changes such as atrophy, hypertrophy, hyperplasia, and metaplasia; when these adaptations fail, cell death occurs.  This article covers accidental cell death (necrosis) and regulated cell death (RCD) (apoptosis and others), with emphasis on apoptosis.

# Classification

Cells have 4 survival adaptations (atrophy, hypertrophy, hyperplasia, metaplasia) in response to stress.  However, cell death occurs when these mechanisms are overwhelmed due to severe and irreversible injury.  There are 2 broad categories of cell death ((Video 1)):

-   Accidental cell death (ie, **necrosis**).
-   RCD, including **apoptosis** and additional forms (eg, necroptosis, pyroptosis).

## Accidental cell death

Accidental cell death is synonymous with **necrosis**.  It refers to cellular destruction in response to extreme ischemic (eg, infarction), biochemical (eg, bacterial toxins), chemical (eg, osmotic lysis), or thermal (eg, freeze-rethaw) insults.  Necrosis:

-   Releases lysosomal enzymes that digest cells and surrounding tissue.
-   Occurs all at once, without a defined sequence of events.
-   Ruptures plasma membranes (eg, releasing intracellular contents).
-   Triggers robust acute inflammation and cytokine release.

Necrosis cannot be targeted by pharmacologic agents.

## Regulated cell death

RCD is typically denoted by the suffix "-optosis."  It involves programmed cell destruction in response to unsurvivable insults that do not immediately cause necrosis.  The major forms of RCD are apoptosis and nonapoptotic RCD (pyroptosis, necroptosis, and ferroptosis).  This article focuses primarily on **apoptosis**, but other forms are briefly described.  Apoptosis:

-   Is carried out by "executioner" caspases (tightly regulated proteases).
-   Follows a programmed sequence of events (eg, shrinkage, blebbing, fragmentation).
-   Preserves cell membranes (ie, less release of intracellular antigens).
-   Elicits minimal acute inflammation.

Unlike necrosis, apoptosis can be targeted by pharmacologic agents (eg, BCL-2 inhibitors, caspase inhibitors).

# Necrosis

Necrosis, or accidental cell death, refers to uncontrolled cell destruction accompanied by membrane rupture, release of intracellular contents, and resulting inflammation.  Different patterns of necrosis are identified based on etiology and their gross and microscopic appearance ((Table 1)).

## Coagulative necrosis

Coagulative necrosis occurs when proteins (including caspases and other enzymes) are denatured before they can break down cell components.  This typically occurs during prolonged tissue hypoxia or acidosis (eg, ischemia, infarction).  As a result, autolysis is delayed, so cellular architecture is temporarily preserved.  Dead cells retain their outlines ("ghost" or "silhouette") on histology.  The necrotic tissue has a gel-like consistency, similar to that of coagulated blood.  Coagulative necrosis is primarily seen in all **solid organ infarctions** (eg, heart, kidney, bowel, lung) **except the brain**.  Despite preserved structure, their membranes are compromised, leading to spillage of intracellular contents that elicit acute infiltration (eg, neutrophil migration shortly following acute myocardial infarction) ((Figure 1)).

## Liquefactive necrosis

Liquefactive necrosis occurs when spilled lysosomal enzymes completely digest the dead cells and surrounding tissue.  The tissue is replaced by fluid and amorphous cellular debris.  Liquefactive necrosis is seen mainly in the **brain** following acute ischemic stroke, when neurons (the most ischemia-sensitive cells) quickly rupture and release autodigestive enzymes.  Unlike other solid organs, the brain's extracellular matrix is soft and spongious, offering little resistance to enzymatic breakdown.  Liquefaction is also seen in **suppurative bacterial infections** (eg, necrotizing fasciitis, lung abscess), in which bacterial exotoxins and neutrophil-derived enzymes degrade pathogens and host tissue, forming **pus**.

## Gangrenous necrosis

**Dry** gangrene is ischemic coagulative necrosis of the skin or extremities caused by arterial ischemic events (eg, atherosclerosis, embolism, frostbite).  Venous drainage persists, allowing fluid to exit, leading to gradual desiccation and preventing bacterial superinfection.  The tissue undergoes **mummification**; it shrinks, hardens, and turns brown-black due to hemoglobin breakdown.  A clear line of demarcation forms between dead and viable tissue, often leading to autoamputation.  In contrast, **wet** gangrene occurs when bacterial superinfection adds a liquefactive and often purulent component to the necrosis.

## Fibrinoid necrosis

Fibrinoid necrosis is a specific pattern of necrosis affecting vascular walls.  It occurs when the walls of small arteries and arterioles are damaged by **vasculitic inflammation** (particularly in anti-cytoplasmic antibodies–associated vasculitides such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis or by **malignant hypertension** (eg, eclampsia).  Infiltration of plasma proteins (eg, fibrin) into the vessel walls results in a bright intramural band of proteinaceous material on histology, typically accompanied by acute (neutrophilic) inflammation ((Figure 2)).

## Caseating necrosis

Caseating necrosis is seen with **chronic granulomatous inflammation** due to mycobacterial (eg, tuberculosis) or fungal (eg, histoplasmosis) infections.  The central area of the granuloma undergoes necrosis, forming a soft, cheese-like (caseous) core composed of degenerated lipid and proteinaceous debris.  The necrotic core is surrounded by a rim of epithelioid macrophages, multinucleated giant cells, and lymphocytes.  In later stages of healing, the caseating granuloma may calcify or become fibrotic.

## Fat necrosis

Fat necrosis affects adipose tissue and is typically caused by mechanical trauma (eg, **breast**) or lipase release (eg, **acute pancreatitis**).  In trauma, ruptured adipocytes trigger local inflammation and fibrosis, forming firm nodules; histology shows ruptured, anucleate adipocytes surrounded by lipid-laden macrophages, often with punctate calcification ((Figure 3)).  In acute pancreatitis, lipases digest triglycerides into free fatty acids, which bind calcium to form chalky, white, soap-like deposits (ie, fat saponification) ((Figure 4)).

# Apoptosis

Apoptosis, the classic form of RCD, is a tightly controlled process that systematically dismantles the cell while preserving membrane integrity and limiting inflammation.  It is initiated through 3 major pathways:

-   Intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway ((Figure 5)).
-   Extrinsic (death receptor) pathway ((Figure 6)).
-   Cytotoxic (perforin-granzyme) pathway ((Figure 7)).

Each pathway converges on activation of **executioner caspases** (3, 6, and 7) that carry out controlled demolition of cell structures.

## Intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway

The intrinsic apoptosis pathway involves the release of cytochrome c from the **mitochondria** into the cytoplasm.  It is a response to:

-   Mitochondrial depolarization due to cessation of electron transport (eg, no gradient), free radical (mitochondrial reactive oxygen species) damage, or opening of permeability transition pores (eg, due to massive calcium influx).
-   Genotoxic stress (eg, DNA damage from ionizing radiation, chemotherapy) and activation of oncogenes (eg, p53).
-   Proteotoxic stress (eg, accumulation of misfolded proteins).
-   Loss of survival signals (eg, withdrawal of obligatory growth factors or cytokines).

The mitochondrial outer membrane (OMM) houses **Bax** and **Bak**, proapoptotic proteins that oligomerize in response to the triggers above.  The Bax/Bak complexes create pores in the OMM that allow **cytochrome c** to diffuse from the intermembrane space into the cytoplasm.  In the cytoplasm, cytochrome c recruits **caspase-9**, setting off a proteolytic cascade that activates the final executioner caspases (ie, 3, 6, and 7).

Mitochondria also help regulate intracellular **calcium** levels.  Calcium has the steepest electrochemical gradient of any cellular ion, with concentrations more than 10,000 times higher outside the cell than inside.  When cytosolic calcium rises, the mitochondrial matrix acts as a buffer by sequestering excess calcium and storing it in an inert form as calcium phosphonate.  However, if calcium influx becomes excessive—as can occur during events such as glutamate excitotoxicity ((Figure 8))—this buffering capacity is overwhelmed.  The resulting calcium overload triggers the opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore in the inner membrane, causing mitochondrial depolarization and initiating the intrinsic apoptosis pathway.

## Extrinsic (death receptor) pathway

The extrinsic apoptosis pathway is a form of **immune-mediated RCD** that eliminates cells recognized as **non-self**.  The pathway eliminates diseased cells displaying foreign or abnormal proteins (eg, viral infection, tumor cells) and cells expressing non-self major histocompatibility complexes (MHCs) (eg, allogeneic transplant).

It involves death ligands and death receptors.

-   Briefly, death ligands, such as the **Fas ligand** (CD95) and **tumor necrosis factor–related apoptosis-inducing ligand (TRAIL)**, are **acutely upregulated** in activated natural killer (NK) cells and cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs).
-   At the same time, death receptors, such as Fas receptor (Fas, \[CD95R\]) and TRAIL receptors (DR4/DR5) are **constitutively expressed** in every nucleated cell.

When death ligands engage their receptor counterpart in diseased cells, the death receptor undergoes a conformational change that activates **caspase-8**.  In turn, caspase-8 cleaves and activates executioner caspases 3, 6, and 7.

In **autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome**, defective lymphocyte Fas or caspase-8 leads to apoptosis resistance.  Patients have chronic benign lymphoproliferation (eg, hepatosplenomegaly, bulky lymphadenopathy) accompanied by an immune blood dyscrasia (eg, autoimmune hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia) and have an elevated risk of transformation to lymphoma.

## Cytotoxic (perforin-granzyme) pathway

The cytotoxic pathway is a specialized **immune-mediated** RCD that involves the release of cytolytic enzymes **(perforin, granzymes)** by CTLs and NK cells to destroy infected, neoplastic, or foreign cells.  The pathway is triggered by:

-   Foreign peptides presented on MHC I (eg, allogeneic organ transplant), which activate CTLs.
-   Increased stress ligand (eg, MHC class I chain-related protein A, and chain-related protein B) expression, which activates NK cells.
-   Loss of MHC I expression (ie, "missing self"), a feature of many viral infections, which activates NK cells.
-   Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ie, type 2 hypersensitivity), which activates NK cells ((Figure 9)).

CTL and NK cells synapse with diseased target cells and insert perforin into their membrane, creating small pores.  Granzymes enter through these pores, where they activate caspase-3 to induce apoptosis.  Granzymes can also trigger caspase-independent apoptosis because they have extensive and nonspecific protease activity.

## Common executioner sequence

The chronologic sequence of apoptosis is as follows ((Figure 10)).  After initiation of the caspase cascade by any of the 3 pathways above:

-   Executioner caspases (3, 6, and 7) are activated.  These caspases have 3 major effects:
    -   They activate DNases to fragment genomic DNA, leading to chromatin condensation.
    -   They proteolyze laminin (nuclear envelope protein), leading to nuclear fragmentation (karyorrhexis).
    -   They cleave the actin cytoskeleton, leading to membrane blebs.
-   Blebs separate as membrane-bound apoptotic bodies, enclosing organelles, nuclear fragments, and cellular debris.
-   Apoptotic bodies externalize phosphatidylserine (normally on the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane), which serves as a phagocytic signal for engulfment by macrophages.

The process is noninflammatory because membranes remain intact, preventing the release of destructive (eg, lysosomal) enzymes and the release of intracellular damage-associated molecular patterns \[DAMPs\]).

## Nonapoptotic RCD

Nonapoptotic forms of RCD operate independently of the classic pathway of executioner caspases and are now known to represent >50% of all RCD events.  These cells show quasinecrotic features such as membrane rupture and often trigger **inflammation**; unlike necrosis, however, the cell rupture remains tightly regulated.  The major forms of nonapoptotic RCD include:

-   **Necroptosis**, a backup pathway for extrinsic apoptosis when death receptors (Fas, TRAIL) are activated but caspase-8 is absent or inhibited (eg, by some viruses).  It uses pore-forming proteins to disrupt the plasma membrane, leading to cell lysis and inflammation.
-   **Pyroptosis**, an inflammation-induced RCD that occurs when pathogen-associated molecular patterns and DAMPs ((Table 2)) activate innate immune receptors in conditions such as sepsis and acute respiratory distress syndrome.  It uses a separate set of caspases (eg, 1, 4, 5) distinct from executioner caspases.
-   **Ferroptosis**, a less inflammatory RCD driven by **lipid peroxidation**, which occurs when free iron produces hydroxyl radicals.  Lipid peroxides are normally reduced by intracellular **glutathione**, but this antioxidant defense system can be depleted (eg, certain chemotherapies).
-   **Neutrophil extracellular traps** (ie, **NETosis**), a neutrophil-specific form of RCD in which neutrophils eject webs of chromatin, known as neutrophil extracellular traps, that are laced with antimicrobial proteins that ensnare and kill invading pathogens extracellularly.

# Apoptosis in health and disease

## Normal functions

Accidental cell death (necrosis) is never normal.  However, RCD has several vital roles:

-   Development:  In embryologic contexts, the term **programmed cell death** is used interchangeably with apoptosis.  It enables digit separation ((Figure 11)), neural pruning, canalization of lumens (eg, gastrointestinal tract), and dissolution of temporary structures such as the primitive notocord, müllerian ducts in males, and wolffian ducts in females.
-   Immune tolerance:  Apoptosis (intrinsic pathway) prevents autoimmunity through clonal deletion (ie, negative selection) of self-reactive T and B cells in the thymus and bone marrow.  Apoptosis (extrinsic pathway) also terminates the immune response by destroying activated leukocytes after pathogen clearance.
-   Infection control:  Apoptosis eliminates infected cells, particularly those harboring viruses and intracellular pathogens.  The extrinsic and cytotoxic pathways (ie, NK cells, CTLs) allow pathogen spread to be contained while minimizing inflammation and bystander damage to normal tissue.
-   Antineoplastic:  Apoptosis (intrinsic pathways) defends against neoplasia by eliminating cells with extensive DNA damage, especially if there is concurrent deactivation of tumor suppressor proteins (eg, p53, "guardian of the genome," which is a potent apoptotic stimulus).  Apoptosis (extrinsic and cytotoxic pathways) also eliminates tumor cells that present neoantigens (altered self-proteins) on their MHC.
-   Tissue turnover:  Apoptosis maintains stable cell populations, especially in tissues with high rates of proliferation (eg, epidermis, intestinal mucosa, and bone marrow).  Similarly, it allows for physiologic tissue regression in response to hormone withdrawal (eg, menstrual endometrial shedding, mammary gland involution).

## Dysregulated apoptosis

Defects in apoptosis are seen in many human diseases.

-   Apoptosis is impaired in **cancer**, allowing cancer cells to survive despite otherwise lethal genetic damage.  Many cancers harbor mutations in *TP53* or overexpress Bcl-2, which blocks mitochondrial apoptosis in response to severe DNA damage.  As the cells continue to proliferate, they accumulate even more mutations, developing progressively malignant phenotypes (eg, loss of polarity, dedifferentiation, invasiveness).
-   Apoptosis resistance is also a feature of several **nonmalignant diseases**.  For example, in **pulmonary arterial hypertension**, vascular endothelial and smooth muscle cells proliferate and become abnormally long-lived, contributing to luminal narrowing and eventual right ventricular failure.  In **idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis**, lung fibroblasts acquire an apoptosis-resistant phenotype, leading to persistent activation and collagen deposition.
-   Imperfect apoptosis may underlie several **autoimmune conditions** such as systemic lupus erythematosus and systemic sclerosis (scleroderma).  In such disorders, patients have a small pool of autoreactive lymphocytes that escaped deletion during negative selection, potentially due to a subtle defect in intrinsic apoptosis.  Later in life, minor tissue injuries (eg, sunlight exposure, viral infections) may expose intracellular contents, particularly **nuclear antigens**, especially if apoptotic clearance is already impaired.  This promotes the formation of **antinuclear antibodies** (eg, anti–double-stranded DNA, anticentromere), driving immune-mediated tissue damage.

## Apoptosis as a therapeutic target

Several FDA-approved medications targeting apoptosis are approved for use in oncology.  They include:

-   **Bcl-2 inhibitors** (eg, venetoclax) block Bcl-2, an antiapoptotic protein that prevents the oligomerization of Bax and Bak, thereby inhibiting OMM permeabilization and cytochrome c release.  Bcl-2 is overexpressed in several hematologic malignancies, making the cells resistant to apoptosis.  By blocking Bcl-2, venetoclax restores apoptotic balance; it is used as a chemotherapeutic option for chronic lymphocytic leukemia and acute myelogenous leukemia.
-   **Arsenic trioxide** (ATO) activates the intrinsic (mitochondrial) apoptosis pathway through the generation of reactive oxygen species and the activation of Bax and Bak.  ATO induces the death of myeloblasts in acute promyelocytic leukemia and is often used with all-*trans* retinoic acid as first-line treatment.
-   **Immune checkpoint inhibitors** ((Figure 12)) restore the immune system's ability to attack tumor cells by reactivating T and NK cells.  These immune cells express **programmed death protein-1 (PD-1)**, which normally slows cells' activity and eventually triggers apoptosis, thereby naturally winding down the immune responses and avoiding damage to healthy cells.  However, many tumors exploit this process by **overexpressing** the **PD-1 ligand (PD-L1)**; because PD-L1 chronically activates PD-1, it leads to T-cell exhaustion and apoptosis.  **PD-1 inhibitors** (eg, nivolumab, pembrolizumab) and **PD-L1 inhibitors** (eg, durvalumab, avelumab) block this interaction, restoring T-cell survival and tumor killing.  Cancers with defects in mismatch repair proteins and high microsatellite instability (reflecting DNA polymerase errors during cellular replication) are particularly susceptible to immune recognition because they rapidly accumulate mutations and generate approximately 20-fold more neoantigens than tumor cells that have normal mismatch repair.

Many cancers (especially of solid tumors) have defective apoptotic machinery (eg, loss of p53), making them more resistant to chemotherapy or radiation.  As a result, higher doses are often needed, which shifts the mechanism toward necrosis and leads to more inflammatory adverse effects (eg, acute radiation proctitis).  Combining both treatments either concurrently (ie, chemoradiation) or sequentially (ie, neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by radiation) helps overcome this resistance by disrupting multiple pathways; this can **sensitize** the tumor cells to apoptosis, allowing a synergistic response using relatively lower doses of each.

# Summary

Cell death falls into 2 major categories: accidental cell death (necrosis) and regulated cell death.  Necrosis is never normal and is triggered by extreme damage, resulting in membrane rupture, lysosomal enzyme release, and resultant inflammation.  It takes on distinct forms in different tissues (eg, coagulative, liquefactive, fibrinoid).  In contrast, apoptosis, the classic form of regulated cell death, is a noninflammatory, programmed process triggered via intrinsic (mitochondrial), extrinsic (death receptor), or cytotoxic (granzyme-perforin) pathways, all converging on executioner caspases.  Apoptosis is noninflammatory because it preserves cellular membranes, limiting the release of intracellular contents.  It is essential for many physiologic processes (eg, organ morphogenesis, immune tolerance, infection control, tumor suppression).  However, apoptosis is dysregulated in autoimmune and neoplastic diseases.  Unlike necrosis, apoptosis can be pharmacologically induced (eg, Bcl-2 inhibitors, cytotoxic chemotherapy).

​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​

articles.title: Cell Biology: Cell Adaptation
articles.markdown:
# Cell Biology: Cell Adaptation

# Introduction

Cells face constant stress (eg, mechanical, chemical, genetic, infectious, metabolic) and have 4 principle adaptations that alter their size, number, or phenotype:

-   Atrophy is a decrease in cell (and thus organ) size.
-   Hypertrophy is an increase in cell (and thus organ) size.
-   Hyperplasia is an increase in cell number (and thus organ size).
-   Metaplasia is a replacement of one mature cell type by another.

Some adaptations overlap (eg, myometrial hypertrophy and hyperplasia in the gravid uterus, mucosal atrophy interspersed with intestinal metaplasia with *Helicobacter pylori*–induced gastritis).  They are mostly reversible once the underlying stress is removed.  Cells that are persistently or irreversibly injured may die by apoptosis (regulated cell death) or necrosis.  Diseased cells that fail to adapt can compromise organ function or acquire genetic alterations that drive dysplasia (premalignant transformation).

# Atrophy

Atrophy involves a **decrease in cell size** without a reduction in cell number, leading to diminished organ and tissue mass.  The shrunken cells have lower metabolic demand, allowing them to survive under conditions of scarcity or stress.

## Mechanisms

Atrophy can occur due to loss of mechanical loading (**disuse** atrophy), oxygen and nutrient delivery (**ischemic** atrophy), neuromuscular input (**denervation** atrophy), or paracrine support (**hormonal** atrophy).  In all cases, the common pathway involves:

-   Increased protein degradation via activation of the **ubiquitin-proteasome** system ((Figure 1)) and increased organelle destruction via the **autophagy-lysosome** system ((Figure 2)).
-   Reduced protein synthesis via downregulation of the **phosphoinositide 3-kinase/protein kinase B/mammalian target of rapamycin (PI3K/AKT/mTOR)** axis, leading to decreased ribosomal biogenesis and translational activity ((Figure 3)).  The mTOR pathway is suppressed by a lack of trophic factors (eg, nutrients, hormones, innervation).

## Histopathology

Atrophic cells exhibit reduced cytoplasmic volume due to loss of organelles and structural proteins.  Nuclei are generally shrunken and contain condensed (hyperchromatic) chromatin, reflecting low transcriptional activity.  As a final product of autophagic digestion, **lipofuscin** pigment accumulates (particularly in hepatocytes and cardiac myocytes), giving cells a brownish discoloration ((Figure 4)).  Autophagic vacuoles can be seen on electron microscopy, reflecting lysosomal activity.

## Physiologic

Although atrophy is often regarded as part of normal aging (eg, cerebral volume loss, sarcopenia), it is never considered a physiologic process.

## Pathologic

There are 4 main forms of atrophy, all involving a shift away from protein synthesis (eg, decreased mTOR signaling) and toward protein degradation (eg, proteasome activation):

-   **Disuse atrophy** ("use it or lose it") primarily affects skeletal muscle and is often seen with prolonged limb immobility, bed rest, and mechanical ventilation.
-   **Denervation atrophy** is typically caused by lower motor neuron lesions, such as median nerve entrapment (eg, thenar wasting) and diabetic polyneuropathy (eg, foot atrophy, arch collapse).
-   **Ischemic atrophy** affects tissues experiencing chronic hypoperfusion, such as renal atrophy from renal artery stenosis or testicular atrophy from long-standing varicocele.
-   **Hormonal atrophy** occurs due to withdrawal of endocrine support, such as postmenopausal estrogen decline (eg, endometrial, breast, and vaginal atrophy) or chronic corticosteroid use (eg, adrenal atrophy due to ACTH suppression).

**Cerebral atrophy** (eg, aging) is thought to reflect a combination of disuse (eg, synaptic pruning) and ischemia (eg, microvascular disease).  In contrast, the major gray matter loss seen with neurodegenerative dementias (eg, Alzheimer) primarily reflects apoptosis and gliosis (scarring) rather than atrophy.

**Cachectic atrophy** is seen in the setting of severe malnutrition, chronic illnesses with associated systemic inflammation (eg, tuberculosis, malignancy), advanced heart failure (cardiac cachexia), or end-stage lung disease (pulmonary cachexia).  Inflammatory mediators (eg, tumor necrosis factor–alpha) and catecholamines promote ubiquitination and breakdown of myofibrillar proteins to liberate energy for vital organs.

# Hypertrophy

Hypertrophy involves an **increase in cell size** without an accompanying increase in cell number.  It is the primary adaptive response in postmitotic (terminally differentiated) cells that have minimal proliferative capacity, such as:

-   Skeletal muscle cells.
-   Cardiac myocytes.
-   Adult adipocytes.

(Neurons are also postmitotic, but they do not exhibit hypertrophy.)

The enlarged cells increase their protein and organelle synthesis to adapt to increased mechanical workload (eg, cardiac myocytes with aortic stenosis, skeletal muscle cells with repetitive contractions in focal dystonia) or storage capacity (eg, adipocytes with calorie excess).

The list is not absolute.  For example, ventricular myocytes retain a very limited ability to divide shortly following myocardial infarction.  Some adipocytes can undergo hyperplasia once hypertrophy reaches its upper limit (eg, extreme obesity).

## Mechanism

Hypertrophy can be physiologic (eg, skeletal muscle with exercise) or pathologic (eg, cardiac muscle with hypertension).  The common molecular pathways are the inverse of atrophy, namely:

-   Increased protein synthesis via upregulation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR axis.
-   Decreased protein degradation via ubiquitin-proteasome and autophagy-lysosome pathways (although the relationship is context-dependent).

In skeletal and cardiac muscle, the mTOR pathway is activated by abnormal mechanical loads and wall stress (eg, stretch-activated ion channels, integrins).  In adipose tissue, it is activated by nutrient surplus (eg, insulin and insulin-like growth factor signaling).

## Histopathology

Hypertrophic cells generally appear enlarged, with abundant cytoplasm and organelles:

-   Hypertrophied cardiac myocytes have a large amount of cytoplasm packed with sarcomeric proteins.  Their nuclei are elongated and often described as rectangular **boxcars**, loosely resembling containers on a train ((Figure 5)).  They often undergo DNA replication without cell division, resulting in polyploid nuclei (ie, 4n = 92 chromosomes) to support greater transcriptional output.  Some cells become binucleated as they are pushed to the adaptive limit.
-   Hypertrophied skeletal myocytes display increased thickness, with additional sarcomeres crowding their many nuclei further to the periphery.  They also display greater mitochondrial density to meet higher energy demands.
-   Hypertrophied adipocytes exhibit very large (typically single) cytoplasmic lipid vacuoles that compress the nucleus against the cell membrane.

## Physiologic

In physiologic hypertrophy, capillary density remains proportional to the increased tissue mass (ie, angiogenesis keeps up), fibrosis is absent, and organ function is preserved:

-   Skeletal muscle:  Physiologic hypertrophy is the normal adaptation to resistance training (eg, weight lifting).
-   Left ventricle:  Physiologic hypertrophy is also known as athlete's heart, an adaptive response to exercise ((Figure 6)).  Resistance exercise (eg, weight lifting) promotes concentric hypertrophy to adapt to higher afterload.  Endurance exercise (eg, long-distance running) promotes eccentric hypertrophy to adapt to higher preload.  With eccentric hypertrophy, ventricular thickness (T) increases proportionally to chamber radius (R), such that the wall stress remains constant (based on the law of Laplace: stress ∝ R/T).  This is in contrast to the eccentric remodeling seen with pathologic dilation, discussed later.
-   Adipose tissue:  Physiologic hypertrophy is seen in individuals with overweight or temporary weight gain (eg, "winter weight").  It typically expands the subcutaneous adipose tissue, which remains metabolically healthy (eg, well perfused, insulin sensitive).

## Pathologic

In pathologic hypertrophy, capillary growth is insufficient, parenchymal **fibrosis** develops, and organ function is compromised:

-   Left ventricle:  Pathologic left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) is seen in heart failure ((Figure 7)):
    -   Concentric LVH adds sarcomeres in parallel, increasing ventricular thickness in response to chronic pressure overload (eg, aortic stenosis).  It typically produces **heart failure with preserved ejection fraction**.  Cardiomyocytes outgrow their capillary supply, leading to subendocardial ischemia and diastolic dysfunction, which is further exacerbated by interstitial fibrosis.
    -   Eccentric LVH adds sarcomeres in series, increasing ventricular cavity size in response to chronic volume overload (eg, mitral regurgitation) or hyperdynamic circulation (eg, thyrotoxicosis).  It typically produces **heart failure with reduced ejection fraction**.  Ventricular dilation (ie, ↑↑ R)  is disproportionate to thickness (ie, ↑ T), leading to an increase in wall stress, which promotes further spherical remodeling.
-   Adipose tissue:  Pathologic adiposity is seen in patients with obesity, particularly with a central distribution that involves visceral (eg, omental) fat.  Capillary shortage and intercellular fibrosis in white adipose tissue contribute to local hypoxia, inflammation, and metabolic dysfunction (eg, insulin resistance).

# Hyperplasia

Hyperplasia refers to an **increased number of cells** within a tissue or organ due to regulated proliferation.  Unlike hypertrophy, hyperplasia requires mitotically active differentiated cell populations capable of reentering the cell cycle.  Most cells are capable of hyperplasia, especially epithelium, endothelium, hepatocytes, and mature lymphocytes.

## Mechanism

Hyperplasia is mediated by the **proliferation** of mature cells, as well as by the expansion of stem cells in some instances.  It can be triggered by chronic irritation or inflammation (eg, bronchial epithelial and goblet cell hyperplasia due to cigarette smoke), tissue injury (eg, reactive hyperplasia of type II pneumocytes following pneumonia), or hormone or growth factor stimulation (eg, progesterone-induced endometrial proliferation).  The common molecular pathway involves:

-   Cell cycle progression (particularly **G1/S** transition) via upregulation of cyclins, cyclin-dependent kinases, and S-phase genes (eg, thymidylate synthase, DNA polymerase).  Many growth factors (eg, epidermal growth factor \[EGF\], vascular endothelial growth factor, platelet-derived growth factor, fibroblast growth factor) bind their respective **receptor tyrosine kinases**, triggering the **rat sarcoma–mitogen-activated protein kinase (Ras-MAPK)** cascade, which upregulates these key cell cycle genes ((Figure 8)).
-   Increased protein synthesis via parallel activation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, which enables biomass accumulation necessary prior to mitosis.

## Histopathology

In general, hyperplastic tissues exhibit increased cellularity (ie, more nuclei per high-power field).  Resultant structures (eg, glands, lobules, ducts) are more numerous, but tissue **architecture is preserved**.  Mitotic figures are more frequent, particularly in regenerative hyperplasias, but there is no nuclear atypia (ie, no abnormal spindle formations or pleomorphic nuclei).  Cells are well differentiated and maintain proper polarity.

## Physiologic

Physiologic hyperplasia involves limited cell proliferation that does not lead to malignant transformation.  Tissue **architecture is normal**.  Examples include:

-   Estrogen-mediated endometrial proliferation during the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle.
-   Lactotroph (anterior pituitary) hyperplasia.
-   Compensatory hyperplasia of the liver after partial hepatectomy and of the kidney after nephrectomy.
-   Reactive lymphadenopathy (ie, germinal center expansion, reflecting clonal T- and B-cell hyperplasia) following viral infection.
-   Type II pneumocyte hyperplasia following resolution of acute alveolar injury (eg, aspiration, acute respiratory distress syndrome).
-   Erythroid hyperplasia of the bone marrow in response to chronic hypoxemia (ie, secondary polycythemia) or chronic hemolysis (eg, hereditary spherocytosis).
-   Dihydrotestosterone-driven proliferation of prostatic glands and stroma in benign prostatic hyperplasia.

## Pathologic

Pathologic hyperplasia involves continued cell proliferation, often due to chronic irritation or excessive hormone stimulation.  Most conditions are benign and polyclonal, but malignant transformation may occur in some settings.  Unlike physiologic hyperplasia, tissue **architecture is distorted**.  Examples include:

-   Postmenopausal endometrial hyperplasia due to unopposed estrogen stimulation (eg, obesity, tamoxifen therapy).  It is characterized by an increased gland/stroma ratio and crowded, cystically dilated glands, which may progress to atypia and carcinoma.
-   Hyperplastic colorectal polyps, where certain variants (eg, serrated or serrated lesions) harbor genetic changes (eg, microsatellite instability) that increase the risk for progression to adenocarcinoma.
-   Bronchial goblet cell (mucous gland) hyperplasia due to chronic irritant exposure (eg, cigarette smoking, pollution) or allergic inflammation (eg, asthma).  The Reid index quantifies the gland height relative to airway wall thickness ((Figure 9)), with ratios >0.5 correlating to worse chronic bronchitis and airflow obstruction.
-   Usual ductal hyperplasia of the breast, which features overgrowth of ductal epithelial cells that partially or completely occlude the lumen and is a precursor to atypical ductal hyperplasia or ductal carcinoma in situ.

# Metaplasia

Metaplasia refers to **reversible substitution** of one differentiated cell type by another that is better suited to withstand a noxious stimulus or stress (eg, chronic irritation from cigarette smoke, chronic inflammation from gastroesophageal reflux).  If tissue injury persists, metaplasia can become premalignant (eg, Barrett esophagus), progressing to dysplasia, neoplasia, and eventually invasive carcinoma ((Figure 10)).

## Mechanism

Metaplasia is a 2-step process:

-   Dedifferentiation of a mature cell type to its multipotent stem cell state.
-   Redifferentiation of the multipotent stem cell to a different, better-adapted cell type.

It does *not* arise from direct conversion (transdifferentiation) of one mature cell into another.  The process requires the expression of reprogramming transcription factors (eg, caudal-related homeobox transcription factor 2 for intestinal metaplasia, SRY-box transcription factor 2 for squamous metaplasia) and is further influenced by inflammatory cytokines and paracrine growth factor signaling (eg, EGF, transforming growth-factor-beta).

## Histopathology

Metaplastic epithelia demonstrate replacement with an alternate, well-differentiated epithelium:

-   **Squamous metaplasia** replaces normal columnar epithelium with a protective stratified squamous epithelium.  The multiple layers of flat, keratinized, squamous cells are more resistant to injury, such as from cigarette smoke in the lower respiratory tract and vaginal acidity in the endocervix ((Figure 11)).
-   **Columnar (intestinal) metaplasia** replaces normal squamous epithelium with mucus-secreting columnar epithelium (eg, Barrett esophagus, seen with chronic gastroesophageal reflux).  The tall, mucin-covered, columnar epithelium is better equipped to resist gastric acid and bile ((Figure 12)).  Similar changes are seen in gastric intestinal metaplasia (eg, *H pylori* gastritis), except that the initial gastric epithelium is already columnar but aglandular (not intestinal type).

Mitotic figures may be present due to increased regenerative activity, but nuclear atypia (eg, pleomorphism, hyperchromasia) is absent unless progression to dysplasia has begun.

## Physiologic

**Cervical** squamous metaplasia is a physiologic form of metaplasia that occurs during puberty.  The endocervical canal is normally lined by columnar epithelium, whereas the ectocervix is lined by stratified squamous epithelium.  Rising estrogen levels induce hyperplasia of the endocervical mucosa, everting and exposing it to the more acidic vaginal environment.  In response, these exposed columnar cells undergo squamous metaplasia.

The resulting transformation zone has increased cellular turnover, making it susceptible to infection with high-risk human papillomavirus subtypes, which can promote neoplasia.  Therefore, although the metaplasia is physiologic, the subsequent risk for atypia, dysplasia, and carcinoma represents a pathologic complication.

## Pathologic

Common examples of pathologic metaplasia include:

-   Bronchial squamous metaplasia:  Chronic bronchial irritation (eg, cigarette smoke, pollutants, radon gas) can induce squamous metaplasia, most often involving the **central airways**, which are normally lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium.  It is an early precursor to dysplasia and, eventually, squamous cell lung cancer, which characteristically arises in the hilar bronchi.
-   Bladder squamous metaplasia (schistosomiasis):  The normal bladder is lined by special transitional epithelium (urothelium) of dome-shaped cells capable of stretching.  Chronic inflammation from *Schistosoma haematobium* eggs triggers squamous metaplasia, which can transform to squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder (a distinct entity from typical urothelial carcinoma seen in Western countries).
-   Esophageal columnar metaplasia (Barrett esophagus):  The normal esophagus is lined entirely by squamous epithelium.  Untreated gastroesophageal reflux exposes the distal esophagus to gastric acid and bile, promoting columnar (intestinal) metaplasia.Although this change resists chemical injury, it predisposes to dysplasia and esophageal **adenocarcinoma** in the distal third of the esophagus and near the gastroesophageal junction.  (In contrast, cigarette smoke and alcohol mainly injure the upper esophagus, predisposing to squamous cell dysplasia and carcinoma of the proximal third).
-   Osseous metaplasia: Chronic inflammation or injury (eg, traumatic muscle hematomas, lung abscesses, connective tissue disease \[scleroderma\]) causes differentiation of fibroblasts into osteoblasts, forming mature bone within soft tissues (heterotopic ossification).  This is usually benign but may present as a hard palpable mass.

# Failed adaptation

Acute and severe insults can exceed the capacity for successful adaptation.  In addition, adaptive responses can themselves fail over time.  As a result, tissues may undergo cell-regulated cell death (apoptosis), accidental cell death (necrosis), or neoplasia.  Cell death is discussed in detail in a separate article.

## Apoptosis

Apoptosis is a form of regulated cell death characterized by membrane-enclosed (noninflammatory) destruction of cell components.  Cells commit to apoptosis when damage exceeds a critical threshold, detected by guardian proteins (eg, p53, BH3) that activate mitochondrial proapoptotic effectors (BAX, BAK), leading to mitochondrial permeabilization, cytochrome c release, and caspase activation.  Apoptosis is the preferred response to failed adaptation because it prevents necrotic (and thus inflammatory) cell death or neoplasia.

## Necrosis

Necrosis is an unintentional form of cell death resulting from extreme injury (eg, ischemia, toxins, infections) characterized by membrane rupture, release of intracellular contents, and subsequent acute inflammation.  Necrosis can kill otherwise apoptosis-resistant cells (eg, tumor necrosis due to radiation or chemotherapy).

## Neoplasia

Instead of dying, some damaged cells can bypass apoptotic machinery (eg, due to underlying p53 or inactivation) and continue to accumulate genetic alterations that lead to uncontrolled proliferation, such as mutations in cyclins and tumor suppressors.  Unlike hyperplasia or metaplasia, neoplasia is (almost always) irreversible.  It ranges from in situ carcinoma (eg, cervical intraepithelial neoplasm or ductal carcinoma in situ) to invasive carcinoma.  Tumor cells adaptations that allow them to spread to secondary sites include lossing of intercellular junctions (E-cadherin downregulation), detachment from the basemenet membrane (integrin expression alterations), degradation of the extracellular matrix (type IV collagen production), migration (autocrine chemotactic agents, non-integrin laminin receptor expression,), and dissemination.

# Summary

The 4 principal cell adaptations ((Table 1)) include atrophy (reduction in cell size), hypertrophy (increase in cell size), hyperplasia (increase in cell number), and metaplasia (replacement of one mature cell type with another).  When these adaptive options are overwhelmed, cell death (eg, apoptosis, necrosis) or neoplasia results.

articles.title: Cell And Gene Therapy
articles.markdown: # Cell And Gene Therapy # Introduction Cell and gene therapies are treatments that replace cells or modify their genetic material to treat (and sometimes cure) disease, usually after one dose.  A relatively small number of these treatments have been approved so far, but this is one of the fastest-growing areas of investigational new drug development, with many products showing dramatic and durable efficacy (eg, restoring vision in blinding retinal disease) with a favorable safety profile. # General principles ## Cell therapy Cell-based therapies fall into 2 categories: - **Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)** therapy, which involves engineering a patient's own T cells to express a synthetic immune receptor that recognizes cancer antigens, enabling them to kill tumor cells.  A primary application is the treatment of relapsed and refractory B-cell malignancies. - **Stem cell** therapy, which involves the administration of autologous (from the patient) or allogeneic (from a donor) progenitor cells to repopulate damaged tissue.  Currently, stem cell therapy, in the form of hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) transplant (ie, bone marrow transplant), is used to treat a range of leukemias, lymphomas, and primary immunodeficiencies. ## Gene therapy Gene therapies fall into 2 categories: - **Clustered regularly-interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) gene editing** uses guided endonucleases to introduce targeted changes into the genome to correct harmful mutations or change gene expression (eg, in sickle cell disease). - **Vector gene therapy** uses a virus, typically adeno-associated virus **(AAV)**, to deliver a therapeutic gene (ie, transgene) into diseased cells.  It is used to restore certain **loss-of-function** disorders, in which a defective gene product lacks normal activity (eg, some forms of retinitis pigmentosa). ## Antisense RNA therapy Antisense RNA therapy uses synthetic oligonucleotides that bind specific mRNA transcripts to block translation, promote degradation, or modulate splicing.  It can be used for **gain-of-function** disorders, in which an overactive or aberrant gene product causes disease (eg, some *PCSK9* mutations in familial hypercholesterolemia). # Cell therapy ## Chimeric antigen receptor  therapy The immune system can be harnessed to kill malignant cells.  To accomplish this, an antigen receptor is engineered, consisting of a hybrid ("chimera") between ((Figure 1)): - An extracellular antigen recognition domain for an antigen overexpressed in a tumor; this domain is based on the antigen-binding region (Fab) of an antibody that recognizes this antigen. - An intracellular stimulatory T-cell signaling domain that promotes T-cell activation/proliferation and tumor-killing activity; this domain is based on the signaling subunits of the T-cell receptor and its costimulatory signals (CD3 and CD28). To produce these cells, some of the patient's circulating leukocytes are extracted via apheresis, expanded with growth factors, and genetically engineered to insert the CAR sequence (using retrovirus), before being reinfused into the patient.  Currently, the process takes 2-3 weeks from collection to infusion. **CAR T cells** (eg, tisagenlecleucel, axicabtagene ciloleucel) are the main example of this therapy.  Their receptor targets **CD19**, the universal B cell marker, inducing a potent T-cell–mediated cytotoxic response against B cells.  Therefore, CAR T-cell therapy is used mainly for the treatment of relapsed or **refractory B-cell lymphomas**, producing a cure rate approximating 50% even after multiple lines of chemotherapy have failed. Adverse effects include cytokine release syndrome (CRS), a systemic inflammatory response caused by the rapid activation of CAR T cells.  CRS manifests with flu-like symptoms that can sometimes progress to severe multisystem dysfunction such as neurotoxicity (eg, encephalopathy due to inflammatory disruption of the blood-brain barrier).  A chronic adverse effect is prolonged hypogammaglobulinemia, which is caused by continued depletion of normal B cells by CAR T cells, and may persist for many years. Beyond lymphoma, anti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy is nearing approval for autoimmune disorders, particularly systemic lupus erythematosus.  Beyond CD19, CAR-T is evolving to treat solid tumors (eg, anti–epidermal growth factor receptor T cells for breast cancer), nonmalignant conditions such as fibrosis (eg, antifibroblast T cells for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis), and infectious diseases (eg, anti-hepatitis B surface antigen T cells for chronic infection with hepatitis B virus).  In addition, CAR natural killer cells are being developed to leverage innate immune killing (eg, perforin, FasL death ligand pathway) of tumors that evade T cells through major histocompatibility complex downregulation (a common tactic used by many cancer types). ## Stem cell therapy Stem cell therapy involves the use of progenitor cells with the ability to differentiate into other cell types to repair or regenerate damaged tissues.  Stem cells are categorized by their developmental potential:  **Pluripotent** stem cells can differentiate into any cell type, whereas **multipotent** stem cells can differentiate into a restricted range of lineages. There are 5 major forms of stem cell therapy: - **HSCs** (approved) are multipotent bone marrow progenitors that can give rise to myeloid cells (eg, granulocytes, red blood cells, platelets) and lymphoid cells (eg, T and B cells) ((Figure 2)).  HSC transplantation is an established treatment option for many leukemias, lymphomas, and primary immunodeficiencies.  Patients first receive myeloablative chemotherapy, a regimen of highly cytotoxic medications that irreversibly kill existing hematopoietic stem cells (and also causes temporary, prfound immunosuppressiong during which the risk of infection, including reactivation of certain infections).  Once pancytopenia is established, patients then receive an infusion of donor HSCs, which engraft in the bone marrow, proliferate, and subsequently reconstitute peripheral blood cells.  With autologus transplanation, there is no risk of graft rejection (host cells attack graft \[ie, donor\] cells) or graft versus host disease (graft \[ie, donor\] cells attack host cells). - **Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs)** (mostly investigational) are nonhematopoietic, multipotent progenitor cells capable of differentiating into connective tissue cell types, including osteoblasts, chondrocytes, and adipocytes.  However, they are used primarily for their **paracrine secretory effect** (trophic support), rather than for regeneration of bone, cartilage, or fat.  MSCs secrete a variety of immunomodulatory cytokines that can reduce inflammation (eg, treatment of corticosteroid-refractory graft-versus-host disease).  MSCs also hold promise for treating tissue loss (eg, scarring after myocardial infarction). - **Tissue-specific stem cells** (investigational) are self-renewing multipotent progenitors found in organs that replenish mature cell types within that tissue.  For example, type 2 pneumocytes differentiate into alveolar epithelium to repopulate damaged areas.  Although they have a narrow differentiation capacity, they maintain their identity more stably and predictably.  Potential applications include retinal progenitor cells for macular degeneration. - **Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC)** (investigational) are cells created by resetting generic adult somatic cells (eg, skin fibroblasts) into an embryonic-like state using a cocktail of 4 transcription factors (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc).  This process erases the adult gene expression program and reverts the cells to pluripotency.  Research is ongoing for a wide range of conditions such as cardiomyopathies and retinal degeneration. - **Embryonic stem cells (ESCs)** (investigational, restricted) are pluripotent cells derived from the inner cell mass of blastocyst-stage embryos (days 5-7).  ESCs have largely been replaced by iPSCs, which bypass the ethical concerns surrounding the destruction of embryos.  However, ESCs may offer some advantages, including more consistent differentiation and high clonal efficiency. ## Other cell therapies Besides CAR therapy and stem cells, cell-based interventions include: - **Dendritic cell vaccines** "prime" (ie, load) autologous dendritic cells with tumor antigens ex vivo (to reinforce antigen presentation) and then reinfuse them into the patient (to activate a stronger T-cell response).  One such therapy (sipuleucel-T) is approved for the treatment of metastatic or castration-resistant prostate cancer. - **Tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL)** therapy involves extracting T cells from a **surgically resected** tumor or tumor fragment.  These infiltrating T cells recognize cancer antigens but are suppressed by the tumor microenvironment.  They are expanded and activated ex vivo before being infused back into the patient to mount a stronger immune response.  TIL therapy is approved for **advanced melanoma** (eg, lifileucel) and is being evaluated for cervical cancer and non–small cell lung cancer. - **Pancreatic islet cell transplantation** involves the infusion of deceased donor pancreatic islets into the portal vein of patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus, particularly with brittle hypoglycemia due to alpha-cell failure.  They then engraft in the liver and secrete insulin and glucagon.  The therapy is approved in some parts of the world.  Limitations include the need for immunosuppression (to prevent rejection) and loss of islet graft function over time. # Gene (DNA) therapy ## CRISPR gene editing Gene editing refers to the permanent correction of disease-causing mutations by modifying the genome directly.  CRISPR-Cas technology is based on the bacterial Cas endonuclease; this ancient "immune system" is used by many bacteria to excise foreign DNA introduced by viruses (bacteriophages).  The process removes defective DNA and replaces it with a new desired sequence, using 3 main components ((Figure 3)): - A guide RNA, designed to match the target DNA sequence to be excised. - The **Cas endonuclease**, typically Cas9, which introduces a double-stranded break at the target site. - A DNA repair template with the desired genetic sequence, which gets ligated across the break (by homology-directed repair). CRISPR can be performed ex vivo (cells edited outside of the patient and then reintroduced) or in vivo (components injected into the organ of interest). An ex vivo CRISPR-Cas therapy (exagamglogene autotemcel) is approved for the treatment of **sickle cell disease** and beta-thalassemia.  It edits HSCs to reactivate fetal hemoglobin (HbF), which is normally repressed after birth.  HbF does not sickle (unlike hemoglobin S, which predominates in sickle cell disease) and compensates for defective beta-globin (the cause of the chronic hemolytic anemia seen in beta-thalassemia).  The edited stem cells are reinfused to allow durable repopulation with HbF-producing erythrocytes.  This therapy has around a 90% cure rate (ie, no further vasoocclusive crises or need for transfusions).  However, to make room for the reinfused cells, bone marrow eradication with chemotherapy is required, which is associated with toxicity (eg, adverse events, cytopenias, infection).  Additional investigational uses of CRISPR-based therapies include transthyretin amyloidosis and Leber congenital amaurosis. Several in vivo CRISPR strategies, such as infusing the components into the portal vein to correct abnormal liver-synthesized proteins (eg, transthyretin amyloidosis), are being developed.  Limitations of in vivo CRISPR include **mosaic correction** (ie, edits some cells but not others, leading to a partial or variable response) and potential for off-target or random mutagenesis (eg, requires 15 years of monitoring for malignancies). ## Vector gene delivery Vector-based gene therapy delivers a functional gene copy into cells using viral vectors, typically with AAVs.  Different AAV serotypes target different tissues; once the virus infects a cell, its capsid is trafficked to the nucleus, and its engineered single-stranded DNA is converted by host enzymes into double-stranded DNA for transcription.  The functional "transgene" is typically designed with a highly active promoter sequence (enabling constant, long-lasting, and high levels of expression) and remains **episomal** (ie, in the nucleus but not integrated into native genome.  Alternate names include **gene augmentation** or gene replacement because the treatment restores deficient proteins. These therapies typically have the name "*\-gene*" (for the gene) and "*\-parvovec*" (for AAV vector, a parvovirus).  Therapies are approved to treat spinal muscle atrophy (onasemnogene abeparvovec), hemophilia B (etranacogene dezaparvovec), retinitis pigmentosa (eg, voretigene neparvovec), and other conditions.  AAV gene therapy is intended as a one-time treatment.  Protein expression remains stable for many years.  Episome retention is best in tissues with low mitotic turnover (eg, retinal epithelium). AAV vectors have limitations:  The size of the genes they can deliver is limited (eg, <4.7 kilobases), and immunogenicity (due to formation of anti-AAV neutralizing antibodies) can prevent the uptake of subsequent doses.  An adverse effect includes transient inflammation at the site of delivery.  Long-term, real-world safety data are encouraging, with no major complications occurring in approximately 1,500 patients treated over the last 15 years in the United States. Other nonviral vectors for gene delivery (eg, lipid nanoparticles) are being developed and have lower immunogenicity but also reduced transduction efficiency. # RNA antisense therapy RNA **antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs)** are short synthetic strands of nucleotides, typically 15-25 bases in length, designed to bind complementary sequences in pre-mRNA or mRNA.  They alter how mRNA or pre-mRNA is processed, affecting gene expression at the posttranscriptional level.  ASOs are broadly classified as inhibitory ASOs or splice-switching ASOs. ## Inhibitory ASOs Inhibitory ASOs reduce protein production by degrading the mRNA transcript before it can be translated. - **RNase-activating ASOs** recruit RNase H, an endogenous nuclease that cleaves the mRNA-ASO complex.  For example, mipomersen (withdrawn due to concerns over hepatotoxicity) was an ASO used to treat homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia by targeting ApoB-100 mRNA for degradation. - **Small interfering RNA (siRNA)**, although technically not an ASO, also cleaves complementary mRNA targets by activating the RNA interference machinery ((Figure 4)).  For example, patisiran is an siRNA that targets transthyretin mRNA to treat hereditary amyloidosis. ## Splice-switching ASOs Splice-switching ASOs result in alternative splicing of pre-mRNA, a posttranscriptional process in which exons of one transcribed gene can be variably included or excluded to create multiple mature mRNA transcripts of different lengths ((Figure 5)).  Splice-switching ASOs can be designed to: - Promote **inclusion of normal exons** that are abnormally skipped due to mutations in the splice regulatory site.  In spinal muscular atrophy, deletion of *SMN1* exon 7 causes a deficiency of SMN protein, which normally supports spliceosome function in motor neurons.  It does not affect *SMN2*, a nearly identical gene that normally excludes exon 7 during splicing and produces little functional SMN protein.  The ASO nusinersen promotes inclusion of exon 7 in *SMN2* pre-mRNA, thereby restoring the synthesis of full-length SMN protein. - Promote **exclusion of abnormal exons** that contain pathogenic mutations.  In Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), mutations in specific DMD exons disrupt the reading frame, leading to truncated, nonfunctional dystrophin.  The ASO eteplirsen promotes skipping of exon 51 in DMD pre-mRNA to maintain the reading frame and enable production of a partially functional dystrophin protein. # Summary Cell and gene therapies represent a rapidly advancing field that aims to correct or replace dysfunctional cells and genes to treat disease, often with a single dose. - Cell therapies mainly encompass chimeric antigen receptor T and stem cells.  Chimeric antigen receptor therapy involves engineering autologous T cells to express receptors against cancer antigens (eg, anti-CD19 T cells for relapsed B-cell lymphoma).  Stem cell therapies range from hematopoietic stem cell transplants (established treatment) to mesenchymal, tissue-specific, induced pluripotent stem cells for tissue regeneration (investigational treatments). - Gene therapies encompass clustered regularly-interspaced short palindromic repeats–Cas (CRISPR-Cas) gene editing and vector gene delivery.  CRISPR uses the Cas9 endonuclease and a guide RNA to permanently correct mutations in the genome.  Vector gene delivery uses adeno-associated viruses to insert functional genes into cells, restoring protein production in loss-of-function mutations. - Finally, antisense oligonucleotides affect the processing of mRNA or pre-mRNA, either by degrading harmful transcripts or correcting splicing errors. Many of these therapies have an excellent safety profile and transformative clinical benefits for patients in whom other treatment options have been exhausted. ​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​​​​​​​​‌​​​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌

articles.title: Bone Formation And Remodeling
articles.markdown: # Bone Formation And Remodeling # Introduction Bone remodeling is a dynamic process that maintains skeletal strength and contributes to mineral homeostasis.  It involves the resorption of old or damaged bone and the deposition and mineralization of new bone matrix.  Approximately 10% of the human skeletal structure undergoes remodeling annually.  In children, adolescents, and young adults, bone formation generally exceeds resorption;
